message.content: Donald Trump initially anticipated a career in show business, but in 1964 he enrolled at Fordham University to remain close to home in New York City. During his first year he took part in ROTC, wearing a military uniform each Wednesday, but he dropped the program in his second year. He left football after a few weeks and was a middling player in squash and tennis, though his Fordham peers introduced him to golf. In his junior year he transferred to the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, frequently commuting to his father’s office on weekends. He graduated in May 1968 with a Bachelor of Science in economics, though he was not among the top students and was not listed among Wharton honors recipients. By that time, he was eyeing a career in real estate. He was exempted from the Vietnam War draft due to bone spurs in his heels, and despite five years in military school, he had no interest in going to war.

During his second presidency, observers described a period with fewer guardrails against conflicts of interest and a departure from decades of ethical norms. He continued to own a publicly traded enterprise, the Trump Media & Technology Group, while expanding a portfolio into financial services. His overseas real estate activities included deals with entities linked to state interests. Concurrently, he engaged in branding and licensing arrangements to market Trump-branded merchandise and benefited from events hosted at his hotels and golf courses. He did not place his personal assets in a blind trust, unlike some predecessors. A disclosure published in August 2025 stated that since taking office he had made roughly 690 purchases of municipal bonds and corporate stock, totaling at least $104 million, including holdings in companies affected by shifts in federal policy.

Michael Jackson received the MTV Video Vanguard Award in 1988, and in 2001 the award was renamed the Michael Jackson Video Vanguard Award in his honor. The music video for "Black or White" premiered on November 14, 1991, in 27 countries and attracted an estimated audience of about 500 million, at the time the largest viewership for a music video; the clip featured Macaulay Culkin, Peggy Lipton, and George Wendt. It helped introduce morphing as a visual technique in music videos. The video also generated controversy for scenes in which Jackson rubs his crotch, vandalizes cars, and throws a garbage can through a storefront, prompting an apology from Jackson and the removal of the final scene.

Michael Jackson's philanthropic work included organizing and performing at benefit concerts to raise funds for charitable causes, and he donated concert tickets to groups supporting underprivileged children. He regularly visited ill children in hospitals around the world to offer encouragement, and he contributed personal and professional memorabilia to charity auctions to aid fundraising. His efforts earned him numerous philanthropic honors, including two presidential awards, and Guinness World Records recognized him for the breadth of his charitable activities.

Following the First World War, pacifist sentiment persisted in many European countries, yet irredentist and revanchist nationalism gained traction in several states, most notably Germany. The emergence of these attitudes was closely linked to the territorial, colonial, and financial losses imposed by the Treaty of Versailles. Germany relinquished roughly 13 percent of its prewar territory and forfeited all overseas possessions, while the treaty also prohibited German annexations of other states and imposed substantial reparations. In addition, it restricted the size and capability of the German armed forces. Together, these provisions fostered a climate of grievance and revisionism that helped shape the conditions leading to World War II.

The Second World War began to draw in the United States after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor and other Allied territories in December 1941, compelling the United States to wage war against Japan and, subsequently, Germany. Japanese forces expanded their control across coastal China and much of Southeast Asia, but their advance was halted at the Battle of Midway in June 1942. By early 1943, the Axis powers were turning back on multiple fronts, with decisive defeats in North Africa and at Stalingrad on the Eastern Front. That year also saw Allied successes in the Mediterranean; the invasion of Sicily and mainland Italy contributed to the collapse of Fascist Italy. Across theaters, Allied offensives steadily pushed the Axis back. In 1944, Western Allies opened a major front in Europe with the invasion of France at Normandy, while the Soviet Union reconquered pre-war territory, and the United States and its allies crippled Japan’s navy and seized key Pacific islands. In 1945, Allied forces liberated German-occupied areas and pushed into Germany from both east and west, culminating in the fall of Berlin and Germany’s surrender on May 8. Atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima on August 6 and Nagasaki on August 9, and Japan announced its surrender on August 15, with the formal signing of surrender on September 2.

The 1951 census, the first conducted after independence, recorded a population of 361 million. Since then, medical advances and the Green Revolution have coincided with rapid population growth over the past five decades. Life expectancy is approximately 70 years overall, with female life expectancy around 71.5 years and male life expectancy around 68.7 years. The country has about 93 physicians per 100,000 people.

India's Constitution, completed in 1950, established a secular, democratic republic. Beginning in the 1980s, economic liberalisation opened markets and encouraged modernization, while close collaboration with the Soviet Union provided access to technical knowledge. These developments contributed to the growth of a large urban middle class, positioned India as a rapidly expanding economy, and enhanced its geopolitical influence. The nation continues to grapple with multiple challenges, including persistent rural and urban poverty; religious and caste-related violence; Maoist-inspired Naxalite insurgencies; and separatist movements in Jammu and Kashmir and the Northeast. Territorial disputes with China and Pakistan remain unresolved. India has maintained sustained democratic freedoms among newer nations, but freedom from want for disadvantaged populations remains unachieved.

Trump Tower Manila, also referred to as Trump Tower at Century City, is a residential skyscraper located in Makati, part of Metro Manila in the Philippines. It sits within the Century City mixed-use complex in the Makati Poblacion district. The tower ranks as the third-tallest building in the Philippines and the second-tallest in the Makati skyline.

The showroom for Trump Tower Manila opened in early 2012, following unit reservations that began in September 2011. A groundbreaking ceremony was held in June 2012, with the project scheduled to open in November 2017. By November 2016, construction was nearly complete, and the development is valued at $150 million; upon completion, the tower would stand 57 stories tall.

During World War II, the Nazi regime designated certain forms of music as entartete Musik, or degenerate music, in a broader effort that paralleled the suppression of degenerate art. The designation was grounded in racial, ethnic, and political criteria, and it led to the exclusion and censorship of works associated with those categories. Works by Jewish composers or others deemed non-Aryan were banned, including the classical figures Gustav Mahler, Felix Mendelssohn, Arnold Schoenberg, George Gershwin, and Claude Debussy. In a related move, Irving Berlin’s popular songs were banned in their entirety due to his Jewish background, illustrating the regime’s extensive cultural suppression aligned with its ideological aims.

Music in World War II reflects the complex interplay of state policy, enforcement, and audience practice within Nazi Germany and its fascist ally, Italy. German music during the war is best understood through the regime’s official cultural policy, the degree to which it was enforced, and the diversity of other music that listeners engaged with beyond party restrictions. As the defeated power, German music and songs associated with Nazism did not achieve the same heroic status accorded to American and British popular music in postwar memory. Some observers contend that the music produced under the regime possessed a notable level of artistic quality that, in certain assessments, surpasses that of contemporary American and British popular music. Fascist Italian music of the period is viewed similarly to German music in this regard, reflecting comparable policy frameworks and debates about cultural value.

In September 2023, the British band Keane announced a 2024 tour spanning the United Kingdom, Europe, and America to commemorate the twentieth anniversary of their debut album Hopes and Fears. The excursion began in May 2024 and ran through December, with the May start overlapping the reissue of Hopes and Fears.

Keane signed a publishing deal with BMG in April 2002, though they had not yet secured a recording contract. In early 2002, Tim Rice-Oxley wrote "Everybody's Changing," which was developed into a demo by July, while a "Walnut Tree" demo was completed in May. The year proved difficult, with recording and live performances halted and internal doubts among the group, before they resumed live shows in December. A Betsey Trotwood gig in London drew Simon Williams of Fierce Panda Records, who offered to release the band's first commercial single, "Everybody's Changing." The track was named single of the week by Steve Lamacq on Lamacq Live on 14 April 2003, and its CD single appeared on 12 May 2003. The release, together with the band's growing live reputation, sparked a bidding war among major labels. Keane signed with Island Records in the summer of 2003. Island's A&R head Ferdy Unger-Hamilton was attracted by industry buzz and by hearing "Everybody's Changing" on the radio; after hearing five songs, he was impressed by each and by the band's live show. The decision to align with Island was influenced by a strong rapport with Unger-Hamilton and the belief that he would resist pressuring changes to the band's sound.

Celeste rose to prominence in 2019 after topping the BBC's Sound of... poll and winning the Brit Awards Rising Star award. In 2021, her debut studio album Not Your Muse was released and entered the UK Albums Chart at number one. That year also saw Brit Awards nominations for Album of the Year, Best Female Solo Artist, and Best New Artist, along with a Mercury Prize nomination. Additionally, she earned an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Hear My Voice" from The Trial of the Chicago 7 (2020).

Celeste released in October 2017 the promotional single Not For Me, a track addressing unrequited love and the singer’s growing estrangement from London, the city where she was raised. She had initially intended to include the song on her debut EP The Milk and the Honey, but the file was lost in the digital filing system; after rediscovering it several months later, she issued it as an independent single. In October 2017 she also began her third supporting tour of the United Kingdom and Europe with Skinny Living, and in late November 2017 she performed her final show supporting Roy Ayers at The Jazz Café in London.

Radio Times redacted several contact details—specifically addresses, telephone numbers, and email addresses—in order to prevent readers from donating to charity appeals that had already closed and to comply with legal requirements. In addition, certain names and trademark terms were removed from its content. These removals were undertaken for legal reasons and reflect a cautious editorial approach to avoid potential liability or misdirection of donations.

Radio Times and its television editions document the publication’s handling of television listings in the immediate postwar period; during the span from 7 June 1946 to 15 August 1952, the magazine occasionally carried a complete television listings section that extended to six pages, though the full six-page listing was not included in every issue.

Cristiano Ronaldo was reported in April 2017 to be under investigation by the Las Vegas Police Department in connection with a rape allegation dating from 2009. Documents, confirmed by Ronaldo's lawyers, indicated that he paid a $375,000 settlement to a woman under a non-disclosure agreement. Ronaldo and his representatives denied the accusations, portraying the situation as part of a deliberate defamation campaign and contending that substantial portions of the reporting had been altered or fabricated. Der Spiegel denied the claim that any parts of its report had been altered or fabricated.

Following the period in question, Ronaldo was linked with a move to Real Madrid, although Manchester United filed a tampering complaint with FIFA over Madrid's pursuit; FIFA declined to take action, and Ronaldo remained with United for another season. He later delivered a decisive 40-yard strike in the second leg against Porto, a goal that helped Manchester United advance and earned him the inaugural FIFA Puskás Award, an achievement he described as the best goal he had ever scored. United progressed to the final in Rome, where Ronaldo had little impact in the 2–0 defeat to Barcelona.

Cameron Jibril Thomaz, widely known by his stage name Wiz Khalifa, was born on September 8, 1987, in Minot, North Dakota, to parents who served in the United States Air Force. His parents divorced when he was about three years old, and he spent much of his youth as a military child, moving frequently due to his family's assignments. He lived in Germany, the United Kingdom, and Japan before relocating with his mother to Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, around 1996. In Pittsburgh, he attended Taylor Allderdice High School. Soon after the move, he began writing and performing his own lyrics prior to reaching adolescence.

Wiz Khalifa parted ways with Warner Bros. Records in July 2009 after delays in releasing his planned debut album for the label, First Flight. In an interview with the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette, he stated that his time with the label had taught him a great deal and helped him mature as an artist, expressing enthusiasm about moving forward with his own material and gaining greater control over his future projects. The split was publicly announced at a July 31, 2009 concert at the Amphitheatre at Station Square in Pittsburgh, where he performed alongside acts such as Girl Talk, Modey Lemon, Donora, Grand Buffet, and Don Caballero.

Elon Musk has received numerous prestigious honors in recognition of his contributions to aerospace and engineering. In 2008, he was awarded the George Low Transportation Award by the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics for his work on the Falcon rockets. In 2010, he received the Fédération Aéronautique Internationale Gold Space Medal. In 2012, the Royal Aeronautical Society awarded him its Gold Medal. In 2015, Yale University conferred an Honorary Doctorate in Engineering and Technology, and the IEEE granted him Honorary Membership. In 2018, he was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society (FRS). In 2022, he was elected to the National Academy of Engineering.

Ashley St. Clair claimed on the social media platform X that she had given birth to Musk's son Romulus five months earlier, with various media outlets reporting the child as Musk's thirteenth, though the claim remained unverified. On February 22, 2025, St. Clair filed for sole custody of the child and for Musk to be recognized as the father. On March 31, 2025, Musk stated he was unsure whether he was the father but acknowledged payments totaling $2.5 million to St. Clair and said he would continue paying $500,000 per year. The Wall Street Journal subsequently reported that $1 million of these payments was structured as a loan.

Skycity (Mandaluyong) refers to a development project in Mandaluyong, Philippines. In 2010, the Second Division of the Supreme Court rejected the challenges brought by the GEA, and the court deferred to the Housing and Land Use Regulatory Board (HLURB) for its regulatory expertise on the matter. Following the decision, the developer, EGI, stated that construction could resume.

Skycity in Mandaluyong is a development project located in Mandaluyong, Philippines. As of 2020, the excavation area linked to the project had come to be described colloquially as the "big hole." The site was overgrown with moss, and there were no visible signs of construction resumption.

CITIC Plaza is a high-rise complex located in Guangzhou’s Tianhe District. It forms part of the CITIC Plaza development, which also includes two 38-storey residential towers. The complex is situated near a new railway station that serves the Guangzhou–Shenzhen and Guangzhou–Hong Kong routes, and is adjacent to a new metro station as well as the Tianhe Sports Center, a venue that hosted events during the 6th National Games and portions of the 2010 Asian Games. It lies on the same axis as the East and West Towers in Zhujiang New City and the Pearl Observation Tower, and is surrounded by a cluster of other tall buildings. Collectively, these features reflect Guangzhou’s growing wealth and its expanding role as a major urban and economic center.

All Nippon Airways' Guangzhou office was formerly located in unit 2605 of CITIC Plaza until May 2, 2011; beginning on May 3, 2011, it relocated to Tower A of Victory Plaza, where it has since been housed.

In preparation for UEFA Euro 2024, UEFA announced the appointment of 20 video match officials to assist in officiating matches, and separately confirmed a group of 12 support match officials. The latter group is designated to serve as the fourth official or as reserve assistant referees during games, providing additional officiating coverage as needed.

UEFA Euro 2024 featured several notable absences, including Sweden, Russia, and Wales. Sweden failed to reach the finals for the first time since Euro 1996, and also missed the 2022 World Cup, marking their second consecutive major tournament absence. Russia were barred from the qualifiers as a consequence of the invasion of Ukraine. Wales, who had progressed to the knockout stages in the two preceding editions, including a 2016 semi-final, were eliminated after a penalty shootout defeat by Poland in the play-offs. North Macedonia and Finland, who had made their debuts at Euro 2020, failed to qualify for Euro 2024.

The Guild of Music Supervisors Award for Best Song Written and/or Recording Created for a Film is a category within the Guild of Music Supervisors Awards that recognizes songs written and/or recorded specifically for feature films. It is presented annually as part of the awards program, honoring music that was created directly for cinematic releases. The category was introduced at the Guild's sixth annual awards ceremony and has been awarded each year since its inception.

The 2023–24 Czech Cup marks the 31st edition of the Czech Republic's annual knockout football cup competition. Due to sponsorship arrangements, the tournament is widely referred to as the MOL Cup. The competition's champions earn a berth in the third qualifying round of the 2024–25 UEFA Europa League.

On 14 August, the draw for the second round of the 2023–24 Czech Cup was held. A total of 27 matches were planned for this stage, involving 54 teams overall: 43 qualifiers from the preceding round and 11 new entrants.

During the early years of World War II, Sobhuza II was the king of Eswatini. He brokered an agreement with the British government whereby Swaziland would contribute volunteers to the Allied war effort in exchange for the prospect of greater autonomy in the future. A few thousand Swazi men volunteered to fight for the Allies, enlisting in the African Auxiliary Pioneer Corps. The corps served in Egypt and Libya as part of the Western Desert campaign in North Africa, and later participated in the Allied invasion of Italy. A notable Swazi veteran was Mnikwa Dlamini, who would later become the Chief of Hhelehhele.

During World War II, Eswatini—then known as Swaziland—remained a British protectorate and supported the Allies in their fight against the Axis Powers. Although no large-scale battles or major military operations occurred in or near the territory, Swaziland contributed troops to the Allied war effort. The war era also brought several notable domestic developments to Eswatini, reflecting changes within its administration and society under wartime conditions.

Elizabeth II's Platinum Jubilee celebrations began on 6 February 2022, marking seventy years since her accession to the throne. In her accession day message, she renewed her commitment to a lifetime of public service, a pledge she originally articulated in 1947.

Elizabeth II's eldest son, Prince Charles, was born in November 1948. About a month earlier, the king issued letters patent permitting Elizabeth's children to bear the style and title of a royal prince or princess, since their father was no longer a royal prince. The couple's second child, Princess Anne, was born in August 1950.

Megan Twohey was born in Washington, D.C., and was raised in Evanston, Illinois. Her mother, Mary Jane Twohey, was a television news producer, while her father, John Twohey, served as an editor for the Chicago Tribune.

Megan Twohey, whose surname is pronounced "TOO-ee," is an American journalist and an investigative reporter for The New York Times. She has previously reported for Reuters, the Chicago Tribune, and the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel.

What Was I Made For? is a song by American singer Billie Eilish, released on July 13, 2023, as part of the soundtrack for the 2023 film Barbie. Eilish announced the track on July 6, 2023 through social media, describing the song as meaning the world to her and expressing the hope that it would change lives, while urging fans to prepare to sob. A short snippet was shown in a trailer for the film on July 10, 2023. She continued to tease the single and its music video on Twitter on July 12, 2023. In the film, the song accompanies a scene in which Barbie meets the spirit of her creator, Ruth Handler.

The music video for What Was I Made For? was released on July 13, 2023, alongside the single, and was directed by Billie Eilish herself, with the footage filmed in a single continuous take. Eilish appears in a yellow dress paired with a blonde wig, bangs, and a high ponytail reminiscent of a 1959 Barbie, set at a lone school desk inside an empty monochromatic space. A Barbie-themed case containing miniature doll clothing that mirrors outfits Eilish has worn publicly serves as the central prop. In the sequence, she removes and examines the doll garments, organizing them on a miniature hanging rack while facing interruptions from a brief earthquake, strong wind, and rain that threaten progress. After the rain subsides, she stuffs the clothes back into the case and leaves with the case in hand, and she briefly returns after the song’s ending to collect a forgotten accessory before exiting again.

Longkou West Station is a Guangzhou Metro station on Line 11. The station commenced operations on 28 December 2024. It is located underground at the intersection of Longkou Road West and Zhongyue Road in Tianhe District, Guangzhou. The station is referred to by its Chinese names as Simplified Chinese 龙口西站 and Traditional Chinese 龍口西站, with the pinyin transcription Lóngkǒuxī Zhàn and the Cantonese Yale transcription Lǔngháusāi Jaahm.

Longkou West station is a station on Line 11 that underwent several name changes during its development: during the planning stage it was designated Longkou East, and during construction it was renamed Tianhe East. In June 2023, it was announced as part of Line 11’s initial naming plan that the station would be called Longkou West, and in May 2024 the name Longkou West was officially approved. On 20 September 2024, the station completed the three-rights transfer.

Vox Media, Inc. is an American mass media company founded in November 2011 in Washington, D.C., by Jim Bankoff and Trei Brundrett. It is headquartered in Lower Manhattan, New York City. The company was created to oversee SB Nation, a sports blog network established in 2003 by Tyler Bleszinski, Markos Moulitsas, and Jerome Armstrong, and The Verge, a technology news website that launched concurrently with Vox Media. Bankoff had served as chief executive of SB Nation since 2009 prior to Vox Media's founding.

In February 2018, Vox Media laid off approximately 50 employees, predominantly from its video production teams, a reduction that comprised about 5% of its workforce. The move followed CEO Jim Bankoff’s prior indication that Vox planned to exit native video on Facebook due to inconsistent monetization and limited promotional reach. An internal layoff memo stated that, despite its success, native video would not constitute a viable driver of audience growth or revenue compared with other investments. As a result, Vox redirected its strategy to place greater emphasis on podcasting and Vox Entertainment.

By June 2012, the United States Navy had four minesweepers deployed to the Persian Gulf in response to regional instabilities. The Royal Navy maintains four minesweepers stationed in the Persian Gulf as part of the 9th Mine Counter-Measures Squadron.

During World War II, significant advances in minesweeping emerged as nations reoriented and repurposed vessels for mine clearance duties. Several states adapted ships for minesweeping, with Australia converting 35 civilian vessels into auxiliary minesweepers to bolster coastal and convoy protection. Both the Allied and Axis powers relied heavily on minesweeping operations throughout the conflict, reflecting the central role of naval mines in wartime strategy. In the Kriegsmarine, minesweepers formed a substantial portion of overall strength and are regarded as an essential, though often overlooked, component of German maritime power. The threat posed by naval mines did not end with hostilities, as minesweeping crews remained active after VJ Day to clear contested waters and safeguard postwar navigation.

Set during the Second Sino-Japanese War, the Battle of South Shanxi unfolded amid deteriorating Kuomintang–Communist relations after the New Fourth Army incident in early 1941. In the surrounding area, the Eighth Route Army declined to come to the aid of the encircled Nationalist forces, effectively leaving them to fight without Communist support. The engagement concluded in a heavy Nationalist defeat, an outcome that is remembered in China as one of the war's worst defeats.

The Battle of South Shanxi featured the leadership of Major General Wang Jun (王竣), who commanded the newly formed 27th Division of the 80th Corps as part of the operation. Wang Jun led the division during the engagement, and he was subsequently posthumously promoted to lieutenant general.

China International Center is a 62-storey skyscraper in Guangzhou, China, rising to a height of 270 metres (890 feet and completed in 2007. The building’s name is rendered in Simplified Chinese as 中华国际中心 and in Traditional Chinese as 中華國際中心, with the pinyin transcription Zhōnghuá Guójì Zhōngxīn.

Discovery Primea is a 68-storey mixed-use residential tower located along Ayala Avenue in Makati, and is among the tallest buildings in the Philippines. It was erected on the site of the former Gilarmi Apartments, which were co-owned by Armi Kuusela, the first Miss Universe, and her ex-husband Virgilio Hilario. As one of the early urban residential condominiums in the Makati Central Business District, the project was developed by JTKC, Inc., a pioneer among residential condo developers in the Philippines. JTKC, Inc. also owns Discovery Suites, a serviced apartment complex in Ortigas Center, Mandaluyong. The residential tower opened in February 2015.

In 2013, the top floor of the Discovery Primea Tower reached its final height, signaling the completion of the tower’s construction. As a result, the building stood among the tallest structures in the Philippines.

Miss Universe 1952 saw a series of withdrawals before the competition took place. Elisabeth van Proosdij, representing the Netherlands, withdrew after it emerged she was married during her reign, despite the pageant permitting married contestants. Leila Teresa Tuma, representing Syria, also withdrew due to political tensions in the country. In addition, Brazil and the Republic of China were invited but chose to withdraw because their national pageants were not sufficiently prepared to select representatives.

Miss Universe 1952 was set to be staged in Long Beach, California, after the city pledged $30,000 to host the competition. The pageant was scheduled for June 23–30, 1952. Executive producer Oliver Reinhardt secured sponsorship arrangements with Pan American World Airways and Catalina Swimwear, while Yolande Betbeze, Miss America 1951, refused to pose in a Catalina Swimwear swimsuit for publicity.

Operation Musketeer I, II, and III, conducted from 1944 to 1945, were a series of World War II operations carried out by United States and Filipino forces with the objective of defeating and expelling the Imperial Japanese forces occupying the Philippines.

In 1944, the German operation Margarethe led to the occupation of Hungary during World War II. Döme Sztójay, a pro-Nazi figure, was subsequently appointed Hungary’s prime minister, with his installation aided by a German military governor who operated within the occupation authorities.

The Porter-class destroyers comprised eight large ships of about 1,850 tons standard displacement in the United States Navy. Construction was authorized by Congress on 26 April 1916, but funding was delayed. The design conformed to the London Naval Treaty’s 1,850-ton limit, which allowed thirteen ships of this size, with a later Somers class built to satisfy the limit. The first four vessels were laid down in 1933 by New York Shipbuilding in Camden, New Jersey, and the remaining four in 1934 by Bethlehem Steel in Quincy, Massachusetts. All boats were commissioned in 1936 except Winslow, which entered service in 1937. The class was developed in response to Japan’s large Fubuki-class destroyers and was initially designated to serve as flotilla leaders. During World War II, Porter-class ships saw extensive service across the Pacific, the Atlantic, and the Americas. Porter was the sole loss of the class, sunk at the Battle of the Santa Cruz Islands on 26 October 1942.

Porter-class destroyers consisted of seven vessels: Porter, McDougal, Winslow, Moffett, Selfridge, Phelps, and Balch. In August 1941, three of them—McDougal, Winslow, and Moffett—took part in the escort group that supported the Atlantic Charter conference at Placentia Bay alongside five destroyers and two cruisers. Selfridge and Phelps were in port during the attack on Pearl Harbor and engaged incoming aircraft. The class operated in both major theaters of World War II, seeing action in the Battle of the Atlantic and the Pacific War while also escorting convoys in the Americas. Phelps fought at the Coral Sea and Midway, where she scuttled the disabled aircraft carrier Lexington and helped rescue its crew. Balch assisted in Midway by rescuing Yorktown survivors. Moffett contributed to the destruction of two U-boats, U-128 and U-604, while stationed near Trinidad in the Caribbean. Other ships of the class also took part in the Guadalcanal invasion and the Marianas campaign. By September 1944, the class had become concentrated in the Atlantic theater. Porter suffered the class’s sole loss, at the Battle of the Santa Cruz Islands on 26 October 1942. Selfridge lost her bow to a torpedo at the Naval Battle of Vella Lavella on 6 October 1943, but was subsequently repaired. In September 1945 McDougal and Winslow were redesignated AG-126 and AG-127 and modified for anti-kamikaze research, in a configuration akin to Gearing-class radar-picket destroyers. With the end of the war, all ships except Winslow were scrapped; Winslow, used as a training vessel, remained in service until 1950 and was scrapped in 1959, making it the most enduring destroyer commissioned in the 1930s and the last of the class to be scrapped.

The Continuation War was a conflict between Finland and the Soviet Union that ran from 1941 to 1944, in alignment with Germany’s campaign against the Soviet Union. On June 25, 1941, a Soviet air raid on Finnish cities prompted Finland to declare war and to permit German troops to operate within Finnish territory. By September 1941 Finland had regained post‑Winter War concessions in Karelia. The Finnish Army advanced beyond the 1939 border into East Karelia, reaching about 30–32 kilometers from the center of Leningrad and taking part in the siege by cutting northern supply routes and holding positions until 1944. In Lapland, German–Finnish forces failed to capture Murmansk or to sever the Kirov Railway. In 1944, the Soviet Vyborg–Petrozavodsk offensive in June and August drove Finns from much of the territories they had gained, but the Finnish Army halted the offensive in August 1944.

During the Continuation War, Finland held a substantial number of Soviet prisoners of war, with estimates placing the total at around 64,000 and about 56,000 captured in 1941. A subset of these, between 2,600 and 2,800, were transferred to Germany in exchange for roughly 2,200 Finnish POWs. In Finnish captivity, at least 18,318 Soviet POWs died. Mortality was highest in the largest camps, approaching 41 percent, while smaller camps recorded rates of under 5 percent. Approximately 85 percent of deaths occurred between November 1941 and September 1942, and peak monthly fatalities reached 2,665 in February 1942, with 92 deaths in February 1943. Scholars such as Oula Silvennoinen attribute the deaths to overcrowding, inadequate preparation, insufficient warm clothing, and limited food—often diverted by camp staff—and to disease. Antti Kujala states that around 1,200 prisoners were shot, most of them illegally.

From 2013 through 2015, Barack Obama articulated a nuanced stance on Israel and its security, balancing advocacy for regional stability with support for Israel’s right to defend itself. In 2013, journalist Jeffrey Goldberg reported that Obama believed each new settlement announcement pushed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government toward broad international isolation. In 2014, he drew a parallel between the Zionist movement and the U.S. civil rights movement, arguing that both pursue justice and equal rights for historically persecuted peoples, and he reiterated that being pro-Israel and pro-Jewish was part of the political values he had long fought for. During the 2014 Israel–Gaza conflict, Obama affirmed Israel’s right to defend itself. The following year, he faced sharp criticism from Israel after advocating for and signing the Iran nuclear deal. Netanyahu opposed the agreement, urging the U.S. Congress to reject it and labeling it dangerous and bad.

During his presidency, Barack Obama authorized a 2011 drone strike in Yemen aimed at Anwar al-Awlaki, an American imam believed to have been a senior figure within Al-Qaeda. Al-Awlaki thus became the first U.S. citizen to be targeted and killed by a U.S. drone strike. The Department of Justice released a memo asserting that the operation was a lawful act of war under the authorization for use of military force, a stance that civil liberties advocates characterized as a violation of due process and that provoked substantial controversy. In the aftermath, al-Awlaki's teenage son and younger daughter, both American citizens, were killed in separate U.S. military actions, though not targeted directly.

In October 2017, investigations by the New York Police Department, the Metropolitan Police Service, and the Los Angeles Police Department were reviewing allegations against Harvey Weinstein. In London, the investigative operation known as Operation Kaguyak reportedly examined fifteen alleged sexual assaults attributed to Weinstein dating from the 1990s. Separately, the United Kingdom's Crown Prosecution Service authorised charging Weinstein in connection with alleged indecent assaults said to have occurred in 1996.

In October 2017, investigations by The New York Times and The New Yorker reported that dozens of women had accused Harvey Weinstein of rape, sexual assault, and sexual abuse spanning at least three decades, with the number of accusers in the film industry later rising to more than eighty. Weinstein denied that he had engaged in any non-consensual sex. In the wake of the revelations, he was dismissed from The Weinstein Company and subsequently expelled from the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, along with several other professional associations. He then withdrew from public life.

The Western Hubei Operation was a military engagement of the Second Sino-Japanese War between the National Revolutionary Army and the Imperial Japanese Army. The 13th Division contributed three infantry regiments, one cavalry regiment, and one artillery regiment to the operation. Elements of this division crossed to the south bank of the Yangtze River near Ichang to attack Chinese positions in the area.

On February 11, 1993, The New York Times published a report by Carol Lawson detailing Mattel’s plan to render Ken more gender-fluid in order to appeal to both boys and girls following his Toy Fair debut. Some observers viewed a connection to Barbie’s 1992 voice-box line as a subtle acknowledgment of Ken’s departure from strict gender norms. The same year, Mattel and other toy makers experimented with cross-selling strategies, marketing products across traditional gender boundaries. Mattel executive Lisa McKendall described the shift as requiring updated appearances, noting an increased presence of earrings on male dolls and stressing that Ken would need ongoing updates to stay current. The gender-bending article about Ken was syndicated across North American newspapers, including the Seattle Post-Intelligencer, the Vancouver Sun, and the Philadelphia Daily News.

Earring Magic Ken is a Ken doll model released by Mattel in 1993 as part of the Earring Magic Barbie line. It served as a companion to the Earring Magic Barbie figure and was one of five dolls produced in the series. The doll has also been referred to by the nicknames Gay Ken and Fey Ken in various sources.

Psychodrama features Fraser T. Smith as co-executive producer, a longtime collaborator who has known Dave since he was seventeen. While Smith was working on Stormzy's Gang Signs and Prayer, Dave's managers, Jack Foster and Benny Scarrs, introduced him to the artist; they connected immediately, and a studio session followed. During that session, they wrote the track "Picture Me." That early collaboration established a productive working relationship, and Smith later contributed to Dave's first and second EPs, 6 Paths and Game Over, in addition to his role on Psychodrama.

Psychodrama is a concept album by British rapper Dave that unfolds through a three-act structure, with Act I centered on environment, Act II on relationships, and Act III on a social compass. According to Smith, Dave spent a long period developing the title and concept, and the project was intended to be highly ambitious. The overarching theme chronicles Dave's life up to the present, detailing his upbringing and experiences growing up as a young Black man in South London, as well as his struggles, joys, uncertainty, ambitions, hopes, and fears. Mental health is a central thread, with a particular emphasis on depression. The album opens with Dave speaking to a therapist, a motif that recurs throughout the work.

The Dubai project known as the Trump International Hotel and Tower, developed by Nakheel, was officially cancelled in February 2011. The site later hosted Al Ittihad Park, which opened in November 2012. In 2025, plans were renewed to revive the development.

Trump International Hotel and Tower (Dubai) is a proposed tower designed by HHCP Architecture, with construction planned to begin by the end of the next year. The design blends traditional Arab and Islamic design philosophies with a contemporary sensibility, producing an architectural form that is both striking and inspirational. The concept pays homage to the forward-looking spirit of the “new” Dubai, and the project is positioned to embody the Trump brand's stylistic approach in the region.

Seal served as one of the four vocal coaches on The Voice Australia during its first season in 2012, mentoring Karise Eden, who won the competition. He returned for the second season, which began on 7 April 2013, and again acted as the winning coach, guiding Harrison Craig to victory. He did not participate in the third season in 2014, with the Nine Network stating that he would take a break to focus on music and a new album. On 8 November 2016, Nine announced that Seal would return as a coach for the 2017 season, joining Delta Goodrem and replacing Jessie J after a three-year hiatus.

Seal's early critical reception was positive, and his singles—particularly "Crazy," "Future Love Paradise," and his cover of "Killer"—performed well on the charts. "Crazy" became an international hit in 1991, peaking at number two in the United Kingdom and reaching number seven on the U.S. Billboard Hot 100. At the 1992 Brit Awards in London’s Hammersmith Odeon, he achieved the first hat-trick of wins in a single ceremony, securing Best British Male, Best British Video for "Killer," and Best British Album for the self-titled album Seal.

Guangzhou's print media are dominated by three Chinese-language groups: Guangzhou Daily Press Group, Nanfang Press Corporation, and Yangcheng Evening News Group. The city is home to two leading newspapers, Guangzhou Daily and Southern Metropolis Daily; Guangzhou Daily circulates about 1.8 million copies and has been the most successful Chinese newspaper in terms of advertising revenue for fourteen years, while Southern Metropolis Daily is regarded as one of the most liberal publications on the mainland. In addition to Chinese-language outlets, Guangzhou publishes a small number of English-language magazines and newspapers, the most prominent of which is That's Guangzhou. Launched more than a decade ago, That's Guangzhou has expanded into That's PRD, a branch that publishes expatriate magazines in Beijing and Shanghai, and it also produces In the Red.

Guangzhou is the contemporary name of the city, which was previously known as Panyu (Punyü; 番禺). The Panyu toponym remains in use for a Guangzhou district near the city center. The origin of the name Panyu is uncertain, with eleven proposed explanations, including a possible allusion to two local mountains. The city has also been referred to as Guangzhou Fu or Guangfu in acknowledgment of its status as the capital of a prefecture. In medieval Persian sources, Guangzhou Fu was called Khanfu (خانفو) by Al-Masudi and Ibn Khordadbeh. Under the Southern Han, the metropolis was renamed Xingwang Fu (興王府).

Red Hot + Dance elicited a mixed reception among major publications. Entertainment Weekly praised the project for its charitable aims and artistic scope, describing it as a concise excursion through contemporary dance beats that fulfills its purpose. The Los Angeles Times highlighted three new Michael tracks, ranking “Too Funky” among his best and suggesting he focus on dance-oriented material. The Toronto Star’s Peter Howell found “Supernatural” unremarkable and alluded to Madonna’s “Like a Prayer,” while the remix of “Unbelievable” was noted as highly danceable but at the expense of the group’s vocals, evoking a 1990s Saturday Night Fever vibe. The Washington Post offered a broader appraisal of the lineup, noting George Michael’s three contributions including “Too Funky” while arguing they do not fully live up to their reputation; it also observed that “Supernatural” contains interesting lyrics but rests on a fatigued “Pull Up to the Bumper” beat, praised Knuckles’s “Change” remix for its spare elegance, and highlighted Young Disciples’ “Stevie Wonder-ful” and Sabrina Johnston’s “Peace” as notable tracks, with Brian Eno’s ambient-house treatment of “Unbelievable” expanding sonic textures without sacrificing danceability. Deseret News critic Ray Boren suggested renaming the EMF remix “Unrecognizable” and viewed it as more party-ready than its predecessor.

Red Hot + Dance is a 1992 compilation album produced by the Red Hot Organization, a charity collective dedicated to raising funds and awareness in the fight against HIV/AIDS. Released on July 6, 1992, the album features a substantial contribution from George Michael, who provided three newly recorded tracks. These songs were originally intended for a follow-up to Listen Without Prejudice Vol. 1 but were donated to the Red Hot + Dance project, and they are exclusive to the compilation. Additionally, the track "Too Funky" was issued separately as a charity single, with a music video featuring several supermodels, and is not exclusive to the album.

Tel Aviv is a central transportation hub in Israel, supported by an extensive public transit system. The city lies along a substantial portion of the national transportation network’s principal routes, making it a critical link in regional mobility. In 2023, 56% of residents commuted to work without using a car, reflecting a high rate of non-auto travel. A plan exists to raise non-car commuting to about 70% by the end of the decade, aiming to further reduce car dependency and enhance urban mobility.

Tel Aviv is regarded as a major international nightlife hub, featuring a wide range of bars, dance venues, and nightclubs that operate well past midnight. The Tel Aviv port constitutes the city’s largest area for nightlife, attracting sizable crowds of young clubbers from Tel Aviv and neighboring municipalities. In the southern part of the city, Haoman 17 anchors a center of alternative clubbing, complemented by underground venues such as Block Club, Comfort 13, Paradise Garage, and a variety of warehouse- and loft-style party spaces. The Allenby/Rothschild corridor also serves as a busy nightlife district, hosting clubs including Pasaz, Radio EPGB, and the Penguin. In 2013, Absolut Vodka released a bottle specially designed for Tel Aviv as part of its international cities series.

In the 1st century, evidence for the romanization of Hebrew appears in Juvenal's Satire 14:96, where several Hebraic terms occur in forms that seem derived from Greek. The words sabbata, Iudaicum, and Moyses are attested, and they appear to be adaptations from Greek rather than direct Latin coinages. This passage thus reflects the early mediation of Hebrew terms into Latin through Hellenic intermediaries, illustrating a facet of the broader process of linguistic contact in the Roman world.

Romanization of Hebrew involves rendering Hebrew terms in the Latin alphabet, enabling readers who are not proficient in the Hebrew script to understand Hebrew terminology or text. In diaspora Jewish prayer books, supplementary romanization is provided for some or all of the Hebrew-language congregational prayers.

During World War II, Dwight D. Eisenhower was elevated to General of the Army on December 20, 1944, joining a small cadre that achieved the five-star rank during the conflict. He and George Marshall, Henry H. “Hap” Arnold, and Douglas MacArthur were the four officers to reach that grade in the war, and together with Omar Bradley they are the only five men to have held the five-star designation since the death of Philip Sheridan in 1888. The five-star rank was created by a temporary act of Congress (Public Law 78-482) dated December 14, 1944, with the understanding that it would lapse six months after hostilities ended; it was made permanent on March 23, 1946 (Public Law 333, 79th Congress), which also provided full pay and allowances in the grade to those on the retired list. The creation of the rank was intended to provide parity with British field marshals and admirals of the fleet.

During December 1944, in the Battle of the Bulge, Allied forces initially faced fierce resistance but were ultimately repelled in early 1945 after Eisenhower reorganized the Allied forces and improved weather enabled intensified air operations. As German defenses weakened on both the Eastern Front and the Western Front, the strategic situation swung in favor of the Allies. Although the British sought to seize Berlin, Eisenhower declined to launch an assault on the city without explicit orders, preferring to proceed within the bounds of authorized operations. Subsequently, London pressed for advances into Czechoslovakia for political reasons, but Washington refused to back Churchill's plan to use Eisenhower for political maneuvering against Moscow. The division of Germany proceeded along the lines previously agreed by Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin. In the final phase, the Soviet Red Army captured Berlin after a costly battle, and Germany surrendered on May 7, 1945.

The article, titled "List of Miss Universe runners-up and finalists," presents a comprehensive record of Miss Universe titleholders as well as those who finished as runners-up, finalists, and semifinalists. Spanning from the pageant's inaugural edition in 1952 to the present, the list documents the outcomes of contestants across the years and serves as a reference for placements and progression within the competition.

Across its history, the Miss Universe pageant has varied how the runner-up ranks are determined. In the editions of 1952–1989, 2001–2014, 2020, and 2024, the crown and the first through fourth runners-up were chosen from the field of five finalists. In contrast, during 1990–1997 and in 2016 the competition expanded to a top-six final round, yet the title and the first two runners-up were declared only from the top three finalists. In the periods 1998–2000, 2015, 2017–2019, and 2021–2023, the finalists were limited to the top five, with only the Miss Universe champion and the first two runners-up determined among the top three. Consequently, several editions did not feature an official third and fourth runner-up, because those positions would correspond to the top-five or top-six finishers.

Jules Verne was a submarine tender of the French Navy during the 1930s, providing logistical support to the submarine service. After France’s capitulation, the vessel served under the Free French Naval Forces during World War II, continuing to operate in support of Allied naval efforts throughout the conflict.

During World War II, the Kriegsmarine found it impractical to operate a large fleet of conventional surface tenders to sustain its submarine forces. To address this limitation, Type XIV submarines were developed and used as at-sea replenishment vessels, supplying fuel, torpedoes, and provisions to other U-boats while underway. This support role earned the submarines the informal nickname "milk cows" among naval personnel.

Scout cruiser was a class of early 20th‑century warships designed for fleet reconnaissance and flotilla leadership. They occupied an intermediate size and armament niche, being smaller, faster, and more lightly protected than protected or light cruisers, yet larger than contemporary destroyers. The ships were intended to perform scouting duties for the fleet and to act as flotilla leaders. Armament typically consisted of six to ten destroyer‑type guns, with calibres ranging from 76 mm (3 in) to 120 mm (4.7 in), and they carried two to four torpedo tubes.

The first three ships of the Omaha class were initially ordered as scout cruisers (CS). In 1920, prior to their launch, the United States Navy revised its cruiser classification system. As a consequence, these vessels, together with the Chesters, were redesignated as light cruisers (CL).

The first BRIT Awards ceremony was held in 1977 and carried a ceremonial name that referenced the British recording industry and Britannia. It was organized to commemorate Queen Elizabeth II’s Silver Jubilee and was televised by Thames Television. An annual ceremony has been held since 1982.

The BRIT Awards were broadcast live through the late 1980s, with the 1989 ceremony—hosted by Samantha Fox and Mick Fleetwood—receiving widespread criticism for deviations from the planned rehearsal. From 1990 to 2006 the event was recorded and broadcast the following night instead of live. In 2007 the ceremony returned to a live ITV broadcast, held on 14 February and hosted by Russell Brand, and that year also saw three awards removed: British Rock Act, British Urban Act, and British Pop Act. The last ceremony at Earls Court in London took place on 16 February 2010, and the awards moved to the O2 Arena in London for the first time in 2011.

During 2020, Yunan County recorded a total population of 532,679, comprising 282,705 males and 249,974 females. The sex ratio stood at 113.09 males per 100 females, reflecting a higher number of male residents relative to female residents.

In 2020, Yunan County recorded 5,936 births, corresponding to a birth rate of 11.14 per 1,000 population, and 4,067 deaths, for a death rate of 7.63 per 1,000. The resulting natural increase amounted to 1,869 people, equating to a growth rate of 3.51 per 1,000.

Henry VI, born during the Hundred Years' War (1337–1453), remains the only English monarch to have been crowned King of France, receiving the coronation at Notre-Dame de Paris in 1431 under the regnal name Henry II. His early years on the throne were governed by a regency, a period that marked the peak of English power in France. When he took full control in 1437, the balance of fortunes shifted, leading to a series of military setbacks in France together with serious political and financial crises at home. Within his government, divisions among the nobility broadened, contributing to a destabilization of governance. Ultimately, his reign saw the near total erosion of English possessions in France.

Historically, a poem has been attributed to Henry VI, reportedly written during his imprisonment. However, a largely identical verse appears in William Baldwin's 1559 The Mirror for Magistrates, a collection of poems written from the perspectives of historical figures. The presence of this similar line in a later work, which adopts the voices of past figures, has led scholars to question the Henry VI attribution, with many considering it contested or unsupported.

The Battle of Manila (1945) caused extensive damage to the Philippine capital's cultural and historical patrimony, a loss widely remembered as a national tragedy. Hundreds of government buildings, universities and colleges, as well as convents, monasteries, and churches, and their treasures dating to the city's founding were ruined or lost. The destruction decimated Manila's diverse cultural heritage—encompassing the confluence of Spanish, American, and Asian influences in the southern Pacific—affecting art, literature, and especially architecture. Once celebrated as the Pearl of the Orient and a living testament to cross-cultural exchange, Manila was virtually wiped out.

By February 12, Iwabuchi's artillery and heavy mortars had been silenced, and the Japanese forces offered no plan to withdraw or regroup as they contended with severe shortages of rations and ammunition. The U.S. 1st Cavalry Division reached Manila Bay on the same day, signaling the point at which the assault on the city would intensify. On February 17, the 148th Regiment captured the Philippine General Hospital, freeing about 7,000 civilians, and also secured the University of the Philippines Padre Faura campus along with Assumption College San Lorenzo's Herran-Dakota campus. The following day, February 18, the 1st Cavalry Division seized Rizal Stadium, which had been used by the Japanese as an ammunition dump, and Fort San Antonio Abad.

James M. Slattery served as chairman of the Illinois Commerce Commission from 1936 to 1939, and later remained on the commission as a member from April 14, 1939, to November 21, 1940, departing only after a duly elected successor had qualified. In 1939, Governor Henry Horner returned to Illinois to oppose acting Governor John Henry Stelle’s attempt to appoint the successor to J. Hamilton Lewis. Slattery was an unsuccessful candidate in the special election to fill the vacancy, and he then returned to practicing law in Chicago. He died at his summer residence in Lake Geneva, Wisconsin, and was buried in Calvary Cemetery in Evanston, Illinois.

James M. Slattery was born in Chicago and educated in local parochial schools as well as St. Ignatius College (now Loyola University Chicago). In 1905 he served as secretary with the building departments of the city of Chicago. He graduated from the Illinois College of Law at Chicago in 1908, was admitted to the bar that year, and began practicing law in Chicago. Slattery was a member of the faculty at the Illinois College of Law from 1909 to 1912 and concurrently served as superintendent of public service for Cook County from 1910 to 1912. He then acted as secretary of Webster College of Law in Chicago from 1912 to 1914. Later in his career, he served as counsel for the Lincoln Park Commission (1933–1934) and for the Chicago Park District (1934–1936).

During the Formosa Air Battle, Task Group 38.1 operated to protect the retiring Canberra group. At 16:15, USS Houston joined TG 38.1 to relieve USS Wichita, which had served as the Wasp’s tow boat. After sunset, at 18:31, a large enemy bogey appeared. Picket ships’ anti-aircraft batteries downed ten aircraft, while additional enemy planes pressed toward the group’s center. At least two torpedoes were fired at Houston; the vessel veered sharply to starboard to avoid the first wake, while a second torpedo passed to port. The first torpedo struck Houston amidships between the keel and the armor belt, causing flooding. The ship began listing about 16 degrees, and many crew members went over the side. An order to abandon ship was almost issued, but USS Boston decided to tow Houston back toward the east.

At about 06:00 hours predawn, four task groups carried out fighter sweeps over Formosa, prompting a Japanese alert and the interception of Grumman F6F Hellcats as anti-aircraft fire ranged from moderate to intense. The fiercest air-to-air engagements occurred over northern and central Formosa, contested by units from Task Group 38.2 under Bogan and Task Group 38.3 under Sherman. Sherman’s forces, operating from USS Lexington and USS Essex, claimed nearly 50 enemy aircraft shot down, while Bogan’s task group, which included three Essex-class carriers—USS Intrepid, USS Bunker Hill, and USS Hancock—also reported over 50 Japanese aircraft destroyed; together, the two groups accounted for approximately 100 enemy aircraft. Japanese losses were later attributed as 17 of 50 operational Formosa-based fighters, per survivor Kazuo Odachi, and many of Japan’s more experienced pilots were killed during the first wave of the American air raid.

During this period, Madonna experienced the loss of several family members. Her elder brother Anthony died in February 2023 at the age of 66. Her younger brother Christopher died on October 4, 2024, in Petoskey, Michigan, at 63, from pancreatic cancer. Christopher's death came about two weeks after the passing of their stepmother Joan. Madonna subsequently posted a lengthy tribute on Instagram to Christopher, expressing admiration, noting that they had reconciled, stating she had done her best to keep him alive as long as possible, referencing the pain he endured at the end, and saying that there would never be anyone like him.

Madonna’s deliberate use of sexual imagery has been credited with boosting her career while fueling public discourse on sexuality and feminism. The Times argued that she catalyzed a revolution among women in music and compelled the public to reconsider attitudes toward sex, nudity, style, and sexuality. Scholarly perspectives such as John Fiske’s link empowerment to the ability to shape the meanings attached to the self, sexuality, and social relations. In Doing Gender in Media, Art and Culture (2009), Madonna is described as complicating feminist reflections and debates in her capacities as a female celebrity, performer, and pop icon. Sheila Jeffreys contends that she embodies women’s empowerment within the realm of sex by embracing the sexual expectations placed on women. Additionally, media theorist Sut Jhally characterized Madonna as a figure who occupies a near-sacred status within feminist iconography.

Formosa lies across the Tropic of Cancer and is shaped by the East Asian monsoon, producing a climate that varies across the island. The northern region experiences a humid subtropical climate with notable seasonal differences in temperature, while central and much of the southern areas fall under a tropical monsoon regime with less variation in temperature and generally warm to hot conditions. During the winter months from November to March, the northeast tends to receive steady rainfall, whereas central and southern Taiwan are typically sunny. The summer monsoon, from May to October, brings the majority of annual rainfall, accounting for about 90 percent of precipitation in the south and roughly 60 percent in the north. Across the island, average annual rainfall is about 2,600 millimeters.

Formosa's contemporary economy is dominated by natural resources that are largely agricultural in nature. In western Taiwan, sugarcane and rice have been grown since the 17th century, forming enduring staples of the rural economy. From the late 19th century through the first half of the 20th century, camphor production and sugar refining stood as major export industries, connecting the island to broader international markets. The subsequent decline of these sectors was driven primarily by a reduction in global demand rather than by the depletion of the underlying resources, reflecting shifts in international trade and production patterns rather than environmental exhaustion.

Lime Grove Studios, a long-standing BBC film and television production site in west London, closed in July 1991 after 76 years of operation. On 26 August 1991, the BBC broadcast The Lime Grove Story, a day of programming that commemorated the closure by highlighting programmes and films produced at Lime Grove over its 76-year history. Nearby, the BBC Television Theatre, situated near Shepherd's Bush Green, reverted to being the Shepherd's Bush Empire.

Built by the Gaumont Film Company in 1915, the Lime Grove complex was located on Lime Grove, a residential street in Shepherd's Bush. At its opening, Gaumont described it as the finest studio in Great Britain and the first building in the country erected solely for the production of films. From the early 1930s, a number of Gainsborough Pictures productions were made there, and its sister studio, Islington Studios, was also used by Gainsborough; films were often shot partly at Islington and partly at Lime Grove.

Dubai is an international financial centre in the United Arab Emirates. In 2007, City Mayors ranked Dubai 44th among the world's leading financial cities, and a 2012 City Mayors assessment placed Dubai as the 27th richest city globally by purchasing power parity. The MasterCard Worldwide Centres of Commerce Index for 2007 ranked Dubai 37th among the top 50 global financial cities, and named it the leading financial centre in the Middle East. Following its opening in September 2004, the Dubai IFC has attracted many international firms as a regional hub. It also established NASDAQ Dubai, which lists equities, derivatives, structured products, sukuk, and other bonds. The Dubai IFC operates under an independent, risk-based regulatory regime and a legal framework aligned with English common law.

Dubai experiences a hot desert climate (Köppen BWh). Summers are exceptionally hot, extended, windy, and humid, with typical daytime highs near 40 °C and overnight lows around 30 °C in August, the hottest month of the year. The area generally receives abundant sunshine on the majority of days throughout the year. Winters are mild to warm, with average daytime temperatures around 24 °C and overnight lows near 14 °C in January, the coolest month.

At the conclusion of World War I, destroyers assigned to screen battleships weighed about 1,100 tons displacement and were armed with four 4-inch guns and six or more torpedoes. The Italian navy advanced with the Mirabello-class esploratori, which were roughly seventy percent larger than contemporaneous destroyers. Under the Washington Naval Treaty framework, major powers pursued differing paths: the United Kingdom remained satisfied with the V and W-class destroyers, the United States favored Wickes and Clemson-class hulls, while signatories with smaller fleets explored configurations that bridged destroyers and cruisers. Italy continued expansion by launching three additional Leone-class esploratori, and France introduced six Chacal-class contre-torpilleur super destroyers to augment its surface forces. In Japan, developments followed with the light cruiser Yūbari and then the Fubuki-class special-type destroyers (Tokugata), whose extended endurance enabled them to accompany and protect the Kido Butai aircraft carrier force across the Pacific.

Destroyer leader (DL) was a United States Navy hull designation applied to large destroyers during the early Cold War, beginning on 9 February 1951. Vessels bearing the DL designation were formally considered frigates from 1 January 1955 through 1975. In the 1975 ship reclassification, smaller DLs were redesignated as destroyers while the larger DLs were reclassified as cruisers. This reorganization also aimed to align the designation of destroyer escorts with international usage by allowing them to be redesignated as frigates.

The Right to Financial Privacy Act of 1978 (RFPA) is a United States federal law enacted as Title XI of the Financial Institutions Regulatory and Interest Rate Control Act of 1978. It is codified at 12 U.S.C. chapter 35, beginning with section 3401, and establishes protections for the privacy of customers’ financial records by governing the manner and extent to which government authorities may access those records, thereby granting individuals a measure of privacy from government searches.

The Right to Financial Privacy Act (RFPA) governs access to individuals' financial records held by financial institutions. Originally, it required the FBI to demonstrate that the target of a records request was a foreign power or an agent of a foreign power in order to obtain records through a national security letter. Compliance with such letters was voluntary, and many states' privacy laws permitted financial institutions to decline the requests. In 1986, Congress amended the RFPA to authorize the government to compel disclosure of the requested information. The act was later amended by the USA PATRIOT Act of 2001.

Julie Gold is an American songwriter best known for composing the ballad “From a Distance,” which was first recorded by Nanci Griffith. Griffith also recorded several other Gold songs, including “Heaven,” “Southbound Train,” “Good Night New York,” and “Mountain of Sorrow.” Gold’s work has been performed by a range of artists, among them Patti LaBelle, Patti LuPone, Lea Salonga, and Andrea Marcovicci. Her songs have also been featured in film, with “Thanks to You” appearing in the 1993 movie Andre and “Dream Loud” in the 2002 film Unfaithful.

Julie Gold was born in Havertown, Pennsylvania, and later relocated to Philadelphia. She completed her secondary education at the Philadelphia High School for Girls, graduating in 1974, and went on to earn a degree from Temple University in 1978. In the Philadelphia area, she performed as a featured act in coffee houses and other entertainment venues, including the Main Point and the Bijou Cafe. From 1990 to 1994, she was a member of the Four Bitchin' Babes, alongside Christine Lavin, Megon McDonough, and Sally Fingerett.

Scuttling is a method of disposing ships that can offer economic benefits by eliminating ongoing costs associated with maintaining seaworthiness and related obligations. The practice is controversial. A notable case involved the USS Oriskany, which was sunk with approximately 700 pounds of polychlorinated biphenyls remaining on board, components formerly used in cable insulation; the action violated the Stockholm Convention, which prohibits the dumping of PCBs into marine environments. The planned scuttling of HMAS Adelaide at Avoca Beach, New South Wales, in March 2010 was postponed amid resident concerns about tidal effects and whether hazardous substances had been properly removed; after additional cleanup orders, the hulk was eventually sunk on 13 April 2011.
In March 2022, Ukraine scuttled the Hetman Sahaidachny, a Krivak-class frigate, to prevent its seizure by advancing Russian offensive operations that threatened to capture the vessel.

Chlothar II, though only nine years old in 593, commanded a Frankish force at the Battle of Droizy and repelled an invasion of Neustria led by Austrasia's Duke Wintrio. In 596, he and Fredegund captured Paris, a city that had been intended to be held in common; Fredegund, acting as regent for her son, then dispatched a force to Laffaux, contributing to the defeat of the armies of Theudebert and Theuderic. In 597, Fredegund died, leaving Chlothar II to rule Neustria alone, although the young king did not achieve any significant milestones for two more years.

Chlothar II, who ruled the Franks for several decades, presided over a lengthy reign by contemporary standards but presided over a period in which royal authority gradually eroded as power shifted toward the French nobility and the church amid ongoing Merovingian feuding. The Edict of Paris of 614 addressed royal appointments and administration, though modern historians differ in their interpretations of its exact scope and impact. In 617, he established the office of mayor of the palace as a lifelong post, a decisive step toward transforming that office into the de facto head of government and, eventually, a foundation for monarchic power that would culminate with Pepin the Short in 751. In 623, Chlothar II ceded rule over Austrasia to his young son Dagobert I.

Arlo Parks signed with Transgressive Records following the release of her track Cola. In January 2019 she issued the title track of her forthcoming EP, Super Sad Generation. Critics, including Robin Murray of Clash, noted the song’s display of precise artistic control and wordplay that captures the volatile emotions of youth. In March 2019 Parks released her third single, Romantic Garbage, and in early April 2019 released the four-track EP Super Sad Generation. The record was created largely in Parks’s home in South West London and at an Airbnb in London’s Angel district, with Gianluca Buccellati serving as producer and co-writer.

Arlo Parks adopted a distinctive stage name inspired by King Krule and Frank Ocean. In 2018 she began uploading demos to BBC Music Introducing, which drew the attention of radio presenters across the United Kingdom and led Ali Raymond of Beatnik Creative to begin managing her. Her solo debut arrived with the release of Cola through Beatnik Records in November 2018, and she subsequently announced the forthcoming debut EP, Super Sad Generation. The track received critical notice, with Line of Best Fit describing it as underscoring the inevitability of betrayal among pretty people who believe flowers can solve everything. Olivia Swash observed that Parks’s vocal performance benefits from her writing background, delivering a delicate tone atop plodding guitars and vinyl crackle. By November 2019, Cola had amassed over three million streams on Spotify.

Guangdong Provincial People's Stadium, located in Guangzhou, was used by Japanese forces as a transport and supplies depot during the occupation of Guangzhou. The facility was subsequently bombed at the time of Guangzhou's liberation.

Guangdong Provincial People's Stadium (Chinese: 广东省人民体育场) is a multi-purpose stadium in Guangzhou, China. It is primarily used for football matches and has a seating capacity of 15,000. The venue is most easily accessed via Guangzhou Metro Line 1, with Martyrs' Park Station serving as the nearest stop.

Flags accompanying players indicate the national team designation as defined by FIFA eligibility rules, although a few limited exceptions to this convention exist. Additionally, some players may hold more than one non-FIFA nationality, meaning multiple non-FIFA nationalities can be listed.

The 2023–24 season marked MFK Karviná's 119th year of existence and represented the club's return to the Czech First League, the top tier of Czech football. During the campaign, the team also competed in the Czech Cup.

Huangcun station (黄村站; Cantonese Yale: Wòhngchyūn Jaahm), which was formerly planned to be named Olympic Sports Center station, is an interchange on the Guangzhou Metro serving Lines 4 and 21 and functions as the northern terminus of Line 4. The underground facility is situated beneath the Guangdong Olympic Stadium in the Huangcun Subdistrict of Tianhe District, and it opened on 25 September 2010. Line 4 links the Asian Games New Town area outside Haibang Station with the Guangdong Olympic Stadium and played a significant role in facilitating transportation during the Guangzhou Asian Games. The station became a transfer point with Line 21 on 20 December 2019. It is located in proximity to Tianhe East railway station.

Corvettes are relatively small, highly versatile warships designed for operations near coasts. In the United States, the Navy has pursued the Littoral Combat Ship (LCS) program, with vessels that are essentially large corvettes. Their expansive hulls accommodate modular mission packages, allowing them to be configured for a range of duties that previously required specialized ships. Consequently, LCS can perform tasks such as mine countermeasures and anti-submarine warfare, roles formerly carried out by dedicated platforms like the Oliver Hazard Perry-class frigates.
The Imperial Marinheiro was an Imperial Marinheiro-class corvette launched in 1955 and based in Porto Velho, Brazil. It was scrapped in 2023 after partially sinking at its moorings.

Guangzhou Twin Towers comprises two high-rise buildings situated in Zhujiang New Town, Guangzhou's central business district in the Tianhe District. The western tower, known as the Guangzhou International Finance Center, was designed by Wilkinson Eyre and became operational in 2010. The eastern tower, called the Guangzhou Chow Tai Fook Finance Centre, was designed by Kohn Pedersen Fox and opened in 2016.

Guangzhou Twin Towers are two skyscrapers located in Guangzhou, Guangdong Province, China. They constitute the tallest pair of high-rise buildings in the city, surpassing all other structures in Guangzhou. In Chinese, the towers are known as 广州双塔 and 广州双子塔.

Emmanuel Macron met Vladimir Putin on 29 May 2017 at the Palace of Versailles. During the discussions, Macron criticized Russia Today and Sputnik as instruments of influence and propaganda, accusing them of spreading deceptive narratives. He urged international cooperation in the fight against ISIS and warned that France would respond with force in Syria if chemical weapons were used. In response to the 2018 Douma chemical attack, Macron directed French participation in airstrikes against Syrian government targets, carried out in coordination with the United States and the United Kingdom.

In March 2017, Mounir Mahjoubi, who oversaw Emmanuel Macron's digital campaign, told Sky News that Russia was behind high-profile attacks targeting Macron. He contended that Russian state media were the principal source of disinformation, specifically identifying RT (Russia Today) and Sputnik News as the first outlets to propagate false information about Macron.

Nanfang Building (南方大厦) is a historic high-rise in Guangzhou, China. Completed in 1922, it was the tallest building in the country at the time of its completion. Since then, the building has housed offices, department stores, electronics markets, and hotels.

Martin-Michel-Charles Gaudin was a French politician who served as a deputy representing the Aisne department during the Bourbon Restoration. His tenure lasted from 22 August 1815 until 17 July 1819, and he was aligned with the constitutional party.

Martin-Michel-Charles Gaudin was a French statesman who served as Napoleon Bonaparte's Minister of Finance until 1814. He reorganized the system of direct contributions and reintroduced direct taxation, known as droits réunis, and he founded both the Banque de France and the Cour des comptes to strengthen fiscal administration. Gaudin also established the first cadaster as the basis for taxation, thereby linking land ownership records to fiscal policy. In 1809, he was granted the duché grand-fief of Gaeta and the title of duc de Gaëte in the Kingdom of Naples, effectively creating a life peerage. During the Hundred Days, Napoleon reserved a seat for Gaudin in the planned imperial Chamber of Peers, but the chamber never materialised.

Christine Lavin (born January 2, 1952) is a singer-songwriter based in New York City and a promoter of contemporary folk music. She has released numerous solo albums and has also recorded under the name Four Bitchin' Babes with three bandmates. Lavin is noted for her sense of humor expressed in both her music and onstage performances, and many of her songs alternate between comedic moments and emotional reflections on romance.

Christine Lavin began her career performing at Caffe Lena in Saratoga Springs, New York. She was persuaded by Dave Van Ronk to move to New York City to pursue a career as a singer-songwriter, and she accepted his offer of guitar lessons. In New York, she served as the original host of Sunday Breakfast on WFUV. In 1990 she became a founding member of the Four Bitchin' Babes.

Laura González was born in Cali, Colombia, and moved to Cartagena when she was six months old. She is of Lebanese descent. She completed high school at Cartagena Modern Gymnasium and pursued Dramatic Art at the School of Education Actoral House Ensemble. She speaks Spanish, English, and French.

Laura González was crowned Miss Colombia 2017 on 20 March 2017. She represented Colombia at Miss Universe 2017, where she finished as the first runner-up. This achievement continued Colombia's streak of top-three finishes at Miss Universe for a fourth consecutive year.

The Streets released their debut studio album, Original Pirate Material, in March 2002. The record garnered critical acclaim and commercial success in the United Kingdom. It received a nomination for the Mercury Prize. At the 2003 BRIT Awards, Original Pirate Material was nominated for British Album of the Year, and The Streets were nominated in three additional categories: British Urban Act, British Breakthrough Act, and British Male Solo Artist. NME named Original Pirate Material the third-best album of 2002. Subsequent singles from the album included "Don't Mug Yourself," "Weak Become Heroes," and "Let's Push Things Forward."

The Streets is an English musical project led by Mike Skinner, who performs as vocalist and multi-instrumentalist.
