Uruguay rather than California, detailing a 1942 Pacific-transport itinerary beginning with a departure from Brooklyn on 3 March 1942 carrying United States troops, followed by a transit via the Panama Canal and Bora Bora to Auckland, New Zealand, where it arrived on 9 April 1942, then proceeding to Melbourne before returning to New Zealand. The vessel allegedly departed Wellington Harbour on 28 April 1942 carrying Royal New Zealand Air Force cadets and reached San Francisco on 14 May 1942; on 26 May 1942 it sailed from San Francisco with additional U.S. troops, arriving again in Auckland on 12 June 1942.

Originally named California, the vessel was renamed SS Uruguay in 1938. From 1942 to 1946, it was operated by agents of the War Shipping Administration as a troopship under the Uruguay designation. After the war, it returned to civilian service as SS Uruguay in 1948. The ship was laid up in 1954 and was ultimately scrapped in 1964.

Off the Grid is widely regarded as one of the album’s strongest tracks, receiving favorable responses from both critics and fans. Complex named the song the best track of 2021, highlighting its standout quality within the year’s releases. Pitchfork reviewer Matthew Ritchie offered a positive assessment, praising Fivio Foreign’s vocal contribution. The Ringer’s Rob Harvilla described the track as a notably claustrophobic Brooklyn drill excursion, emphasizing its atmospherics and intensity.

Off the Grid was first officially previewed on August 5 during a listening party held at Mercedes-Benz Stadium, and it was previewed again on August 26 at Soldier Field, where West contributed an additional verse at the end.

On 2 September 1945, with Japan’s surrender formalized, the USS J. Franklin Bell proceeded to the Western Pacific on 21 September, transporting troops to Eniwetok, Okinawa, and Leyte. After taking on homebound passengers at Leyte, she sailed on 27 October 1945 and arrived in Seattle on 12 November 1945. Beginning on 22 November 1945, the vessel conducted coastal operations, shuttling between ports in Washington and California.

Departing on the 22nd with 862 casualties bound for Saipan, the USS J. Franklin Bell subsequently proceeded to Espiritu Santo and Nouméa to embark additional homebound casualties. It left Nouméa on 11 July with more than 1,700 passengers aboard and arrived in San Francisco on the 27th.

On the morning of 28 July 1904 (Old Style 10 August 1904), Vice Admiral Vitgeft’s Russian squadron departed Port Arthur with the aim of breaking the blockade and heading for Vladivostok. At about 9:00 a.m. the Russian fleet sailed out, initially forming a line abreast to clear the mining channel along the Shandong Peninsula coast. By 10:30 the force had reached open waters, roughly half of the torpedo boats turning back to Port Arthur while the remaining ships adjusted their course to the southeast at eight knots (approximately 15 km/h; 9.2 mph). Around 11:30 the two principal fleets converged and became visible through the haze, the leading ships about 12 nautical miles apart. The Japanese fleet was arranged with Mikasa at the head, followed in line by Asahi, Fuji, Shikishima, Kasuga, and Nisshin. Admiral Tōgō Heihachirō then executed a decisive maneuver: once directly in front of the enemy line, his ships simultaneously turned to port, placing the Russian fleet behind them.

During the Battle of the Yellow Sea, the combat lasted nearly seven hours, with the two fleets exchanging fire and about 7,382 shells launched at a hit rate of roughly 1.7 percent. In a notable action, Schensnovich steered his battleship directly into Admiral Tōgō's battleline, effectively ending the battleship fleet duel and saving the Russian flagship from destruction. Schensnovich died in January 1911 from wounds received in the engagement, aged 57.

Wuhan Institute of Physical Education maintains a campus with a total building area of 657,862.91 square meters as of December 31, 2024, comprising an office building area of 16,907.16 m² and other areas totaling 640,955.75 m². The institute operates a fleet of 21 official vehicles, distributed as two for top leadership, eight for emergency support, three for specialized professional use, and eight for other purposes; the remaining vehicles are predominantly non-motorized, including electric two-wheeled patrol units and electric garbage-collection vehicles. In terms of equipment, the institution houses 83 general equipment units priced above 500,000 yuan each and 32 special equipment units priced above 1,000,000 yuan each.

Wuhan Institute of Physical Education (Chinese: 武汉体育学院; 武漢體育學院), commonly abbreviated as 武体, is a provincial public research and education institution based in Wuhan, Hubei Province, China. It is branded as Wuhan Sports University for teaching and athletic training programs, and as Wuhan Institute of Physical Education in research communications. The institute was established through a joint initiative of the General Administration of Sport of China and the People's Government of Hubei Province. It is affiliated with the Wuhan Institute Group (WIG), an association of ten ministerial and provincial higher education institutions in Wuhan.

Mixed Personalities portrays a romantic partner who experiences mood swings, with vocal processing that employs Auto-Tune in a manner reminiscent of Kanye West's 808s & Heartbreak era (2008). The track also samples dialogue spoken by R. Lee Ermey in the 1987 film Full Metal Jacket; Ermey is noted as a late former Marine drill instructor who later pursued acting.

In mid-2018, Kanye West expanded his collaborations to include artists from a younger generation, working with Lil Pump on “I Love It,” XXXTentacion posthumously on “One Minute” and “The Storm,” and 6ix9ine on “Mama” and “Kanga.” West was introduced to YNW Melly’s music by CyHi the Prynce, and he flew Melly to Los Angeles for a meeting. Melly previewed a number of songs from his project We All Shine for West, among them the track titled “Mixed Personalities,” after which West requested to be featured on the track.

Barbie: Big City, Big Dreams presents Malibu Barbie and Brooklyn Barbie as they navigate fame and friendship in the urban setting. Malibu develops admiration for pop star Emmie after seeing a poster in the subway, while Brooklyn explains that Emmie is an old childhood friend whom she has not seen in many years. The two vow that rising stardom will not jeopardize their close relationship. Emmie makes a surprise appearance at Handler Arts Academy in disguise, seeking to be treated as a normal student. Concurrently, Dean Morrison announces that the Spotlight Solo will be livestreamed from Times Square, underscoring the show's high-profile reach. During the course of events, Malibu and Brooklyn meet Rafael (Rafa), a costume-design student, and his dog Gato, and Rafael provides them with sequined dresses intended to sparkle, though the remote control used to light them up fails to operate properly.

Barbie: Big City, Big Dreams follows Malibu Barbie as she begins at a prestigious city academy and encounters difficulties across all of her classes during the opening week. Ken phones to check on her, but she responds with mixed feelings about his concern. The group of girls who share the Barbie surname, along with Rafa, discover that Emmie is attending the school in disguise. Emmie explains that she had lost contact with Brooklyn Barbie due to her strict manager father, and the two are able to rekindle their friendship. The Barbie-named group and Rafa pledge to keep Emmie's undercover status secret.

The article titled "List of George Michael live performances" is a structured, neutral catalog that documents the English singer-songwriter George Michael’s live appearances, with an emphasis on concert tours and other notable performances. Covering the artist who lived from 1963 to 2016, the entry compiles verifiable information about his live acts and presents them in an organized, reference-oriented format suitable for readers seeking an overview of his stage career.

In December 2009, President Barack Obama signed the Fiscal Year 2010 Defense Appropriations Bill, which allocated $130 million for the Marine One program, including $100 million to recover technology from the VH-71 Kestrel and $30 million to support the Navy’s initial VH-XX studies. In February 2010, the Navy issued a request for information to the aviation industry as part of evaluating options for the program. In April 2010, Lockheed Martin announced a collaboration with Sikorsky to offer the Sikorsky S-92 as the proposed replacement rather than the VH-71. In June 2010, Boeing explored a U.S.-built licensed version of the AgustaWestland AW101 for the renewed VXX program, alongside the V-22 Osprey and CH-47 Chinook.

Lockheed Martin VH-71 Kestrel traces its origins to the AW101, originally designated EH101, which was developed and produced by EH Industries, a joint venture between Westland Helicopters of the United Kingdom and Agusta of Italy. Following the 2001 merger of Westland and Agusta to form AgustaWestland, the company identified strong export potential for the AW101, including opportunities for overseas manufacturing collaborations. On 23 July 2002, Lockheed Martin and AgustaWestland signed a ten-year agreement to jointly market, manufacture, and support a United States–based derivative of the AW101. The derivative, known as US101, would be 65 percent American in content. The proposed roles for the US101 included United States Air Force combat search and rescue, United States Coast Guard search and rescue, and United States Marine Corps executive transport.

General Reinsurance Corporation (Gen Re) is a global reinsurer with an international office network. In Latin America, it operates from Mexico City and São Paulo; in Europe and the Middle East, it maintains offices in Cologne, Copenhagen, Dubai, London, Madrid, Milan, Moscow, Paris, and Vienna; in Africa, it has a presence in Cape Town and Johannesburg; in Asia, it conducts activities from Beijing, Hong Kong, Mumbai, Seoul, Shanghai, Singapore, Taipei, and Tokyo; and in Australasia, it maintains offices in Auckland and Sydney.

John Houldsworth, the chief executive officer of Cologne Re Dublin, agreed to become a cooperating witness for the United States Department of Justice and the Securities and Exchange Commission in exchange for a plea bargain. He pleaded guilty to conspiring to commit securities fraud. He faces a maximum sentence of five years in prison and fines up to $250,000. Sentencing was stayed pending related SEC prosecutions.

Since the early 1980s, the Chinese Communist Party has pursued engagement with European social democratic movements, marking its first sustained effort to establish cordial party-to-party relations with non-communist parties. A brief deviation occurred in the 1970s when the CCP interacted with far-right parties as a strategic step to counter Soviet expansionism. This shift reflected a reorientation from an originally negative view of social democracy—rooted in the Second International and Marxist-Leninist critique—toward a belief that the model could be studied and learned from. By the mid- to late 1980s, the CCP dispatched delegates across Europe to observe social democratic practices, noting that many of these parties were experiencing electoral decline and self-reform. Attention centered on reform trajectories within the British Labour Party and the Social Democratic Party of Germany (SPD), with the CCP concluding that these parties remained viable due to modernization—privatization, smaller government, a revised welfare state, and a more market-oriented stance. As a result, the CCP shifted its traditional base away from trade unions toward entrepreneurs, younger voters, and students, while crediting European social democrats with fostering a form of capitalism tempered by social policy.

Some historians regard the May Fourth Movement as the starting point of the revolutionary struggle that culminated in the founding of the People's Republic of China. In the period following the movement, trends toward social transformation intensified and reshaped the political landscape. In a 1939 assessment, Mao Zedong argued that the movement indicated the bourgeois revolution against imperialism had advanced to a new stage, though the proletariat would lead the completion of the revolution. The movement also produced radical intellectuals who mobilized peasants and workers, thereby strengthening the organizational base of the Chinese Communist Revolution and contributing to the growth of the CCP. Among the period’s most influential Marxist promoters were Chen and Li. The Chinese Communist Party embraces the May Fourth Movement and regards itself as part of its legacy.

Boundaries for the Black Belt in the American South are defined using Census data to identify rural Southern counties with substantial African American populations, applying a threshold of at least 25 percent African American residents. Under these criteria, such counties comprised 29 percent of the Southern United States population in 1980 and declined to 23 percent by 2005. In the same set of counties, the White population’s share of the Southern population fell from 23 percent in 1980 to 17 percent in 2005, while the Black population grew from 6.7 million in 1980 to 8.4 million in 2005. The White population within these counties numbered 10.7 million in 1980 and 11.7 million in 2005.

W. E. B. Du Bois is regarded as the most prominent analyst of the Black Belt in the American South, distinguishing his work by employing statistically grounded studies of family life, economic cooperation, and social conditions within the region. In the early twentieth century he also served as editor for The Atlantic University Publications. His 1903 volume The Souls of Black Folk offers extensive analysis and reflective consideration of the experiences and structures of Black communities in the South. Albany, Georgia, located in Dougherty County, is identified as the heart of the Black Belt, a designation linked to its historical role in plantation agriculture, with Du Bois describing the area as preserving the vestiges of the vast plantation system.

Solar power is the conversion of energy from sunlight into electricity. It can be produced directly using photovoltaic technologies that rely on the photovoltaic effect to generate electric current, or indirectly through concentrated solar power systems that use lenses or mirrors along with solar tracking to concentrate sunlight onto a receiver. In CSP setups, the focused light creates a hot spot whose thermal energy is typically used to drive a steam turbine or other heat engine to generate electricity.

Solar power potential is greatest in regions that experience very high annual solar radiation, particularly the arid tropics and subtropics. In low-latitude deserts, the sky is often clear and daily sunshine typically exceeds ten hours, creating favorable conditions for both photovoltaic and solar-thermal technologies. These hot deserts form the Global Sun Belt, a belt that encircles the globe. The Global Sun Belt includes extensive desert regions in Northern and Southern Africa, Southwest Asia and the Middle East, and Australia, along with smaller deserts in the Americas.

Bhutan experienced internal strife in the 1870s, arising from power struggles between the Paro and Tongsa valleys. Ugyen Wangchuck, the penlop of Trongsa, rose to ascendancy amid these conflicts. From his base in central Bhutan, he defeated his political opponents and, following a period of civil wars and uprisings from 1882 to 1885, united the country under his leadership.

Bhutan encompasses a diverse flora, featuring over 5,400 plant species, including Pedicularis cacuminidenta. Fungi form a vital part of Bhutan's ecosystems, with mycorrhizal species aiding forest trees by supplying mineral nutrients essential for growth. In addition, wood-decay and litter-decomposing fungi play a crucial role in the natural recycling of nutrients, helping to sustain the country's ecological processes.

The Grammy Award for Best Country Song, sometimes known as the Country Songwriter's Award, is a category within the Grammy Awards that has been presented since 1965. It honors the songwriter or songwriters of a given country song, rather than the performing artist, unless the artist is also credited as the songwriter.

Years shown for the Grammy Award for Best Country Song reflect the year of the ceremony, recognizing works released in the preceding year. In terms of individual achievement, Lori McKenna, Josh Kear, Chris Stapleton, and Kacey Musgraves are tied for the most wins in this category, each having earned three awards.

Walter M. Schirra, Jr., piloted the Mercury-Atlas 8 mission, Sigma 7, launching on October 3, 1962, at 7:15 a.m. The flight experienced a minor early deviation in the trajectory but successfully reached orbit. During the mission, Schirra manually demonstrated spacecraft control using the reaction control system, reflecting NASA and Schirra’s emphasis on engineering and human factors in manual capsule operation in the wake of Scott Carpenter’s Aurora 7 issues. The suit temperature rose to about 32 °C (90 °F), prompting a manual adjustment of the cooling system. He tested control inputs in zero gravity without sight and demonstrated the ability to back up automatic controls and fly the capsule manually. After six orbits, he reoriented the spacecraft to pass over Africa and performed retrofire for reentry. The capsule landed roughly five miles (eight kilometers) from the recovery ship USS Kearsarge in the central Pacific. Schirra then activated the explosive hatch to exit and sustained a sizable bruise; this incident has been cited in discussions about whether Gus Grissom deliberately opened the Liberty Bell 7 hatch. On October 16, 1962, Schirra and his family were received by President John F. Kennedy in the White House Oval Office.

Walter M. Schirra earned his naval aviator wings in 1948 and joined Fighter Squadron 71 (VF-71) at Quonset Point, Rhode Island, where he flew the F8F Bearcat. As VF-71 prepared to transition to jet aircraft, he undertook transition training in the F-80 Shooting Star while the squadron moved toward the F9F Panther. With the outbreak of the Korean War, he deployed to the Mediterranean aboard the USS Midway in June 1950. He later applied for and was selected to participate in a United States Air Force exchange program to gain combat experience, training in the F-84 Thunderjet.

During Christian IV's reign (1588–1648), Copenhagen grew rapidly, marking a period of substantial urban expansion. In the early 17th century, the Tøjhus Arsenal and the Børsen on Slotsholmen were completed, emblematic of the city's increasing military and commercial prominence. The East India Company was founded in 1616 to promote international trade and maritime enterprise. The district of Christianshavn was developed to the east of the old town, featuring canals and ramparts and drawing on Dutch planning traditions; though designed as a fortified trading centre, Christianshavn was eventually incorporated into Copenhagen. Christian IV sponsored a number of major construction projects, including Rosenborg Castle and the Rundetårn. In 1658–1659, Copenhagen withstood a Swedish siege under Charles X and repelled a major assault, underscoring the city’s resilience during that conflict.

As of 2014, Copenhagen had 15 Michelin-starred restaurants, the most of any city in Scandinavia, underscoring its international reputation as a gourmet destination. Notable Michelin-starred establishments include Den Røde Cottage, Formel B Restaurant, Grønbech & Churchill, Søllerød Kro, Kadeau, Kiin Kiin (Denmark’s first Michelin-starred Asian restaurant), Kong Hans Kælder, Relæ, Restaurant AOC (two stars), Noma, and Geranium (three stars). Noma, whose name translates to Nordic food (nordisk mad), was ranked the world’s best restaurant by Restaurant magazine in 2010, 2011, 2012, and 2014. This sustained acclaim helped spur interest in New Nordic Cuisine, a culinary movement closely associated with Copenhagen’s dining scene.

Among 480 cities surveyed for atmospheric particulate matter, Dammam, Saudi Arabia, was identified as the worst-performing locality. PM2.5 concentrations increased by 111.1 μg/m3, signaling a substantial rise in fine particulate pollution. The city is a major hub of the Saudi oil industry and hosts what is described as the largest airport in the world, as well as the largest port in the Persian Gulf, factors associated with its elevated pollution profile. Consequently, Dammam is presently the most polluted city in the surveyed set.

Atmospheric particulate matter, particularly fine particles known as PM2.5, is consistently and independently linked to serious health effects, including an elevated risk of lung cancer and mortality from cardiovascular and respiratory diseases. The connection between particulate pollution and adverse health outcomes was first demonstrated in the early 1970s and has been corroborated by numerous studies since. In the United States, estimates from around 2000 place PM-related deaths in the tens of thousands annually, ranging approximately from 22,000 to 52,000. In Europe, PM pollution was attributed to about 370,000 premature deaths in 2005. Globally, the Global Burden of Disease collaboration estimated roughly 3.22 million deaths associated with PM pollution in 2010. More recently, the European Environment Agency estimated that premature deaths in the 27 European Union member states in 2019 due to fine particle pollution were about 307,000.

Active rock is a radio format used by numerous commercial radio stations in the United States and Canada. It blends contemporary hard rock with selected classic rock tracks, aiming to provide a balance between current hard-edged songs and established favorites. The format places emphasis on the tougher aspect of mainstream rock and the album-oriented rock tradition, often highlighting heavier material within the broader rock spectrum.

Active rock is a radio format that lacks a single, universally accepted definition. In the late 1990s, Sean Ross, then editor of Airplay Monitor, described it as essentially AOR with a stronger emphasis on the harder end of the rock spectrum. Radio & Records characterized the format as featuring current rock hits in heavy rotation and directed toward a male audience aged 18 to 34. The same publication also noted that its approach resembled that of contemporary hit radio stations.

Half Rate is a speech codec variant that operates at a bitrate of 5.6 kilobits per second, roughly half the bandwidth required by the Full Rate codec and thereby doubling the network capacity available for voice traffic. This reduction in bitrate comes with a trade-off of diminished audio quality relative to the Full Rate solution. The encoding process uses an 8 kHz sampling rate with 13-bit samples, and data are organized into frames of 160 samples (20 milliseconds), which are further divided into 40-sample subframes (5 milliseconds).

GSM Half Rate is a speech coding option defined for the Global System for Mobile Communications by the European Telecommunications Standards Institute in EN 300 969 (GSM 06.20). It uses a form of the Vector-Sum Excitation Linear Prediction (VSELP) algorithm to encode speech at a reduced bit rate. The Half Rate specification succeeded the earlier ETSI ETS 300 581–2, whose first edition was published in December 1995.

UH-Downtown station is a METRORail stop located in Houston's downtown area. The One Main Building sits immediately beside the station, at 1 Main Street. A short stroll from the station brings visitors to the Willow Street Pump Station, which is situated at 811 North San Jacinto Street.

The UH-Downtown station features an unusually narrow platform due to the limited space at its site. As a consequence of these spatial constraints, ticket vending machines are situated on the University of Houston–Downtown campus to serve passengers.

Velocity made good (VMG) is a measure of a sailing vessel’s progress toward a specified mark, combining the boat’s speed with the direction of travel toward the target. The heading that yields the highest VMG is typically about 60 degrees off the true wind, corresponding to a course roughly toward the northeast or the northwest depending on wind direction. Sailing too close to the wind upwind reduces progress because the vessel slows substantially, whereas sailing further downwind increases speed but moves the boat away from the mark to an extent that the speed gain does not meaningfully improve advance toward the target. In practice, VMG reflects the trade-off between speed and angle to the mark, guiding sailors in choosing a balance that maximizes effective progress.

Velocity made good (VMG) denotes the rate at which a vessel makes progress toward a designated course. A GPS device that reports VMG presents the vessel’s progress along the chosen course, reflecting the boat’s movement relative to that course. To derive an accurate VMG, however, wind speed and wind direction must be measured in addition to the boat’s speed and heading, since wind conditions influence the true component of velocity toward the target.

The presidential standard of Georgia is derived from the national flag, with the Georgian coat of arms displayed at its center. Official copies are exhibited in the president's office, at the Chancellery Building, and at other state agencies. It is also used as a car flag on vehicles carrying the president within Georgia.

The presidency of Georgia was established on 10 March 1992 to address a legitimacy gap after the post-coup transition, with Eduard Shevardnadze as the first head of state. The 1995 Constitution restored the presidency, and Shevardnadze was elected in November 1995 and then reelected in April 2000. Following the Rose Revolution, he resigned on 23 November 2003, with Nino Burjanadze serving briefly as acting president. Mikheil Saakashvili was elected on 4 January 2004. In 2007 he did not complete his first term and resigned to defuse tensions, leading to the presidential election being moved forward from autumn 2008; he was reelected on 5 January 2008. From 2013 to 2018, executive powers were curtailed in favor of the prime minister and government, as the country shifted toward a parliamentary system. Giorgi Margvelashvili was elected president in October 2013, marking the completion of the transition to a parliamentary republic. In November 2018, Salome Zourabichvili became Georgia’s first female president in permanent capacity and the last president elected by direct vote under the new constitution.

Stefan Reuter earned 69 international caps for West Germany, making his senior international debut on 18 April 1987 in Cologne as a substitute for Wolfgang Rolff in the 63rd minute of a goalless draw with Italy. He scored his first international goal on 12 December 1987 in Brasília, netting a 90th-minute equalizer to secure a 1–1 draw with Brazil, the first of his two international goals.

Stefan Reuter was briefly linked with a move to Liverpool following West Germany's World Cup victory, but the transfer did not materialize, and he instead joined Juventus for the 1991–92 season before returning to Germany to sign for Borussia Dortmund. During his time with Dortmund, he helped the club win the Bundesliga in 1994–95, 1995–96, and 2001–02, and he was part of the squad that captured the UEFA Champions League title in 1996–97. The club also reached the UEFA Cup finals in 1993 and 2002. Over his Dortmund career, he made 307 Bundesliga appearances and scored 11 goals, and he retired from professional football in 2004.

John F. Walter was born in Buffalo, New York. He earned a Bachelor of Arts degree from Loyola University of Los Angeles in 1966 and a Juris Doctor from Loyola University of Los Angeles School of Law in 1969. He then worked in private legal practice in California from 1969 to 1970, served as an Assistant United States Attorney for the Central District of California from 1970 to 1972, and subsequently returned to private practice in California from 1972 to 2002.

John F. Walter is a United States district judge serving in the Central District of California. He was nominated to the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California on January 23, 2002, by President George W. Bush to fill the seat that had been vacated by John Davies. The Senate subsequently confirmed him on April 25, 2002, and he received his official judicial commission on May 1, 2002.

Mollusca, a highly diverse phylum, exhibits unresolved relationships among its major lineages, which complicates the identification of ancestral traits. Debates center on metamerism in their origins: some researchers propose a non‑metameric last common ancestor with later segmentation, while Sigwart (2007) argues for a segmented founder accompanied by a creeping foot and a mineralized shell. If the earliest molluscs were metameric, an annelid‑like origin has been suggested as a possibility. In contrast, Giribet et al. (2006) concluded that features such as repeated gills and retractor muscles of the foot are derived characteristics rather than ancestral traits. Additionally, in certain lineages, the evolution of conchiferan shells has been proposed to derive from spicules of aplacophorans, though this scenario is difficult to reconcile with the embryological origin of spicules.

Mollusc cultivation for pearls involves implanting either cultured seed material or beads into oysters to initiate pearl formation. The seed method uses grains ground from the shells of freshwater mussels. Overharvesting for seed material has endangered several freshwater mussel species in the southeastern United States. In some regions, the pearl industry holds substantial economic importance. Consequently, significant funds are allocated to monitoring the health of farmed molluscs to support production and safeguard populations.

In December 2017, Ziff Davis acquired Mashable for $50 million, a price described by Recode as a distressed sale. At that time, Mashable had not met its advertising targets and reported a loss of $4.2 million for the quarter ended September 2017. Following the acquisition, the company laid off about 50 staff while preserving its senior management. Under Ziff Davis, Mashable expanded into numerous countries across Europe, Asia, the Middle East, and Australia, producing content in several languages.

Mashable was founded in July 2004 by Pete Cashmore while he was living in Aberdeen, Scotland. The site began as a simple WordPress blog with Cashmore as its sole author. It quickly gained prominence, and Time magazine named it one of the 25 best blogs of 2009. By November 2015, Mashable had amassed more than 6,000,000 followers on Twitter and more than 3,200,000 fans on Facebook. In June 2016, Mashable expanded its media presence by acquiring the CineFix YouTube channel from Whalerock Industries.

Wuzhou Wu is a variety of Southern Wu Chinese spoken in and around the city of Jinhua in Zhejiang province. The dialect exhibits limited mutual intelligibility with Taihu Wu, with speakers typically unable to understand Taihu Wu to a meaningful degree. The name traces back to Wuzhou County, an historic prefecture in the area corresponding to present-day Jinhua. It is also known by the names 婺州話 (Wuzhou hua) and 務州片 (Wuzhou pian).

On the fifteenth day of the war, Drona inflicted heavy losses on the Pandava forces, among whom Virata fell in an archery duel and Drupada was slain in a sword fight. After these events, Drona lamented the deterioration of his friendship with Drupada and paid his respects to Drupada's corpse. Alongside his son Ashwatthama, Drona then unleashed a renewed and devastating assault on the Pandava army that day.

On the thirteenth day of the Kurukshetra War, Drona deployed the Chakravyuha, a complex circular formation designed to ensnare Yudhishthira. He believed that only Arjuna and Krishna possessed the means to penetrate it. The Trigartas diverted Arjuna and Krishna to another portion of the battlefield, and this distraction enabled the main Kaurava army to surge through the Pandava ranks.

In 1958, Archbishop Joseph Cordeiro was appointed archbishop of Karachi and invited a community of contemplative nuns to the diocese. In December 1959, nine nuns from the Los Angeles monastery arrived in Pakistan to establish the Karachi monastery. On July 20, 1968, the convent moved from Ingle Road to the Landhi area of Karachi.

Monastery of the Angels is a religious community whose nuns earn a modest income by baking and selling bread. The institution’s bread has drawn attention from writers, with Salman Rushdie describing its qualities as having a pale crumb, a crisp crust, and a flavorful taste.

Burroughs Corporation's early large-system lineage began with the B5000, introduced in 1961 as the cornerstone of the Burroughs Large Systems family. A few years afterward the B5500 followed, employing large rotating disks for external memory rather than drums. The B5000 Series is noted for implementing what is widely regarded as the world’s first virtual memory with a multi-programming operating system. In the late 1960s, its successors included the B6500 and B6700, with the B7700 appearing in the mid-1970s and the A-series in the 1980s. Across generations, the architecture remained broadly consistent and continues in the Unisys ClearPath MCP line of stack-based machines programmed in extended Algol 60. The operating system, Master Control Program, gave its name to the Tron project; MCP was originally programmed in ESPOL (an extension of Algol), DCALGOL, and later NEWP, extended variants of Algol developed nearly a decade before Unix. The command interface evolved into WFL (Work Flow Language), a compiled, structured language featuring declarations, statements, and procedures.

Burroughs Corporation manufactured military computers, including the D825, which was developed at the Great Valley Laboratory in Paoli, Pennsylvania, with the prefix “D” indicating defense-industrial use. Some scholars regard the D825 as the first true multiprocessor computer. The same Paoli site also housed the Defense and Space Group Marketing Division.

In February 2011, amid negotiations over the border dispute, Thai and Cambodian troops clashed within Cambodian territory near the Preah Vihear temple. The fighting produced casualties on both sides and involved artillery bombardment in the vicinity. The Cambodian government claimed that the Preah Vihear temple had sustained damage as a result of the clashes, while a UNESCO mission concluded that the damage was caused by gunfire from both Cambodian and Thai forces.

Preah Vihear was constructed largely from local gray and yellow sandstone, with timber employed extensively to form the roof support that supported a terracotta tile covering. In the arches, small bricks were used in place of large rock slabs to shape the corbelled structures, bricks being more suitable for such roofs because they can be mortared together and are more compact and solid than stone slabs. The main tower rises from exceptionally large sandstone blocks, each weighing at least five tons, and several of these blocks incorporate holes intended for lifting during construction.

The Flathead River originates from a system of forks in the Rocky Mountains of northwestern Montana. Its largest tributary, the North Fork, begins in the Canadian province of British Columbia and flows southward, and is sometimes regarded as the river’s main stem. Near West Glacier the North Fork merges with the Middle Fork to form the principal Flathead River. The stream then runs west to join the South Fork and cuts through Bad Rock Canyon between the Whitefish Range and the Swan Range. All of the headwater forks are designated, wholly or partly, as National Wild and Scenic Rivers. After emerging from the canyon, it enters the broad Flathead Valley and curves southwest, passing Columbia Falls and Kalispell. It is joined by the Stillwater River and its Whitefish River tributary before emptying into Flathead Lake, where the Swan River joins the Flathead River.

On February 9, 2010, the Government of British Columbia announced that it would not permit mining, oil and gas development, or coalbed gas extraction within its portion of the Flathead Valley, including the Flathead River area. The decision was welcomed by environmental groups and by U.S. Senators from Montana, who praised it as a protective measure for the region.

Work sampling is a statistical method used to estimate the share of time workers devote to predefined activity categories, such as setting up a machine, assembling components, or remaining idle. By conducting intermittent observations over a work period, the approach yields data on how time is distributed across activities and aids in evaluating efficiency and overall workflow. The resulting information can inform the evaluation and refinement of job responsibilities, tasks, performance competencies, and organizational processes. The technique is also referred to by several alternative names, including activity sampling, occurrence sampling, and ratio-delay study.

Planning a work sampling study necessitates allocating sufficient time to carry out observations and record the results. These studies typically require a substantial period to complete, with the available window generally extending to several weeks or more in order to obtain representative samples.

NuttX was first released in 2007 under the BSD license. In December 2019, the project entered incubation at the Apache Software Foundation. The license subsequently changed from BSD to the Apache License, though the exact date is not specified in the available information. In November 2022, NuttX graduated to a top-level Apache project, marking its full integration within the Apache ecosystem.

NuttX is a free and open-source real-time operating system designed for embedded systems. It emphasizes adherence to technical standards while maintaining a compact footprint, and it is scalable from 8-bit microcontrollers to 64-bit processor environments. The project aims to conform to POSIX and ANSI specifications while also incorporating Unix-like APIs and interfaces from other RTOSes, such as those found in VxWorks, to provide functionality not available under POSIX/ANSI or not suitable for deeply embedded contexts. For example, the fork() system call, common in general-purpose Unix environments, is not appropriate for embedded environments, so NuttX provides alternative mechanisms aligned with resource-constrained operation.

Kaohsiung County was a county in southern Taiwan until its dissolution following a major administrative reorganization in 2010. On 16 August 1950, the southern portion was separated to form Pingtung County, leaving the remainder of Kaohsiung County comprised of areas previously known as Hōzan (Fengshan), Okayama (Kangshan), and Kizan (Chishan) from the Japanese era. In the ensuing period, the county’s districts were abolished, and all townships were placed under direct administration by the Kaohsiung County Government. On 25 December 2010, Kaohsiung County merged with Kaohsiung City to form a larger single special municipality.

Kaohsiung County was established on December 6, 1945 within the territory of Takao Prefecture (高雄州) shortly after the end of World War II. In its early years, the county covered most of Takao Prefecture except for the urban areas surrounding the cities of Takao (now Kaohsiung) and Heitō (now Pingtung). The county was organized into districts (區), which were formed from the reformed Japanese districts (郡), and those districts were further subdivided into townships.

Tenebrism is a painting style characterized by stark light and shadow, in which darkness serves as a dominant element. The name stems from the Italian tenebroso, meaning "dark, gloomy, mysterious," and the approach is sometimes referred to as dramatic illumination. The technique aims to heighten theatricality by means of a spotlight-like beam that illuminates certain figures or moments against a dark field. It is frequently associated with Baroque painting, where it was widely employed to intensify emotional impact. In relation to the broader practice of chiaroscuro, tenebrism adopts far more intense and abrupt contrasts of light and dark to convey drama, whereas chiaroscuro encompasses subtler shifts in value intended to model form and three-dimensionality.

Tenebrism is a painting style that emphasizes intense contrasts between light and shadow. Although Caravaggio is widely credited with inventing the approach, earlier artists had employed similar effects. Albrecht Dürer used the technique in several self-portraits, while Tintoretto integrated it into his dramatic religious canvases, with The Miracle of St Mark cited as a notable example. El Greco produced three versions of a composition in which a boy, a man, and a monkey are clustered in darkness around a single flame, illustrating a pronounced interplay of light and darkness. Adam Elsheimer is also associated with night scenes that feature restricted, narrowly focused illumination. In art historical usage, the term tenebrism is typically applied to artists from the 17th century onward.

Protests in Portland during 2025 drew national attention after President Donald Trump described the city as anarchic on September 5. He later characterized Portland as war-ravaged and claimed that federal buildings were under siege by Antifa and other domestic extremists, announcing on September 28 a plan to send troops and authorize force in the city. The Oregon Attorney General filed suit arguing that Trump overstated the threat in order to justify illegally seizing control of state National Guard units. On October 4, 2025, U.S. District Judge Karin Immergut blocked the deployment of Oregon National Guardsmen, limiting the federal government's ability to deploy troops in the state.

During the 2025 Portland protests, a demonstrator wearing an inflatable frog costume drew attention after federal officers sprayed pepper spray at the respiratory opening of the costume’s headpiece. In the wake of the incident, the protester launched a website titled Operation Inflation. A TikTok video of the event garnered approximately 1.4 million likes, amplifying online attention. NBC News described the frog as a symbol of nonviolent protest, while Hindustan Times noted that the Portland Frog attracted widespread social media interest through videos and images featuring the inflatable costume. The Telegraph suggested that the protester had risen to notoriety and become a symbol of resistance, and Willamette Week referred to the figure as an icon. The Independent described Portland's “antifa frog” as the unofficial mascot of the No Kings protest movement.

King Levinsky, a boxer who later entered professional wrestling, was at times managed by his sister Lena (Kraków) Levy. Known by the nickname "Leapin Lena," she was a colorful figure famed for using salty language and for loudly supporting her brother during his bouts. In its February 1939 issue, Esquire profiled Levinsky's transition into a career as a professional wrestler, marking a notable shift in his sporting path.

King Levinsky (10 September 1910 – 30 September 1991), also known as Kingfish Levinsky, was an American heavyweight boxer who competed during the 1930s. Born Harris Kraków, he hailed from the Kraków family of fish sellers based in Maxwell Street, Chicago's historic Jewish ghetto. He was consistently regarded as one of the era's leading heavyweights, with The Ring magazine ranking him among its top ten heavyweights for four consecutive years from 1931 to 1934, attaining his highest position of third in 1933.

The 1970 United States census reported that the national population had risen to more than 204 million. In a shift within state rankings, California overtook New York to become the most populous state, replacing the previous leader. Four states experienced population declines compared with the 1960 census, with West Virginia recording the largest decrease at roughly seven percent.

The 1970 United States census was carried out by the U.S. Census Bureau. The official count placed the resident population at 203,392,031, representing a 13.4 percent increase from the 1960 census, which recorded 179,323,175 people.

Internet radio enabled the combination of music with advocacy messages. In February 1999, Zero24-7 Web Radio was launched, becoming the first internet radio station to be crowdsourced and programmed by professional broadcasters. The project was crowdfunded by a partnership of individuals, charities, and businesses, and was based in Washington, D.C. Its programming blended progressive music with environmentally oriented messaging. It was created by Mark Daley, a veteran of the BBC and WHFS.

Internet radio drew significant media and investor attention in the late 1990s as streaming audio over the web gained prominence. In 1998, Broadcast.com’s initial public offering set a record for the largest one-day price jump among United States stock offerings, with an IPO price of $18 and shares opening at $68 on the first trading day. The company was operating at a loss, and its SEC prospectus warned that losses were expected to continue indefinitely. On July 20, 1999, Yahoo! acquired Broadcast.com for $5.7 billion.

Wursten Frisian is a historical variant of the Frisian language associated with the Wursten region in present-day Lower Saxony, Germany. It is chiefly notable for containing the only fully preserved sentence attributed to the language, which exists in its original form and is interpreted as an imperative inviting someone to come closer so that information can be conveyed. In English, this line is rendered as a direct request for the listener to approach so that the speaker can tell them something.

The Wursten region, not part of the original Frisian settlement area, was colonised by Frisians in the 8th century CE and developed into an independent municipality. By the fifteenth century East Frisian began to decline, gradually giving way to West Low German dialects in the zone between the Lauwers and Weser rivers. In Wursten, the East Frisian language persisted somewhat longer than in East Frisia proper and in Ommelanden (now part of the Netherlands).

By 2006, tourism had become Nicaragua's second-largest sector of the economy. Over seven years, the sector expanded by about 70 percent nationwide, with annual growth typically between 10 and 16 percent, and tourism income increased by more than 300 percent over a decade. The rapid expansion benefited related industries, including agriculture, commerce, finance, and construction. President Daniel Ortega indicated an intention to leverage tourism as a means to reduce poverty across the country. In 2010, Nicaragua welcomed one million tourists in a calendar year for the first time.

During 1980, the Carter administration provided roughly $60 million in assistance to Nicaragua under the Sandinista government. The program was halted after evidence emerged that Nicaragua had been shipping arms to Salvadoran rebels. At the time, public opinion generally favored Nicaragua in its dispute with the Sandinista leadership.

In 2000, the Clinton administration ended the military-use restrictions on GPS signals, thereby opening the United States GPS satellite system to full commercial access. This policy shift enabled broader adoption of GPS navigation devices and related civilian applications.

GPS navigation devices have become integrated into smartphones, with mobile operating systems offering free mapping and routing services that typically require an active data connection to function. Some platforms allow users to purchase and download maps for offline use, though interest in offline maps has waned as caching enables faster access to data. A broad range of navigation applications exists, with new versions continually being released. Major apps such as Google Maps Navigation, Apple Maps, and Waze rely on data connections for map content and live traffic information. By contrast, certain apps on specific platforms can operate offline by using locally cached maps; examples include iGo for Android, and Maverick and HERE for Windows Phone. Consequently, almost any smartphone can function as a personal navigation assistant.

Members of the National Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences (NARAS), including media companies and individual professionals, nominate recordings for consideration. Submissions are made online. For each submitted entry, review sessions are conducted with the participation of more than 150 recording industry experts, whose assessments determine that the work is entered in the correct category.

The Special Grammy Award of Merit is awarded occasionally by the Recording Academy to recognize ongoing contributions and influence in the recording field. It has been presented under different names at various ceremonies, including the Grammy Legend Award and the Grammy Living Legend Award. As of 2018, fourteen solo musicians and one band had received the award.

The Royal Dutch Football Association is the governing body for football in the Netherlands. Its official Dutch designation is Koninklijke Nederlandse Voetbalbond, abbreviated KNVB, with phonetic pronunciations provided for both the Dutch name and the acronym. The organization oversees the country’s main leagues—the Eredivisie and the Eerste Divisie—as well as the amateur leagues, and it administers the KNVB Cup. It also supervises the Dutch national teams for both men and women.

The Royal Dutch Football Association (KNVB) is the governing body of football in the Netherlands. It traces its origins to 1889 with the founding of the Nederlandse Voetbal en Athletiek Bond, and internal disagreements subsequently led to the formation of the Koninklijke Nederlandse Voetbalbond, which would later adopt the organization’s current title. The KNVB was a founding member of FIFA in 1904, making it one of the earliest non-British European football associations to join the international governing body. The Netherlands’ first football club had already been established in Haarlem in 1879, and the Netherlands Football League Championship existed unofficially for about a decade before the KNVB’s founding. In 1909 the federation took a firm stand against professionalism, vowing to protest by all means necessary. In 2012, the KNVB launched an 11-point plan titled “Football for Everyone” to encourage openly gay players to come out, complemented by a 30-second video, “Gay? It doesn’t matter,” prepared by broadcaster BNN and aired during the Netherlands’ World Cup qualifier against Andorra in October 2012.

British Standard Pipe employs parallel, non-tapered pipe threads. A pressure-tight joint is produced by compressing a soft sealing material, such as an O-ring or washer, between the end face of the male thread and the face of the mating socket or nipple. The seal is formed as the backnut is tightened, drawing the components together to compress the sealing element.

British Standard Pipe specifies thread forms used to join pipes in which a pressure-tight joint is produced by the engagement of a male and a female thread. The male thread is always tapered, while the female thread may be either parallel or tapered. In European practice, tapered female pipe threads are not commonly used.

On 11 June 2008, the building owner and InterContinental Hotels Group (IHG) reached an agreement to operate the InterContinental Hanoi Landmark 72, a 359-room hotel occupying nine floors from the 62nd to the 70th, with the Club Lounge located on the 71st floor.

AON Hanoi Landmark Tower is a multi-tower complex in Hanoi. By November 2010, the main tower had reached about 300 metres, becoming the tallest building and structure in Vietnam at that time. On 24 January 2011, the main tower topped out at 350 metres, the tallest building in the country, while the two additional towers had already reached 212 metres. The complex officially opened on 18 May 2012. It remained Vietnam’s tallest building until Landmark 81 surpassed it in 2018.

Following the 1954 Yangtze floods, planners advanced a set of ambitious flood-control schemes that would redefine the region's infrastructure and hydrology. The proposals included a bridge intended to span a deep gorge, creating a navigable thoroughfare for vessels. Upstream defenses, including stone walls to the west, were conceived to restrain rainfall associated with Wushan and thus reduce flood risk. The hydrological consequence envisioned was the creation of a smooth lake that would rise within the narrow gorges, signaling reservoir formation and substantial changes to watershed dynamics. Taken together, the plans would markedly alter both the landscape and water regimes, reflecting a scale of transformation not previously seen in the area. Symbolically, the project was framed with mythic imagery, suggesting the mountain goddess might marvel at the transformed world. The rhetoric employed a contrast between progress and inertia, with sails driven by the wind symbolizing advancement while a tortoise and snake remaining still signifying persistence or stagnation.

From June to September 1954, the Yangtze River floods primarily impacted Hubei Province in China as unusually heavy precipitation and a particularly long rainy season along the middle Yangtze in late spring contributed to the disaster. The river began rising above normal levels in late June, and three flood gates were opened to divert water. Nevertheless, flood levels continued to rise despite these mitigation efforts. Peak water levels reached 44.67 meters (146.6 feet) at Jingzhou, Hubei, and 29.73 meters (97.5 feet) in Wuhan. The disaster killed approximately 33,000 people, including deaths from plague in the aftermath.

An album's music is organized into units called tracks, each representing a distinct song or instrumental recording. In popular music, these tracks are commonly referred to as album tracks, a designation that also applies to EPs and singles. In older physical formats, track identification could be determined visually on vinyl by the grooves, and album sleeves or covers often displayed the track numbers for each side. On compact discs, tracks are indexed with numbers that enable players to jump directly to the start of a given track. In digital marketplaces such as iTunes, the term song is frequently used interchangeably with track, even when the recording contains no vocal content.

The long-playing disc, introduced by Columbia Records in 1948, arrived in 10-inch and 12-inch formats and was pressed on 33 1/3 rpm microgroove vinyl. Compared with the typical offerings on earlier 78 rpm records, a single LP generally carried a similar number of tracks, enabling a fuller listening experience within a single disc. The LP quickly became the standard format adopted by the recording industry for presenting albums. Since its introduction, the format has undergone only minor refinements, and the later incorporation of stereophonic sound, yet it has remained the prevailing medium for vinyl albums.

Kangwon Province is a province of North Korea located on the eastern side of the Korean Peninsula. It is bordered to the north by South Hamgyŏng, to the west by South P'yŏngan and North Hwanghae, and to the south by Kaesŏng. To the east it has a coastline along the Sea of Japan. Across the Korean Demilitarized Zone lie its South Korean counterparts, Gangwon Province and Gyeonggi Province.

Kangwŏn Province (North Korea) is part of the broader Gwandong region, a designation that also encompasses Gangwŏn Province. Geographically, the Taebaek Mountains serve as a natural divider within this region, with the western portion referred to as Yŏngsŏ and the eastern portion designated Yŏngdong.

San Juan del Sur is a coastal town and municipality in Nicaragua, with an estimated population of 15,553. Its economic and demographic profile includes many families engaged in fishing, tourism, or the food and beverage sector, and it hosts a notable presence of foreigners from the United States, Canada, and Europe. Over the past two decades, the local economy has shifted from fishing and shipping toward tourism. In October 2002, the community commemorated its 150th anniversary and was designated as the Port of San Juan del Sur and as a Tourism City of Nicaragua.

San Juan del Sur is a Pacific port town in Nicaragua. It has long been a focal point in both historic and contemporary proposals for a Nicaragua Canal. The site's appeal largely stems from its location on the narrow Isthmus of Rivas, which lies between the Pacific Ocean and Lake Nicaragua and offers a strategic crossing point that has shaped discussions about potential canal routes.

The XR-10 was a larger derivative of the XR-8, featuring twin engines mounted in nacelles on the sides of the fuselage, rotors driven by long driveshafts, and an all-metal skin. The first of two prototypes took to the air on 24 April 1947, and at that time was the largest rotorcraft to have flown in the United States. Early test flights revealed the same rotor-system problem encountered on the XR-8, with blades from the two rotors colliding in flight, though subsequent fixes allowed continued flight testing. On 3 October 1949, the first prototype was lost in a crash caused by a control-system failure, and Kellett's chief test pilot, Dave Driskill, was killed. The program was abandoned shortly afterward, and a 16-seat civil version, designated KH-2, remained only on drawing boards.

The Kellett XR-10 was a 1940s United States military transport helicopter designed by the company Kellett. It flew only in prototype form. It was conceived in response to a United States Army Air Forces directive seeking an enclosed-fuselage helicopter capable of transporting passengers, cargo, or wounded personnel. The XR-10 followed Kellett’s XR-8 layout and employed twin intermeshing rotors. The Air Force accepted the XR-10 on 16 October, ahead of competing proposals from Sikorsky, Bell, and Platt-LePage.

Bill Mack was a songwriter in the country music industry. His most famous composition is “Blue,” which LeAnn Rimes recorded, and the track earned the Grammy Award for Best Country Song in 1997. Mack also wrote “Drinking Champagne,” a song that has been recorded by a variety of artists; Cal Smith scored a 1968 hit with it, and George Strait included a version on his 1990 album Livin’ It Up, helping to keep the song in the public ear. Other notable artists who recorded Mack’s material include Dean Martin, Ray Price, Jerry Lee Lewis, and George Jones.

Bill Mack, a songwriter, hosted a radio program on WBAP. After his tenure, Eric Harley succeeded him as the host of the WBAP show. The program was subsequently renamed the Midnight Radio Network, and several years later it was rebranded again as Red Eye Radio.

The Red Rose of Lancaster is traditionally traced to Edward I’s gold rose badge, with his brother, the Earl of Lancaster, adopting a red variant. It is widely regarded as the Lancastrian emblem during the Wars of the Roses. Some lines of evidence point to land tenure records that require tenants to render an annual red rose for a manor held from Henry VI, suggesting a symbolic association with the house. Yet, scholars have questioned whether the red rose functioned as a definitive Lancastrian emblem in the fighting between houses. Historian Adrian Ailes argues that the red rose’s popular use was probably reinforced by Henry VII’s prompt response to the pre-existing Yorkist white rose, helping to shape Tudor-era symbolism.

In 1345, Edward III launched a three-pronged invasion of France, with the campaigns proceeding from Brittany, Flanders, and Aquitaine under the leadership associated with the Earl of Northampton, Edward, and Henry, respectively. Henry of Lancaster achieved a notable victory at the Battle of Auberoche against Comte d'Isle, an achievement regarded as Lancaster's greatest military success, and the campaign yielded a substantial prisoner ransom estimated at £50,000. In recognition of his leadership, Henry was named a founding knight of the Order of the Garter and was later elevated to the rank of Duke of Lancaster. The creation of the dukedom marked a relatively new ducal title in the realm, Cornwall having been the only prior duchy established. Additionally, Lancaster was granted palatinate authority over Lancashire, conferring a distinct administration independent of the Crown. Other palatine counties in England included Durham, an ancient ecclesiastical palatinate, and Chester, which was held as crown property.

On 14 June, the cruiser Yakumo was designated as the flagship for Vice Admiral Kataoka Shichirō, who commanded the Imperial Japanese Navy's Third Fleet. The assignment formed part of the operation to capture Sakhalin in July.

Yakumo's secondary armament consisted of twelve Elswick Pattern Z QF 6-inch guns of 40-caliber length, eight of which were mounted in armored casemates on the main and upper decks while the remaining four were placed on unarmored upper-deck mounts protected by gun shields. Each Pattern Z gun fired armor-piercing shells weighing 45.4 kilograms (100 pounds) at a muzzle velocity of about 700 meters per second, with a supply of 150 rounds per gun. In addition, the cruiser carried twelve 40-caliber QF 12-pounder 12-cwt guns for close-range defense, and eight QF 2.5-pounder Yamauchi guns provided further protection against torpedo boats at close range. The 12-pounder guns fired projectiles of 76 mm (3 in) diameter weighing 5.7 kilograms (12.5 pounds) at 719 meters per second.

Patrik Andersson is a Swedish former professional footballer who joined Bayern Munich in June 1999 for around DM 6 million. He made his debut on 22 August 1999 in a 2–0 away defeat to Bayer Leverkusen. During his time with Bayern, he helped the club secure two Bundesliga titles and was part of the squad that won the DFB-Pokal, as well as the UEFA Champions League in the 2000–01 season; in that campaign he scored his only goal for the club, a late and decisive strike against Hamburger SV, and he missed a penalty in the final shootout.

Patrik Andersson is a Swedish footballer who earned 96 caps and scored three goals for the national team. He was part of the Sweden squad that won bronze at the 1994 FIFA World Cup and contributed to the team's run to the Euro 1992 semi-finals. He was selected for Sweden's squads at Euro 2000 and the 2002 FIFA World Cup, and he also represented the nation at the 1992 Summer Olympics in Barcelona. At Euro 2000, Andersson received a red card for a foul on Bart Goor of Belgium. On the eve of Sweden’s opening match at the 2002 World Cup against England, he was injured in the final training session and did not play, with Andreas Jakobsson taking his place.

Paul IV pursued a notably stricter anti-Jewish policy than the comparatively lenient measures of the early sixteenth century, seeking to curb what he saw as excessive tolerance. In the Papal States, and especially in Ancona, Marranos benefited for a time from the protections of earlier popes such as Clement VII (1523–34), Paul III (1534–49), and Julius III (1550–55), who had affirmed papal authority over apostasy cases rather than local jurisdiction. Paul IV contended that this leniency had been exploited by Jewish communities and failed to bring about sufficient Christian conversions. Consequently, he imposed harsh restrictions and terminated all dispensations granted to Jews within the papal state, with the aim of coercing Jewish populations to convert.

In Sholem Asch's 1921 historical novel The Witch of Castile, Pope Paul IV is portrayed as a principal antagonist, his figure anchoring the narrative of Jewish oppression. The work is known in Yiddish as Di Kishufmakherin fun Kastilien and in Hebrew as Ha'Machshepha Mi'Castilia. Set in Rome, the story follows a young Sephardi Jewish woman who is falsely accused of witchcraft and burned at the stake, her death framed as that of a Jewish martyr. This depiction is presented within the context of Paul IV's actual persecution of Jews, aligning the fictional tragedy with historical persecutions during his papacy.

Lifelong learning refers to the ongoing pursuit of knowledge and skills across an individual’s life, encompassing formal and informal educational activities aimed at personal and professional development. Lifelong learning institutes are educational organizations dedicated to promoting lifelong learning and providing opportunities aligned with this objective. In addition to these organized institutions, informal lifelong learning communities exist around the world, enabling people to engage in learning through social networks and shared interests.

Lifelong learning is supported in some universities through formal administrative units dedicated to continuing education and related activities. For example, the Academy of Lifelong Learning functions as an administrative unit within the University of Delaware. In Poland, the Jagiellonian University Extension (Wszechnica Uniwersytetu Jagiellonskiego) is one of the most comprehensive centers for lifelong learning, with a focus that includes open learning, organizational learning, and community learning.

Under the May 1939 electoral law, the National Renaissance Front overhauled the franchise and the structure of representative institutions. The voting age was raised to thirty, and participation was conditioned on literacy and employment in one of three sectors: agriculture or manual labor, commerce or industry, or intellectual professions. Electoral districts were reduced to eleven, spanning the ten ținuturi and Bucharest. Senate eligibility was narrowed so that members could be elected only by high-ranking figures within corporations or guilds (bresle). The Senate’s composition was expanded with the creation of lifetime seats in addition to existing holders, and its new ranks included religious leaders and various members associated with the House of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen. A dedicated Senate seat was reserved for Mihai, the heir to the throne and, upon coming of age, the Grand-Voivode of Alba Iulia.

The National Renaissance Front (FRN), established under King Carol II of Romania, has been described as superficially fascist, if at all. It received endorsement from the United Kingdom and France as a defense line against Nazism in the Balkans, and the Western press was largely sympathetic toward the FRN. The organization adopted symbols and discourse associated with fascism. Beginning in January 1939, its members wore uniforms in navy blue or white and ceremonial headgear. The Roman salute was made a mandatory form of greeting within the movement.

Within blood typing, the Rh factor is indicated by a plus or minus suffix. The plus sign denotes the presence of the Rh factor, while the minus sign signifies its absence. For example, A+ denotes type A blood with the Rh factor present, and B− denotes type B blood without the Rh factor.

In various contexts, the terms positive and negative are frequently abbreviated as +ve and −ve, a shorthand that appears in technical and everyday usage. Similarly, batteries and cell terminals are commonly identified by the symbols + and − to indicate their polarity, facilitating correct connections and safe operation.

1987 (What the Fuck Is Going On?) is an album released independently by The JAMs in June 1987. After ABBA lodged a complaint, the Mechanical-Copyright Protection Society ordered the destruction of all unsold copies. In response, The JAMs destroyed a substantial portion of the album's copies through unconventional, highly publicized methods. They later issued 1987 (The JAMs 45 Edits), a version stripped of all unauthorized samples, which produced long silences and minimal audible content, and was formally released as a 12-inch single.

The album 1987 (What the Fuck Is Going On?) opens with the track "Hey Hey We Are Not The Monkees," which initiates with a sequence of simulated sexual noises arranged as rhythm, a texture Drummond described as "sampled breathing" sounds. The first sample is drawn from the Monkees' theme, incorporating the moment of their return. The piece then moves into a cryptic, bleak spoken passage by Drummond, beginning with imagery of emerging from mud and moving from chaos primeval toward a burnt-out sun, bearing only fragmentary rhymes to declare. A dense collage follows, mixing further samples from the Monkees' theme with continued vocal contributions from Drummond, including a self-deprecating remark about not being The Monkees. An original a cappella vocal line interrupts the sequence, later reappearing as part of The KLF's Justified and Ancient, and it conveys a claim of being justified and ancient while signaling a wish not to upset the existing order.

Hose (tubing) refers to flexible conduits used to convey liquids or gases under pressure or suction. Early examples were fashioned from natural materials such as leather, flax, and cotton, providing limited flexibility and chemical resistance. The Second World War stimulated industrial research and the development of synthetic rubber, which offered markedly better chemical resistance and durability for hose applications. In contemporary use, hoses are manufactured from a variety of materials including natural or synthetic rubber, canvas, and helically reinforced wire to provide strength and flexibility. Plastics such as polyvinyl chloride and polytetrafluoroethylene are also employed, offering chemical resistance and temperature performance advantages. For certain services involving cryogenic or low-temperature fluids, hoses are constructed from materials like stainless steel or polyethylene terephthalate, which maintain integrity at very low temperatures (e.g., liquid oxygen and liquid nitrogen).

A hose, also referred to as a hose-pipe, is a flexible hollow tube designed to convey fluids from one location to another. It serves as a portable conduit for liquids and is commonly connected to water sources such as a faucet or a hydrant to facilitate delivery.

LBC News expanded to 24-hour broadcasting on 28 October 2019, enabling continuous transmission across day and night. Previously, the service relayed LBC's programming during the evening and overnight periods. The hours from 23:00 to 06:00 are automated, with the schedule operated without live presentation.

By October 1994, London News Radio had undergone significant upheaval, having first acquired LBC and subsequently been bought by Reuters. At its launch on 5 October 1994, the organization operated under the name London Radio Services. It ran London News on 97.3 FM and London News Talk on 1152 AM. The service initially employed a 20-minute wheel schedule. The inaugural on-air team included Michael Wilson and Clare Catford, with Jonathan Staples presenting the morning sequence and Nicky Broyd handling the afternoon slot. Drivetime was presented by Christopher Terry and Brenda Ellison, while John Terrett served as the evening host.

The United States’ incursion into Cambodia sparked protests at home, and President Richard Nixon pledged to deescalate American involvement. In May 1970, the Kent State University protests culminated in National Guardsmen firing on demonstrators, killing four students and provoking renewed outrage. The administration’s response was widely perceived as callous, fueling the anti-war movement. Nevertheless, the United States continued bombing Cambodia as part of Operation Freedom Deal.

Opposition to the Vietnam War developed early and drew on critiques associated with the Geneva Conference, with critics arguing that Washington’s support for Ngo Dinh Diem and its rejection of elections undermined the democracy the United States professed to defend. As Kennedy served in the Senate, he spoke against deeper U.S. involvement, signaling internal dissent within American political leadership. The draft mobilized substantial protest among young people, helping the antiwar movement gain traction within the broader counterculture of the era. Within the peace movement, some advocates argued for unilateral U.S. withdrawal, while others united against what they viewed as American anti-communism and imperialism, bringing together groups such as the New Left. Individual proponents offered varied ethical foundations, including Stephen Spiro’s invocation of Just War theory to oppose the conflict. In addition, certain activists sought solidarity with the Vietnamese people, with Norman Morrison notably emulating Thích Quảng Đức in an act intended to highlight the war’s human costs.

VF Corporation is an American apparel and footwear company established in 1899 by John Barbey and based in Denver, Colorado. It was known as Vanity Fair Mills until 1969. The corporation oversees eleven brands that are organized into three product categories: Outdoor, Active, and Work.

VF Corporation announced in 2011 its plan to acquire Timberland for approximately $2.2 billion, with the transaction expected to close in September of that year. Subsequently, VF Imagewear was awarded a multimillion-dollar contract on December 21, 2012, to supply uniforms and insignia for officers of the U.S. Customs and Border Protection. In February 2013, the same unit received a $50 million contract to manufacture uniforms for Transportation Security Administration officers.

Truth is closely tied to human practices of inquiry and the pursuit of knowledge. For the American philosopher Charles Sanders Peirce, truth is the eventual outcome of inquiry—that is, the proposition that would be disclosed if inquiry were carried as far as it can profitably go. The core claim of this view is that truth is the opinion destined to be universally accepted by all investigators in the long run.

Truth, within the study of logic, concerns whether a given proposition correctly corresponds to the reasoning it expresses. Logicians analyze patterns in reasoning to determine the validity or truth of statements by examining the relationships between premises and conclusions and the broader implications of arguments. To facilitate precise analysis, they employ formal languages and symbolic frameworks that allow truths to be articulated and evaluated with rigor. In this view, truth is not absolute in a vacuum but is defined relative to an interpretation of the language or to the axioms and inference rules that govern a particular logical system.

In June 2007, two Herald Sun reporters, Michael Harvey and Gerard McManus, were found guilty of contempt of court in the Victorian County Court for refusing to disclose a confidential source. The case related to coverage of Australian Government plans to scale back proposed entitlements for veterans. The verdict sparked renewed debate and calls for reform of Australian law to introduce shield laws that would protect journalists' sources, a movement framed as aligning with professional journalistic ethics.

Following the 2016 Moomba Festival in Melbourne, the Herald Sun initiated a 32-month campaign that framed African communities, particularly Sudanese Australians, through a lens of criminality and alleged gang activity. While civic and state leaders, community members, and the police publicly denied the existence of such gangs, the newspaper maintained extensive coverage, publishing around 130 articles over two years that repeatedly used the terms Sudanese and gang. The publication also produced 173 references to a purported gang named Apex, including 37 editorials, despite limited supporting evidence. This persistent racialised and criminalising portrayal is credited with intensifying racism toward African Australians and creating numerous community difficulties. Academics describe the Herald Sun’s emphasis on crime within the Sudanese Australian community as contributing to a moral panic.

Tatai Wildlife Sanctuary is a protected area in southwest Cambodia that was established in 2016 and comprises about 144,275 hectares (356,510 acres) in the Cardamom Mountains. In 2021, a PADDD (Protected Area Downgrading, Downsizing and Degazettement) process reduced its extent by 26,103 hectares (64,500 acres). The sanctuary contends with ongoing threats including sand dredging and processing, filling of water bodies, and land grabbing. Local communities were displaced into the protected area after the 2014 construction of the 246 MW Stung Tatai hydropower dam by the China National Machinery Industry Corporation.

Tatai Wildlife Sanctuary, located in the Cardamom Mountains of southwestern Cambodia, has been identified as a potential site for tiger conservation and reintroduction efforts. In 2007, the last confirmed sighting of the Indochinese tiger in Cambodia was recorded when a camera trap captured images of the species within the country. By 2016, Cambodia had declared the tiger functionally extinct in the wild. In April 2023, India and Cambodia signed a memorandum of understanding to assist with tiger reintroduction initiatives. The proposed plan envisions reserving at least 90 acres (36 hectares) of the Cardamom rainforest to host Bengal tigers imported from India.

Johns-Manville suppressed a 1943 report that confirmed a link between asbestos exposure and cancer. In the 1960s, 1970s, and 1980s the company faced thousands of individual and class-action lawsuits alleging asbestos-related injuries, including asbestosis, lung cancer, and malignant mesothelioma. Many settlements during this period offered as little as $600 for asbestosis, whereas the FAIR Act proposed $12,000 for that condition.

Johns Manville emerged from Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in 1988 under the name Manville Corporation. In 1997 it reverted to Johns Manville, dropping the hyphen, and this is the name under which the company operates today. In 2001 it became a wholly owned subsidiary of Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE: BRK.A, BRK.B).

Tasty is BuzzFeed's video series devoted to comfort food, produced for Facebook, and by December 2019 it attracted about 100 million followers. The channel generates significantly more views than BuzzFeed's dedicated food site, reflecting its broad reach and engagement. It has given rise to five spin-off segments: Tasty Junior, which was spun off into its own page; Tasty Happy Hour, focusing on alcoholic beverages; Tasty Fresh; Tasty Vegetarian; and Tasty Story, in which celebrities prepare and discuss their own recipes. In addition to its video content, Tasty has released a cookbook.

In February 2015, BuzzFeed editor Cates Holderness became central to a viral discussion on Tumblr concerning the color of a dress. The post drew more than 28 million views in a single day and established a record for the most concurrent visitors to a BuzzFeed post. The episode began when Holderness showed the dress to BuzzFeed's social media team, who argued about its colors, prompting the creation of a simple poll to gauge user opinion. Holderness left work and took the subway to Brooklyn, and on arriving home found her phone overwhelmed with messages as Twitter began to crash, leading her to fear that someone might have died. Later that evening, the page set a new concurrent-visitor record, reaching a peak of 673,000.

Following his death, the autopsy was performed by A. Quinn Strobl, and Prince’s remains were cremated.
