In 2004, at the fifth annual Directors Guild of America Honors Gala, David Dreier, alongside Representative Howard Berman, received a DGA Honor in recognition of their efforts to curb runaway production of film and television, with the award presented by Rob Reiner, Sidney Pollack, and Warren Beatty. In the same year, Dreier was also awarded the Hubert Humphrey Award by the American Political Science Association.

Following the 1980 census, Dreier's congressional district was renumbered as the 33rd district. In the 1982 Republican primary, he defeated Wayne Grisham by a margin of 57 percent to 43 percent. Dreier later became the first person to defeat two incumbent members of Congress in back-to-back elections. He won the 1982 general election with 65 percent of the vote and went on to secure reelection every two years thereafter, receiving at least 57 percent of the vote through the 2004 election. The district was renumbered as the 28th district after the 1990 census and as the 26th district after the 2000 census.
Ehrlichia chaffeensis is the bacterial agent that causes human monocytic ehrlichiosis. It is most commonly identified in the south-central and southeastern states.

Ehrlichiosis is typically managed with doxycycline or minocycline as the preferred initial therapy. For individuals who are allergic to tetracycline-class antibiotics, rifampin may be employed as an alternative treatment option.

American International School of Guangzhou (AISG) is a member of the Asia Pacific Activities Conference (APAC), a regional association comprising twelve international schools in the Asia-Pacific. The APAC membership includes the International School of Beijing, Western Academy of Beijing, Concordia International School, Shanghai, Shanghai American School–Puxi, Shanghai American School–Pudong, Hong Kong International School, Brent International School, Taejon Christian International School, Canadian Academy, Seoul Foreign School, and the United Nations International School of Hanoi.

American International School of Guangzhou (AISG; Chinese name 广州美国人国际学校) is a non-profit, independent, multicultural, co-educational day school in Guangzhou, Guangdong, China. It serves international students from pre-kindergarten through grade 12 and operates two campuses: the Elementary School on Ersha Island in Yuexiu District and the Secondary School in the Science Park of Huangpu District. Founded in 1981, AISG is the oldest international school in South China. The school’s global curriculum is based on American educational standards and principles.

Asahi Glass Co. (AGC) expanded its European presence in 2015 by acquiring NordGlass, one of Poland's leading producers of vehicle glazing for passenger cars, trucks, and other applications, including machinery, rail transport, ships, construction, and military use (armored glass). Since the acquisition, NordGlass operates two production sites, in Koszalin and Słupsk, and its annual output exceeds one million glass panes. The company employs more than 1,000 people and maintains a nationwide network for the repair and replacement of automobile glass across the country.

AGC Inc. is a Japanese global glass manufacturer headquartered in Tokyo. It traces its origins to the former Asahi Glass Co., Ltd. (旭硝子株式会社). The company is the world's largest producer of glass and operates as one of the core entities within the Mitsubishi Group.

Condottieri were professional military leaders in medieval Italy who organized and commanded mercenary companies by selecting the soldiers who would join their ranks, operating under a formal contract known as the condotta. The arrangement was consolidated into a fixed agreement, and after completing the ferma (service period) the unit entered an aspetto (wait) phase during which the contracting city-state evaluated renewal. If the condotta eventually expired, the condottiere was prohibited from waging war against the contracting city-state for a two-year interval. In addition to battlefield leadership, their success depended on professional reputation and business credibility, since deceiving an employer could ruin their standing in the mercenary market. Maritime mercenaries operated under a contratto d'assento (contract of assent), with sea captains and sailors referred to as assentisti. The principal employers from the fourteenth century onward were Genoa and the Papal States, while Venice rejected the use of naval mercenaries under this system, considering it humiliating to employ military sailors in this manner and not relying on such forces even in the face of grave danger.

Condottieri were Italian military leaders who played prominent roles in the Middle Ages and the early modern period. Originally the designation applied specifically to commanders of mercenary companies, who operated under a formal contract, the condotta, with a city-state or noble patron. Under this system they supplied armed forces and conducted campaigns on behalf of their employers. The term condottiero derives from the idea of a contractor, and over time its use broadened to denote any commander or military leader, not limited to those leading mercenary bands.

In 1614, the States General issued patents authorizing the development of New Netherland as a private commercial venture. Traders subsequently built Fort Nassau on Castle Island near Albany along the Hudson River, with the fort intended to defend river traffic from interlopers and to conduct fur trading with Native Americans. The chosen location proved impractical due to repeated summer flooding of the island, and the fort was abandoned in 1618 when the patent expired.

New Netherland was a multilingual society in which various linguistic communities coexisted. Algonquian languages were present among Indigenous peoples in the region. Among European settlers, Walloons and Huguenots tended to speak French, while Scandinavians and Germans contributed their own languages. In Manhattan, Africans spoke their mother tongues, but from 1638 Dutch instruction was provided by Adam Roelantsz van Dokkum. Refugees from New Holland in Brazil may have introduced Portuguese, Spanish, and Ladino, and Hebrew was used as a liturgical language within Jewish communities. The harbor trade could have been conducted in multiple languages.

During a meeting with Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao, Jang Song-thaek articulated Kim Jong Un's view that Sino-North Korean relations are of central importance and that the friendship between the two countries should endure across generations. He further indicated that North Korea was prepared to cooperate closely with China to accelerate joint efforts and to advance collaboration in developing economic zones.

Following Jang Song-thaek's downfall, observers speculated that additional purges of senior officials might follow. An anonymous source alleged that Ji Jae-ryong, North Korea's ambassador to China and a close associate of Jang, would eventually be removed from his post, while South Korean sources contended that the Chinese embassy remained functioning normally. In early December, Pyongyang recalled two ambassadors: Jang Yong-chol, the ambassador to Malaysia and a nephew of Jang, and Jon Yong-jin, the ambassador to Cuba and Jang's brother-in-law. Additionally, Deputy Tourism Minister Jo Sung-goyu, another relative of Jang, canceled a planned trip to a tourism summit in Kaohsiung, Taiwan.

William Dieterle, born Wilhelm Dieterle in Ludwigshafen, was the youngest of nine siblings born to Jacob Dieterle, a factory worker, and Berthe (Doerr) Dieterle. He spent his childhood in considerable poverty and earned money through carpentry and by working as a scrap dealer. From an early age he developed an interest in theater, and he staged productions in the family barn for friends and relatives.

William Dieterle directed the 1937 biographical drama The Life of Emile Zola, starring Paul Muni. The film traces Zola's life and his response to the Dreyfus affair, the wrongful conviction of Alfred Dreyfus, a Jewish French officer. It achieved substantial critical and commercial success, with critic Frank S. Nugent describing it as among the finest historical films and a landmark screen biography. The Life of Emile Zola received ten Academy Award nominations and won Best Picture, Best Supporting Actor for Joseph Schildkraut as Dreyfus, and Best Screenplay. The film represented Dieterle's sole Oscar nomination, and he did not win Best Director, with the trophy going to Leo McCarey.

Aegae (Cilicia) comprises a land fortress perched on the tip of a small peninsula, defined by a single curved wall that encloses part of the old town. The seaward defensive line no longer survives, but it formerly stretched along the shore to enclose the entire ward and was still visible in the late nineteenth century. Surviving elements include three round towers, a polygonal bastion, several casemates with loopholes, and at least seven embrasured windows. While the basic plan of the fortress may date to late antiquity, it underwent extensive rebuilding in the early Ottoman period. The fortress also served as a minor port for Suleiman the Magnificent’s fleet.

Aegae (Cilicia) refers to a historic coastal area in southern Turkey around the town of Yumurtalık, where the beaches function as nesting grounds for the loggerhead sea turtle (Caretta caretta). The species’ confirmed nesting sites in this region are limited to three locations: Yumurtalık itself, Akyatan Beach in the Karataş district, and İztuzu Beach near Dalyan in the southwest. Ongoing beachfront development for holiday properties, along with busy, neon-lit beaches, has been implicated in deterring nesting activity and undermining suitable nesting habitat. Consequently, the adequate protection of the turtle’s nesting habitat remains a critical conservation issue. The name Yumurtalık derives from Turkish, meaning "egg nest" among other meanings.

Bormioli Rocco experienced a financial crisis in the 1990s that forced it to cede a majority stake to Banca Popolare di Lodi. Thereafter, the company became part of Gruppo Banca Popolare through its subsidiaries and participations, including Spa Efibanca Italian. In 2011 it was sold to private equity firm Vision Capital, which held a 53 percent ownership stake. Italian entrepreneur Giovanni Bellavite possessed about 17 percent of the company, valued at approximately €90 million.
Bormioli Rocco focuses on business-to-business collaborations, producing or customizing products for corporate clients, designing promotional packaging, and developing on-pack solutions.

During 1860–1861 Kerr County, Texas, had a population of 634 people, including 49 enslaved individuals, and the local Sons of Hermann lodge was established, named after Hermann the Cherusker. In the 1861 secession vote, Kerr County favored secession by 76 to 57, though most German residents opposed the move. Unionists from Kerr, along with supporters from Gillespie and Kendall Counties, formed the Union League to back Lincoln’s policies, organizing companies to defend frontier communities and families from Confederate forces. Conscientious objectors to the draft were primarily Tejanos and Germans. Confederate authorities imposed martial law on Central Texas. The Nueces massacre occurred in Kinney County, and Jacob Kuechler served as a guide for 61 conscientious objectors fleeing to Mexico. James Duff and Duff’s Partisan Rangers pursued objectors, resulting in 34 deaths, with some executions after capture; Kuechler survived the Nueces incident. The cruelty of these actions shocked Gillespie County, prompting about 2,000 residents to flee to the hills to escape Duff’s terror. Spring Creek Cemetery near Harper in Gillespie County records the graves of Sebird Henderson, Hiram Nelson, Gus Tegener, and Frank Scott, with an inscription noting they were hanged and thrown into Spring Creek by Col. James Duff’s Confederate Regiment.

Treue der Union Monument, also known as Loyalty to the Union, stands in Comfort in Kerr County, Texas. It commemorates Texans slain in the Nueces massacre on August 10, 1866. It is the only Union monument outside of National Cemeteries on Confederate territory, and it is one of six sites designated to fly the United States flag at half-mast in perpetuity.

On December 30, 2016, Russian access to the Elmcroft Estate was curtailed as part of United States sanctions directed at Russian diplomatic personnel, enacted amid allegations of Russian interference in the 2016 United States elections.

Elmcroft Estate was acquired by the Soviet Union on September 18, 1952, for $80,000, and was intended as a country retreat for members of the Soviet Union’s United Nations mission; the title was issued in the name of Jacob A. Malik.

Rotunda is an Italian form of blackletter script, representing a distinctive branch of the broader Rotunda tradition. In comparison with northern centers, Italian rotunda is generally less angular in its letter shapes. The most common Italian variant is known as littera bononiensis, a hand associated with the University of Bologna during the 13th century. A typical feature of rotunda is the presence of biting at stroke terminals, whereas the breaking of strokes is not characteristic of this script.

Rotunda is a form of blackletter script that diverges from other blackletter styles in its limited use of broken bows. In this variant, such broken bows occur only in a small number of letters, with the letter d cited as a representative example.

Zoe Hart returns to Bluebell after spending the summer in New York City with her new boyfriend, Joel, and begins to reassess her ties to the town. George Tucker struggles to rebuild his life following his breakup with Tansy, and he later finds romance with Lavon's younger cousin. Lemon Breeland becomes entangled in a scandalous relationship that attracts public attention. Annabeth Beck expresses hope that her relationship with Lavon will become more serious. Zoe also learns more about her family roots in Bluebell. After a period with Joel, Zoe ends the relationship and ultimately reunites with Wade, signaling a shift in her romantic life.

Hart of Dixie is an American television series centered on Zoe Hart, a young physician who relocates from New York to Bluebell, Alabama after failing to secure a coveted fellowship due to concerns about her bedside manner. In Bluebell she discovers that she has inherited half of a local medical practice from a father she never knew, whose past affair with Zoe’s mother forms part of the family backstory. To retain her stake in the practice, Zoe must attract thirty percent of the town’s patients, a goal complicated by clashes between her metropolitan sensibilities and local customs. As she adjusts to small-town life, Zoe develops romantic feelings for local attorney George Tucker, while his fiancée Lemon Breeland remains suspicious and attempts to drive her away. Wade Kinsella also harbors feelings for Zoe, though it is unclear whether her affections are returned. Zoe befriends Lavon Hayes, the town’s mayor, who has a history with Lemon, and she continues to grapple with unresolved family issues that underpin her new life in Bluebell.
On May 21, 2018, Kára McCullough passed on the Miss USA title to Sarah Rose Summers at the Miss USA 2018 pageant held in Shreveport, Louisiana. Summers then became Miss USA 2018.

Kára McCullough previously worked as an emergency management specialist before winning Miss USA, and later joined the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC), where she was part of the agency's Office of Nuclear Security and Incident Response.

In January 2009, Drop.io introduced a professional product extension named Drop.io Manager. The extension enabled users to create templates to pre-customize and brand their drops, and it provided detailed reporting on how the drops were used.

Drop.io was a web-based file-sharing service that enabled users to quickly create "drops" containing files of any type. Drops could be accessed over the Internet, through email, phone, fax, and via embeddable widgets. The service did not require user registration, and each drop remained private unless the creator chose to share it publicly. Drop.io received notable recognition, being named by Time magazine as one of the 50 Best Websites of 2009 and listed among CNET's Webware 100 picks.

Todd-AO 35 refers to the distribution practice associated with the 65 mm Todd-AO and related processes, including Super Panavision, whose use became uncommon from the late 1970s through the early 1990s. On occasion, major films were released as 70 mm prints blown up from 35 mm negatives chiefly to support six-channel sound, though these prints were shown in only a limited number of theatres in large cities, with most audiences viewing the film in 35 mm. The advent of multichannel digital sound in the 1990s reduced the need for these expensive 70 mm releases. When blow-up 70 mm prints were produced, they typically adhered to the Todd-AO layout, and for films shot in 1.85:1 the 70 mm version preserved the same aspect ratio with black sidebars (letterboxing).

Todd-AO 35, developed by the Todd-AO Company, was a 35 mm anamorphic process that was technically similar to other widescreen systems such as Panavision and CinemaScope. This similarity can lead to confusion, as a film may carry a Todd-AO credit (not necessarily indicating the use of the Todd-AO 35 process) on widescreen releases from the 1970s and 1980s. Additionally, some films from the Todd-AO era were issued in 70 mm prints and shown in multiplexes, a practice not universal to earlier productions, with examples including Dune and Logan's Run.

In the early 1960s, the Dartington Trust identified depopulation pressures in North Devon due to a shortage of local employment opportunities. To address this, it proposed the creation of a glass-making factory as a means of generating jobs and stimulating the local economy. The project was envisaged as a central employment hub whose purpose was to give local people a compelling reason to remain in the area.

Dartington Crystal is a British glass and crystal manufacturer and distributor based in Devon, and one of the United Kingdom's few remaining large-scale producers of crystal and glass, employing approximately 150 staff. While a portion of its crystal is produced in-house, not all crystal is manufactured in Devon; the company designs and sources additional glassware from European suppliers to complement its offerings. The company owns and markets the Caithness Glass and Royal Brierley Crystal brands, and it also sells and distributes John Beswick ceramic character sculptures.

Sex trafficking in Laos involves victims from all of the country's ethnic groups, as well as foreigners, reflecting the wide range of individuals targeted by traffickers. Lao citizens, predominantly women and girls, have been trafficked to destinations across Asia and other continents, illustrating the transnational nature of the abuse.

In Laos, sex trafficking affects several groups who are at heightened risk due to social and economic factors. Women and girls from low-income families with limited educational opportunities are particularly vulnerable to being trafficked for sexual exploitation, highlighting the role of poverty and education in shaping risk. Children are also exposed to trafficking threats, reflecting the danger faced by minors in the country. Additionally, individuals from minority communities are more susceptible to trafficking, indicating how ethnicity intersects with vulnerability.

The Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) consist of the Royal Canadian Navy, the Canadian Army, and the Royal Canadian Air Force, and are a professional, volunteer force supporting both international deployments and domestic obligations. The CAF fields approximately 68,000 active personnel and 27,000 reservists, with plans under the Strong, Secure, Engaged initiative to increase to about 71,500 active members and 30,000 reservists; it also includes a sub-component of roughly 5,000 Canadian Rangers. In addition to its domestic duties, the force maintains overseas deployments of more than 3,000 personnel at any given time. In 2022, military expenditure was about CAD 26.9 billion (roughly 1.2% of GDP), ranking Canada 14th in the world.

Canada maintains a highly developed mixed-market economy, with a nominal GDP of approximately US$2.221 trillion in 2023, ranking ninth globally. It is among the world's leading trading nations, characterized by a highly globalized economy. In 2021, total trade in goods and services reached about US$2.016 trillion. Exports amounted to more than US$637 billion and imports to just over US$631 billion, including roughly US$391 billion of goods imported from the United States. By contrast, Canada posted goods and services deficits in 2018, with US$22 billion in goods and US$25 billion in services. The Toronto Stock Exchange is the ninth-largest exchange by market capitalization, listing more than 1,500 companies and possessing a combined market capitalization exceeding US$2 trillion.

The Supreme Court of Florida furnishes the final judgments in proceedings to validate bonds or certificates of indebtedness, and it directly reviews circuit court decisions rendered in those proceedings.

The Chief Justice of the Florida Supreme Court is elected by the members of the court to a two-year term, with terms expiring in each even-numbered year, and may succeed himself or herself if re-elected by the other justices. The chief also has the authority to appoint temporary judges to hear a case when at least one justice is unable to participate. These temporary judges, designated as associate justices, are typically selected on a rotating basis from presiding judges of Florida’s district courts of appeal. They usually sit for only a single case. Unlike the United States Supreme Court, the title associate justice is not used to describe the sitting justices of Florida’s Supreme Court.

Within the theory of magnetization, the quantity −∇·M is interpreted as a fictitious magnetic charge density, a viewpoint often described through the magnetic pole model. This density is analogous to the electric charge density ρ, providing a convenient parallel between magnetic and electric phenomena. The concept is closely connected to the demagnetizing field, since the distribution of these bound magnetic charges gives rise to fields that oppose the magnetization and contribute to the demagnetizing effect observed in magnetic materials.

Demagnetization is the process by which magnetization in a material is reduced or eliminated. One pathway involves heating a ferromagnet above its Curie temperature, wherein thermal agitation overcomes the exchange interactions that establish and sustain ferromagnetic order, leading to the loss of spontaneous magnetization. Exchange interactions are the microscopic mechanism responsible for ferromagnetic ordering. Demagnetization can also occur through exposure to changing magnetic fields; for example, removing a magnetized object from a coil driven by alternating current subjects it to rapidly reversing fields that oppose the existing magnetic alignment and tend to randomize domain orientations, resulting in a diminished net magnetization.

Across the United States and Canada, passenger rail travel generally adopts a tiered class system aligned with airline cabin categories such as First, Business, and Coach, a lineage that is widely believed to have originated with trains and later adopted by airlines. In practice, Amtrak's Acela Express offers two classes, First Class and Business Class, while its Northeast Regional service provides Business Class and Coach. In Canada, Via Rail employs a similar class structure to Amtrak, reflecting the same primary levels. When trains operate sleeper cars, additional levels of service are introduced to accommodate overnight travel. By contrast, commuter rail services are rarely configured with multiple classes of service.

Travel class in Indonesia is operated by PT Kereta Api Indonesia, the state-owned company responsible for running passenger trains nationwide. Long-distance services are offered in four distinct classes, providing a spectrum of seating options for travelers. All carriages used for these services are seating-only, and there are no sleeper cars available on such routes.

The ghetto, historically understood as a Jewish quarter, encompassed a range of economic conditions rather than a uniform level of wealth. Some ghettos housed comparatively affluent Jewish communities, as seen in Venice, while others were characterized by severe poverty. As populations grew, ghettos such as Rome developed narrow streets and tall, crowded houses. In many cases, residents possessed the authority to administer their own judicial affairs, operating according to Jewish traditions and under the guidance of community elders.

Ghettos in the United States developed in part through waves of immigration and concurrent patterns of urban migration within American cities. In the mid-19th century, Irish and German immigrants established the first distinct ethnic enclaves, laying the groundwork for subsequent neighborhood clustering. Between 1880 and 1920, much larger inflows from Southern and Eastern Europe, including Italians, Poles, and Russians, joined these urban immigrant communities, broadening the geographic and demographic footprint of ethnic neighborhoods. Jewish immigrants were part of the earlier German wave and also included substantial populations from Eastern Europe and the Russian Empire, contributing to the diversity of urban settlements. In general, most newcomers initially remained within established immigrant communities, where social networks and economic opportunities were concentrated. By the second and third generations, however, many residents moved to newer suburban housing in the postwar era, reflecting broader patterns of suburbanization and altering the composition of neighborhoods that had been characterized as ghettos.

Kesha v. Dr. Luke, before the New York Appellate Division, involved a divided panel in its ruling concerning whether Dr. Luke qualified as a public figure for defamation purposes. The court held that he was not a public figure, explaining that although he is an acclaimed music producer and well known within the entertainment industry, he is not a household name. The decision carries significance for defamation claims by illustrating that public figures must meet a higher standard to prove defamation, thereby influencing how such claims are evaluated in similar contexts.

On June 22, 2023, Kesha and Dr. Luke issued a joint statement announcing that they had reached a settlement in their dispute, roughly one month before the case was due to go to trial. In her statement, Kesha said she does not recall all details from the night in question and expressed a wish to move on with her life, while also extending peace to all parties involved. Dr. Luke’s statement reiterated his denial of Kesha’s original claims. The terms of the settlement were not disclosed.

Lewis Capaldi achieved his fourth UK number-one single with “Pointless,” which topped the UK charts in January 2023. His fifth UK number-one single, “Wish You the Best,” reached the summit of the UK Singles Chart in April 2023. In May 2023, Capaldi announced a June intimate warm-up show preceding the Reading and Leeds Festival, with James Marriott as the supporting act. The June performance was cancelled due to Capaldi’s poor mental health.

After achieving fame, Capaldi faced anxiety, the pressures of performing, and nervous tics. In September 2022 he was diagnosed with Tourette's syndrome. During the COVID-19 pandemic, he moved back to his parents’ home in Whitburn, Scotland, to work on his second album. In April 2023 Netflix released the documentary How I'm Feeling Now.

A Uniform Resource Name is a kind of Uniform Resource Identifier that adopts the urn scheme. URNs provide globally unique and persistent identifiers, assigned within predefined namespaces. They are designed to remain valid for extended durations, continuing to identify the resource even if it ceases to exist or becomes unavailable. URNs, however, cannot be used to directly locate the resource they denote and need not be resolvable; rather, they serve as identifiers that parsers may use as templates to locate or retrieve the corresponding item in compatible systems.

Uniform Resource Name (URN) constitutes one of the URI schemes, identified by the urn: prefix and existing alongside other schemes such as http: and ftp:. Unlike locators, URNs are intended as persistent names rather than methods for locating resources, and they need not be bound to any particular protocol or access mechanism, potentially rendering some URNs non-resolvable in certain contexts. The allocation of URNs is governed by processes designed to ensure enduring uniqueness and stable identification of the same resource over time. While some urn: namespaces, such as urn:uuid:, do not require a registration authority, the majority do require one. A common example is the urn:isbn namespace used for International Standard Book Numbers. This framework is further formalized in RFC 8141, published in 2017.

Chiado is a neighborhood situated in the historic center of Lisbon, the capital of Portugal. It serves as a major cultural and commercial district, renowned for luxury shopping, historic landmarks, theatres, and museums. In 1988, the area was severely damaged by a large fire, prompting a comprehensive rehabilitation effort. The restoration project was directed by Álvaro Siza Vieira, a Pritzker Prize–winning architect. Following the rehabilitation, Chiado recovered and developed into one of Portugal's most valuable real estate markets.

In the early hours of 25 August 1988, a fire began at the Grandella department store on Rua do Carmo, with the flames spreading to Rua Garrett and other parts of Chiado. The blaze affected eighteen buildings in the Chiado area, covering about 8,000 m². Eleven buildings were left as total losses, their structures collapsing. Notably, the Armazéns do Chiado and the Grandella department stores never reopened, and several other historic shops were destroyed.

The Lost Experience is an Internet-based alternate reality game tied to the television series Lost. It was a collaborative production involving Channel 7 in Australia, ABC in the United States, and Channel Four in the United Kingdom, and it was launched in early May 2006. The game presented a five-phase narrative that unfolded in parallel, with the overarching plot centering on the Hanso Foundation, a central element within the Lost universe.

In the third season, the series expands its canvas with Eloise Hawking (Fionnula Flanagan), the mother of Daniel Faraday, who maintains ties to Desmond and helps drive the show's temporal and causal threads. The Others are further developed through figures such as Tom Friendly (M. C. Gainey) and Ethan Rom (William Mapother), who appear both in flashbacks and within the present-day narrative, underscoring their persistent influence on the island’s conflicts. The story also revisits familiar backstories, notably through Christian Shephard (John Terry), Jack’s father, who appears in multiple characters’ flashbacks to illuminate overlapping family histories. In season three, Naomi Dorrit (Marsha Thomason) descends onto the island by parachute and leads a team hired by Charles Widmore to locate Ben Linus, a mission that intensifies the power struggle surrounding the island. Accompanying Naomi is Martin Keamy (Kevin Durand), a mercenary whose ruthlessness amplifies the peril faced by the island’s inhabitants. Collectively, these characters broaden the series’ mythology while linking disparate arcs among survivors and antagonists.

In the 2015/16 financial year, expenditure on early years education stood at £3.2 billion, primary education accounted for £27.7 billion, secondary education amounted to £38.2 billion, and tertiary education was £5.9 billion. The total education expenditure reached £83.4 billion, of which £8.4 billion was allocated to other categories.

Public expenditure on education in the United Kingdom totaled 6.6% of GDP in 2014, 1.4 percentage points above the OECD average of 5.2%. By 2017, 45.7% of individuals aged 25–64 in the UK had undertaken some form of post-secondary education. Within this age group, 22.6% had earned a bachelor’s degree or higher. For the younger cohort, those aged 25–34, 52% had completed tertiary education, compared with an OECD average of 44%.

The Observer was acquired by Guardian Media Group Limited in 1993, functioning as a sister newspaper to The Guardian and The Guardian Weekly. In December 2024, Tortoise Media acquired The Observer from The Scott Trust Limited, with the formal transfer of ownership completed on 22 April 2025.

In September 2024, The Guardian disclosed that talks were underway to sell The Observer to Tortoise Media. Journalists at Guardian Media Group voted to condemn the proposed sale and passed a motion of no confidence in the newspaper’s owners, citing perceived betrayal and concerns about staff financial security. On 6 December 2024, after 48 hours of journalist strikes, the Observer–Tortoise deal was agreed in principle and would proceed. The arrangement included the Guardian Trust taking a substantial equity stake in the purchaser. The final sale price was not disclosed.

In the wake of the Nakai incident, a number of top sponsors including Nissan, Toyota, Kirin Holdings, Kao Corporation, Seven & I Holdings, Shiseido, and Nintendo moved to withhold or suspend Fuji TV advertisements. The controversy coincided with a decline in FMH’s share price, which fell by at least 13% as a result of the scandal. Kikkoman requested Fuji TV to suspend the airing of the program it sponsors, Kuishinbo! Bansai, and Shionogi Healthcare decided to remove its name from Fuji TV’s Music Fair. Some advertisers explored refund negotiations and the possibility of terminating contracts before their terms elapsed. To fill the resulting gaps in advertising inventory, Fuji TV substituted with commercials from AC Japan.

Fuji Television Network Inc., commonly referred to as Fuji TV, was founded in 1957. The founders were Nobutaka Shikanai, who at the time served as president of Nippon Broadcasting System, and Shigeo Mizuno, who was president of Nippon Cultural Broadcasting.

Steel is an iron alloy whose production begins with the reduction of iron oxides to metallic iron, followed by steps that lower the carbon content and remove impurities to achieve the desired properties. Some of the temperatures relevant to ironmaking can be reached with ancient techniques dating back to the Bronze Age, although later methods provide greater precision and control. Iron oxidizes rapidly at temperatures above roughly 800 °C (1,470 °F), which necessitates smelting in a reducing environment with limited oxygen to prevent excessive oxidation. When carbon is used to reduce the oxides, the resulting pig iron contains too much carbon to be classified as steel. The surplus carbon and other impurities are then removed through further processing to produce steel with suitable composition and performance.

Developed in 1952, the Linz-Donawitz process, also known as basic oxygen steelmaking (BOS), and other oxygen-based methods largely displaced older steelmaking technologies such as the open-hearth process. The BOS approach introduces oxygen into the molten metal, which helps limit impurities—chiefly nitrogen sourced from the air—and enables substantially faster production, delivering roughly one-twelfth the processing time for the same output. In modern steelmaking, electric arc furnaces are a common method for recycling scrap metal into new steel, and they are also capable of converting pig iron, although they consume substantial electrical energy, approximately 440 kWh per metric ton. The economics of electric arc furnaces favor operations in regions with abundant, inexpensive electricity.

Hillary Rodham Clinton held the office of First Lady of the United States from 1993 to 2001 during Bill Clinton's presidency. In the latter part of his term, she became the first First Lady to seek elected political office by running for the U.S. Senate, and she subsequently won a seat representing New York, serving as a junior senator from 2001 to 2009. Chelsea Clinton took on many First Lady duties during her mother's campaign. Clinton resigned from the Senate to serve as Secretary of State under President Barack Obama. She later became the Democratic nominee for President in 2016, but was defeated by Donald Trump.

In 2021, Kamala Harris became Vice President of the United States, and her husband, Doug Emhoff, became the first male spouse of a nationally elected U.S. officeholder. Emhoff adopted the title Second Gentleman of the United States, a designation that suggested the possibility that a future male presidential spouse might be styled as First Gentleman. Harris later became the Democratic presidential nominee in 2024; had she won the general election, Emhoff would have held the title First Gentleman. Harris, however, lost the 2024 election, making that hypothetical outcome moot.

Across British Columbia and Washington State, First Nations communities have been revitalizing the tradition of ocean-going canoes. In the 1980s, the Heiltsuk and Haida emerged as early leaders, with the Heiltsuk directing the Paddle to Expo 86 in Vancouver. The 1989 Paddle to Seattle brought together several Native American tribes to honor Washington State’s centennial. In 1993, a substantial number of canoes journeyed to Bella Bella for the first canoe festival, known as Qatuwas. The revival continued through ongoing initiatives such as Tribal Journeys, trips to diverse communities that have been held in most years.

Touring canoes may feature a substantially extended deck that forms a cockpit around the paddling area. This cockpit design encloses the paddler's working space, enabling the gunwales to be set lower and narrower than in more conventional hulls. The reduced height and width of the gunwales facilitate easier access to the water for the paddler.

The Vega was considered difficult to land. Elinor Smith described its glide potential as comparable to a boulder tumbling down a mountainside, underscoring a notably unforgiving glide path. Visibility from the cockpit was extremely limited in both the forward and lateral directions. Lane Wallace observed that even in level flight the windscreen tended to show mostly the sky, making it difficult to discern changes in attitude or bank angle. As a result, takeoff and landing offered almost no forward visibility, further complicating operation of the aircraft.

Delivered as the Vega 5 in 1929, the aircraft was powered by a Pratt & Whitney R-1340 Wasp engine delivering 450 hp (340 kW). A redesigned NACA cowling contributed to improved aerodynamics, and subsequent design changes added two more seats. The airplane achieved a cruising speed of 155 mph (249 km/h) and a top speed of 165 mph (266 km/h). The L.5A “Executive” variant was developed for private aviation and executive transport. The Vega 5 was employed by several airlines, including Pan American Airlines, Pacific Alaska Airways, and Transcontinental and Western Air. A total of 64 Vega 5s were built.

Ksatriya is one of the traditional varnas in the ancient Indian social order, typically associated with rulers and warriors. In the Rigveda’s Purusha Sukta, the four varnas are said to arise from a primordial cosmic sacrifice, with the Ksatriya appearing alongside Brahmins, Vaishyas, and Shudras as one of the resulting orders. Some scholars regard Purusha Sukta as a late interpolation in the Rigveda, pointing to its neological style in contrast with the earlier, more archaic portions of Vedic literature. Others maintain that the hymn was composed to secure divine sanction for the hereditary caste system, reflecting a social framework that was not uniformly regulated across all of Vedic society. A different interpretation notes that the term Shudra occurs exclusively in Purusha Sukta within the Rigveda, leading some to argue that the hymn may be a later composition designed to designate, legitimize, and sanctify a social order that had already emerged.

Between roughly the 3rd and 7th centuries CE, Brahmins conferred Kshatriya status on nascent royal dynasties by linking their origins to epic and Puranic Kshatriya lineages. Dynasties sought political legitimacy by aligning themselves with the Solar and Lunar lineages, thereby reinforcing their claim to rule. In exchange, the newly designated Kshatriyas patronized and rewarded Brahmins for their legitimizing role. The Sanskritic culture associated with these Kshatriyas proved highly influential for later periods, helping to establish the stylistic norms that guided subsequent Kshatriya elites. The process occurred across both North India and the Deccan.

The ICF Canoe Slalom World Championships are an international canoeing competition organized by the International Canoe Federation (ICF). From 1949 through 1999 the championships were contested in odd-numbered years. The 2001 edition, scheduled for Ducktown, Tennessee, east of Chattanooga, from September 20–23, was canceled in the wake of the September 11 attacks. Since 2002 the championships have been held annually in non-Summer Olympic years.

The ICF Canoe Slalom World Championships are the premier international competition in the sport organized by the International Canoe Federation, and this article presents the top 10 male paddlers and the top 10 female paddlers based on medal records achieved in individual events at the World Championships, with team events excluded. In these lists, active competitors are indicated in bold, as are those who hold the highest number of medals for each medal type (gold, silver, and bronze). The statistics are current through the 2025 championships.

Amid the widespread use of X-rays and the growing awareness of the hazards of ionizing radiation, there arose a need for standardized measurement concepts. National efforts produced a variety of definitions and methods, leading to inconsistencies across borders. At the 1925 London International Congress of Radiology, proposals were advanced to create a dedicated body to study and harmonize radiation units. This body, the International Commission on Radiation Units and Measurements (ICRU), was established at the Second International Congress of Radiology held in Stockholm in 1928, with Manne Siegbahn as its chairman.

During the early development of X-ray dosimetry, exposure was gauged with an air-filled ionisation chamber that measured ionisation in air. The corresponding unit of exposure, the roentgen (R), was defined as the amount of X-rays producing 1 esu of charge in 1 cm³ of dry air at 0 °C and 1 atm, and the unit was named to honor Wilhelm Röntgen. In 1937, a meeting of the International Commission on Radiation Units and Measurements extended the definition to gamma radiation, thereby standardising exposure across X-ray and gamma sources. This approach, while providing a consistent exposure measure, did not directly assess how much energy was absorbed in matter such as tissue; instead it quantified ionisation in dry air under specified conditions.

The United Nations General Assembly Fourth Committee handles a broad slate of items on the Assembly’s agenda, including issues related to the effects of atomic radiation, questions relating to information, and a comprehensive review of peacekeeping operations along with the ongoing work of special political missions. It also considers the activities of the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestinian Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA) and examines the report of the Special Committee on Israeli Practices. In addition, the committee addresses international cooperation in the peaceful uses of outer space. Through these topics, the Fourth Committee contributes to the General Assembly’s consideration and oversight of political questions and related international cooperation.

The United Nations General Assembly Fourth Committee, officially the Special Political and Decolonization Committee (SPECPOL) and commonly referred to by its code C4, is one of the six principal committees of the General Assembly. It addresses a wide range of political issues, including UN peacekeeping operations and the peaceful uses of outer space. The committee's agenda and workload are heavily influenced by decolonization matters, with significant focus on developments in the Middle East.

Among cases of sexual harassment, male-to-male harassment is often described as gender harassment intended to police deviations from traditional male gender roles. The harasser may perceive the target as not fulfilling conventional masculinity values, such as being gay, young, or inexperienced. In contrast, incidents of women harassing men are reported less frequently than those in which men harass women.

Sexual harassment refers to unwanted conduct of a sexual nature that is generally regarded as unacceptable and harmful in most settings. Those who experience such harassment may recover from the psychological effects it produces, with recovery goals that commonly include maintaining social participation or reintegrating into society and restoring healthy functioning in intimate relationships that have been affected by the related trauma. Additional aims often focus on regaining social acceptance and on the ability to concentrate and perform effectively in educational and professional environments. Coping with the experience typically involves a combination of stress-management techniques, psychotherapy such as cognitive-behavioral therapy, support from friends and family, and advocacy efforts.
During the early modern period, The Wealth of Nations stands as Adam Smith's seminal book, and his work is commonly regarded as the foundation of classical economics.

During the early modern period, French humanism was advanced by scholars such as Guillaume Budé (1467–1540), who applied Italianate philology to the study of antiquity, including coinage and legal history, and produced a detailed commentary on Justinian's Code. Budé maintained royal absolutist views rather than the republican ethos of some Italian humanists, yet he remained actively engaged in public life, serving as a diplomat for Francis I and contributing to higher learning by helping to found the Collège des Lecteurs Royaux, which would later become the Collège de France. In parallel, Marguerite de Navarre, sister of Francis I, emerged as a poet, novelist, and religious mystic who protected and assembled a circle of vernacular writers, among them Clément Marot, Pierre de Ronsard, and François Rabelais. Taken together, these developments illustrate how scholarly inquiry, political authority, and literary culture intersected in early modern France.

Striped bass have been introduced into waters in Ecuador, Iran, Latvia, Mexico, Russia, South Africa, and Turkey. These introductions were primarily undertaken to support sport fishing and to develop aquaculture.

Striped bass (Morone saxatilis) was introduced to the Pacific Coast of North America and to a wide array of large reservoir impoundments across the United States, with introductions carried out by state game and fish commissions. The primary objectives of these introductions were to provide opportunities for recreational fishing and to serve as a predator to help regulate gizzard shad populations in various freshwater systems. Notable introduction sites include Elephant Butte Lake in New Mexico; Lake Ouachita and Lake Norman spanning Arkansas and North Carolina; Lake Norfork, Beaver Lake, and Lake Hamilton in Arkansas; Lake Thunderbird in Illinois; Lake Pleasant and Lake Havasu in Arizona; Lake Powell on the Arizona–Utah border; Castaic Lake, Pyramid Lake, Silverwood Lake, Diamond Valley Lake, and the San Francisco Bay–Delta in California; Lewis Smith Lake in Alabama; Lake Cumberland in Kentucky; Lake George in Florida; Lake Murray in South Carolina; Lake Lanier in Georgia; Watts Bar Lake in Tennessee; Lake Mead in Nevada; Lake Texoma on the Texas–Oklahoma line; Lake Tawakoni, Lake Whitney, Buffalo Springs Lake, Possum Kingdom Lake, and Lake Buchanan in Texas; Raystown Lake and Lake Wallenpaupack in Pennsylvania; the Umpqua River in Oregon; and Smith Mountain Lake and Leesville Reservoir in Virginia.

Humans have inhabited environments beyond the planet’s surface only in a small number of purpose-built deep underground or underwater facilities and in a limited set of orbital space stations. The overwhelming majority of people reside on Earth’s surface and depend on its ecosystems for sustenance and well-being. Since the latter half of the twentieth century, hundreds of individuals have undertaken temporary stays beyond Earth, while only a tiny fraction has reached the Moon.

Earth’s internal structure comprises several concentric layers, including an asthenosphere that lies beneath the rigid lithosphere and acts as a low-viscosity substrate upon which the lithosphere moves. Within the mantle, mineral phase changes occur at roughly 410 and 660 kilometers depth, forming a transition zone that separates the upper mantle from the lower mantle. Beneath the mantle lies a very low‑viscosity liquid outer core that surrounds a solid inner core. The inner core may rotate slightly faster than the rest of the planet, with estimates ranging from about 0.1 to 0.5 degrees per year, though alternative rates have been proposed. The radius of the inner core is approximately one-fifth of Earth’s overall radius. Density increases with depth, and Earth possesses the highest density among Solar System planetary-sized bodies.

On 15 September at 04:30, the Imperial Japanese Army launched an assault on Pyongyang with approximately 23,800 troops advancing from four directions. An artillery barrage came from the east, a feint was executed to the south, and the main assault pressed in from the north. Chinese defenders offered stiff resistance, contributing to some of the war’s fiercest fighting; they did not fire on troops crossing into the city and seemed unprepared for the northern attack. After Japanese forces entered Pyongyang, the defenders were defeated and the survivors withdrew, only to be countered by a separate Japanese force during their retreat. The Japanese captured 35 artillery pieces, hundreds of rifles, and ammunition. Among the Chinese leadership, Hui Muslim general Zuo Baogui fought notably well and was killed in action by Japanese artillery.

The First Sino-Japanese War, fought between the Qing dynasty and the Empire of Japan, ended in a decisive Japanese victory that arose from modernization and industrialization undertaken about two decades earlier. It demonstrated the effectiveness of a Western-style military system in tactics, training, and organization, and the Imperial Japanese Army and Navy defeated China through foresight, endurance, strategy, and strong organization. The victory enhanced Japan’s prestige on the world stage and reflected the Meiji Restoration’s success, with relatively modest losses and, in return, gains including dominance over Taiwan, the Pescadores, and the Liaotung Peninsula. Moreover, Japan’s abandonment of isolation and adoption of Western policies served as a model for other Asian nations, and the triumph elevated Japan to equal status with Western powers and established it as the dominant power in Asia. Access to essential resources such as iron supported continued modernization and expansion, while the victory intensified Japan’s ambitions for further aggression in the region. The settlement stimulated greater Japanese involvement in Chinese affairs, worsening the late-Imperial Chinese crisis and deepening China’s semi-colonial status, even as Western powers tacitly agreed to delimit their benefits from China after Japan’s victory; in the ensuing years they began to partition China with many treaty ports and concessions established in 1897–98, including Guangzhouwan and Port Arthur.

UTC+02:00 denotes a time offset two hours ahead of Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). This offset is indicated by the suffix +02:00 in time representations. In the ISO 8601 standard, times that include this offset are written with the +02:00 designator, as illustrated by the timestamp 2020-11-08T23:41:45+02:00.

The second qualifying round of the 2023–24 UEFA Europa Conference League consisted of sixteen teams, thirteen of whom had been eliminated in the Champions League first qualifying round, while the remaining three were losers from the Champions League preliminary qualifying round.

During the qualifying phase of the 2023–24 UEFA Europa Conference League, a total of 160 clubs competed in the qualifying system. The field was divided into two paths: a Champions Path, which consisted of 23 teams, and a Main Path, comprising 137 clubs. After the conclusion of the play-off round, 22 winners advanced to the group stage, where they were joined by 10 losers of the Europa League play-off round.

Walter Godefroot is a Belgian former professional road cyclist who specialized in one-day classic races. He captured the Belgian national road race championship in 1972 and secured victories in the Tour of Flanders in 1968 and again in 1978, a decade apart, while also triumphing in the Bordeaux–Paris event in 1969 and 1976. Throughout his career, he accumulated numerous runner-up finishes in other major classics, underscoring his sustained prominence in the sport.

Walter Godefroot relinquished his post as team manager prior to the 2006 season, with Olaf Ludwig succeeding him. After Astana–Würth was excluded from the 2006 Tour de France, Godefroot rejoined the organization as manager of Astana. When his contract with Astana expired in July 2007, it was not renewed, and he subsequently withdrew from professional cycling.

The 1954 Australian Championships – Men's singles title was won by Mervyn Rose, who defeated Rex Hartwig in the final. The match was decided over four sets, with Rose taking the first and fourth sets and Hartwig taking the second, resulting in a final score of 6–2, 0–6, 6–4, 6–2.

Ken Rosewall, the defending champion and top seed, was defeated in the semifinals in a five-set match by fifth-seeded Mervyn Rose. Mervyn Rose then went on to win the men's singles title at the 1954 Australian Championships.

In formal logic, a Boolean-valued function often serves as a truth predicate, assigning to each sentence of a formal language a truth value, typically true or false. Such a predicate is interpreted within the surrounding logical framework to express the formal notion that a statement is true. It formalizes the intuitive concept of truth for sentences in a formal system, providing a semantic means to evaluate their status. In some approaches, determining the final truth value may require considerations that extend beyond the syntactic confines of the language, drawing on additional domains or reference structures as needed.

A Boolean-valued function is a mapping from an arbitrary set X into a Boolean domain B, where B is a two-element set such as {0, 1}. The elements of B are interpreted as logical values, with 0 denoting false and 1 denoting true. Consequently, such a function encodes a single bit of information. In mathematical logic and related contexts, it is sometimes referred to as a predicate or a proposition.

Phnom Kulen National Park is situated in Svay Leu District within Siem Reap Province, Cambodia. The park lies roughly 48 kilometers (30 miles) from Siem Reap, the provincial capital, and is about 25 kilometers (16 miles) from Prasat Banteay Srey.

Within Phnom Kulen National Park, the waterfalls vary in size in response to seasonal changes and rainfall, resulting in noticeable differences in their appearance over the year. Consequently, visiting the waterfalls is a popular activity on tours of Phnom Kulen.

A Native American tribe refers to a group that is formally recognized by the United States government. Such tribes possess tribal sovereignty, enabling self-government over their internal affairs and resources. In its relation to the federal government, the tribe’s status is described as that of a domestic dependent, sovereign nation, a characterization that in some contexts resembles a state and in others an autonomous nation. This framework maintains a government-to-government relationship between the tribe and the U.S. federal government, reflecting ongoing official interactions and obligations between tribal and federal authorities.

Under United States federal law, the term tribe encompasses groups that are federally recognized by the Bureau of Indian Affairs as well as Alaska Native tribes created under the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (ANCSA), codified at 43 U.S.C. 1601 et seq. Recognized Alaska Native villages and regional corporations are included among federally recognized tribes. Federally recognized tribes are eligible to participate in certain special programs and services administered by the federal government. The Bureau of Indian Affairs, a component of the Department of the Interior, issues the Certificate of Degree of Indian Blood, a document commonly used as the basis for enrollment in many tribes. Federally recognized tribes function as distinct governmental entities and are not extensions of state or local governments.

Women's Equality Day commemorates a 1920 milestone in United States history when Bainbridge Colby, then the Secretary of State, signed a proclamation announcing that American women had attained the constitutional right to vote. The proclamation came in the context of the certification of the Nineteenth Amendment, which enfranchised women, and the observance honors the achievement of women's suffrage and the broader goal of gender equality in the United States.

Women's Equality Day is observed on August 26 to commemorate the 1920 adoption of the Nineteenth Amendment (Amendment XIX), which guarantees women's suffrage and prohibits denying the right to vote on the basis of sex by both state governments and the federal government. The occasion was first celebrated in 1971, and in 1973 Congress designated it as a national observance; since then, it has been proclaimed annually by the President of the United States.

Established in 1997, the International DOI Foundation (IDF) is a non-profit organization that acts as the governing body of the Digital Object Identifier (DOI) system. It protects the intellectual property rights associated with the DOI framework and oversees the system’s common operational features. The foundation also supports the development and promotion of the DOI system and ensures that improvements to its creation, maintenance, registration, resolution, and policymaking of DOI names are accessible to all registrants. In addition, it safeguards DOI users from the imposition of licensing requirements by third parties beyond those established by the IDF.

Crossref recommends presenting the DOI in plain text rather than hyperlinking it to its URL. The rationale is that, without a clickable link, many users find it difficult to copy the full URL; displaying the complete address enables manual copying and pasting to reach the DOI’s page. The goal of this practice is to ensure that users can access the page identified by the DOI.

Entr'acte, Erik Satie's first publicly performed foray into furniture music, premiered in 1920 as the entr'acte music for a play that had fallen into obscurity. The piece was designed to function as a background sound to the intermission noises of the audience—walking and talking—rather than to be actively listened to. Reportedly, however, spectators did not follow this intention and instead remained in their seats, listening to the music. This reaction has been linked to a habit shaped by incidental music, in which listeners attend to the musical foreground rather than the ambient intermission environment. Frustrated avant-garde musicians attempted to salvage the concept by encouraging the audience to rise, converse, and move about during the break.

Entr'acte, literally meaning "between the acts," denotes a pause that separates two portions of a stage production. It has precise equivalents in other languages, including German Zwischenspiel or Zwischenakt, Italian intermezzo, and Spanish intermedio or intervalo. The term can refer to any interlude within a performance, effectively functioning as a synonym of intermission, though the intermission is the more common term in modern French usage. In English, entr'acte more often designates a musical piece performed between acts rather than the physical pause itself. It is frequently paired with a longer intermission, since an intermission typically occurs between acts; nevertheless, an entr'acte may occur independently between acts without an accompanying intermission.

France's approach to extending the vote to men unfolded in distinct phases during the revolutionary era. The 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen set out principles supporting equal political rights. In 1792 the National Convention was elected by suffrage extended to all men, a measure that proved temporary. In 1795 the Directory revoked the broader male franchise and restored more limited voting rights. Following the upheavals of 1848, voting rights for all men were restored in France.

During the Jacksonian era, spanning roughly the 1820s to the 1850s, voting reforms opened political participation to nearly all white men, achieving broad white male suffrage across states by around 1856. This expansion brought representation to poorer white men, though several states retained tax-paying or similar qualifications; five states preserved such requirements until 1860, two into the early twentieth century, and later generations of poorer whites were disproportionately disenfranchised. The growth of the franchise occurred largely without violence, with the Rhode Island Dorr Rebellion cited as a notable exception. By contrast, most African-American men remained excluded; the Fifteenth Amendment of 1870 barred racial denial of the vote, yet in many jurisdictions rights were effectively denied for about a century. Federal enforcement to secure these rights culminated in the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

Federal Election Commission filings released in April 2018 showed that Kyrsten Sinema had raised more than $8.2 million, a total greater than the combined sum raised by the three leading Republican primary contenders.

An Advocate profile characterizes Kyrsten Sinema as aiming to advance LGBT rights, and she has a long-standing record of policy advocacy on LGBT issues. In 2006, she opposed an Arizona constitutional amendment that would have banned same-sex marriages and civil unions; the measure was defeated, marking the first instance in which a state rejected a ban on same-sex marriage. In 2008, a second Arizona amendment restricting marriage to opposite-sex couples passed, with Sinema again opposing it. She supports same-sex marriage, the recognition of domestic partnerships, and extending anti-discrimination protections to include gender identity.

Richard Meyers, born in Kentucky, moved to New York City in 1966 after dropping out of high school to pursue poetry. There he and his high school friend Tom Miller formed the rock group Neon Boys, which would later evolve into Television in 1973. Miller adopted the stage name Verlaine, reflecting the poet Paul Verlaine, while Meyers chose the surname Richard Hell, a descriptor of his condition that he has stated.

Richard Hell and the Voidoids were a punk rock group from the United States formed in New York City in 1976, with Richard Hell as the frontman. Hell had previously played with the Neon Boys, Television, and the Heartbreakers, before establishing the Voidoids as his principal project.

Maupiti is a volcanic island in the Society hotspot chain. Geologically, it is estimated to be between 3.9 and 4.5 million years old. The island presents as a near-atoll, featuring a central volcanic summit surrounded by a lagoon and a barrier reef. Five motu encircle the lagoon: Auira, Pa'ao, Tuanai, Tiapaa, and Pitiahe. The lagoon covers about 27 square kilometres (10 square miles), while the central landmass measures around 12 square kilometres (4.6 square miles). Its maximum elevation reaches 372 metres (1,220 feet).

Maupiti is an island in the western Leeward Islands of French Polynesia. It is the westernmost volcanic island in the archipelago. The island lies about 315 kilometres (196 miles) northwest of Tahiti and roughly 40 kilometres (25 miles) west of Bora Bora. It has a population of 1,286, and its largest town is Vaiea.

At the Roskilde Festival, a fatal crowd surge occurred during Pearl Jam's performance on the Orange Stage on 30 June 2000, resulting in nine deaths and 26 injuries, three of them serious. All of the deceased were male. The victims included a 26-year-old German; a 23-year-old Dutch national; a 24-year-old Australian who died several days later in hospital; three Swedish men aged 22, 22, and 20; and three Danish men aged 22, 17, and 17.

Roskilde Festival 2009 reflects a long pattern of growth and organizational adjustment that defined the event during the 1990s. As popularity surged, ticket sales were increasingly restricted to safeguard quality, with peak attendance reaching around 125,000 visitors. An additional allocation existed for roughly 25,000 volunteers, 5,000 media personnel, and 3,000 artists, together accounting for 90,000 tickets assigned to these groups. To preserve the festival’s standard, the overall number of participants was limited. The growing distance from the rear of the camping area to the stages had become untenable, prompting a westward expansion in 1994 to create more space without lengthening the travel between camping zones and performance areas. The festival site was divided by a small railway line into two sections, and in 1995 the organizers opened their own train station to facilitate arrivals. In 1997 a second tent, known as the Roskilde Ballroom, was erected to expand capacity and provide additional performance space. If festival visitors were counted as part of Roskilde’s population, the city would rank as the fourth-largest in Denmark.

Cornell University consists of nine privately endowed, non-statutory colleges that operate with a degree of autonomy within the institution. Notable examples include the College of Arts and Sciences; the College of Architecture, Art, and Planning; the College of Engineering; and the Nolan School of Hotel Administration. These colleges function independently of state funding and state oversight, an arrangement that provides them with enhanced autonomy over academic programs, admissions policies, and student advising. Consequently, tuition is not discounted for residents of New York State.

Cornell University's four statutory colleges—the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, the College of Human Ecology, the School of Industrial and Labor Relations, and the College of Veterinary Medicine—function as distinct statutory units within the university. In the 2010–2011 fiscal year, these colleges received $131.9 million in SUNY appropriations to support teaching, research, and service missions, a funding arrangement that ties them to SUNY trustees and state agencies. New York residents enrolled in these colleges are eligible for discounted tuition, though the state regards the colleges' academic activities as private and non-state entities despite the public funding and governance oversight.

The Country Music Association Award for Female Vocalist of the Year is an annual accolade presented by the Country Music Association to recognize outstanding female vocal performances in country music. The inaugural winner was Loretta Lynn in 1967. Miranda Lambert holds the record for the most wins in the category, with seven, while Lambert and Reba McEntire are tied for the most nominations, each with 18. Anne Murray has the most nominations without a win, with six. The current holder is Lainey Wilson, who won the award at the 56th CMA Awards in 2022.

The Country Music Association Award for Female Vocalist of the Year is an annual accolade bestowed by the Country Music Association to honor notable female vocalists for their work in country music during the eligibility cycle. The article presents a list of recipients who have earned the honor over the years. Eligibility criteria encompass distinguished performance on a solo country single or album release and consideration of the artist's overall impact and contributions to the genre within the relevant period.

In 1840, the Cunard Line inaugurated its first regular service carrying both passengers and freight aboard the RMS Britannia. The operation utilized a steamship on the Liverpool–Boston route, marking an early implementation of steam-powered transatlantic crossings.

Today, the dominant propulsion system for steamships is steam turbine technology. Nuclear-powered ships are, in essence, steam-turbine vessels, since their propulsion relies on turbines driven by steam generated without combustion. The boiler in such vessels is heated by heat from a nuclear reactor rather than by burning fuel, illustrating a fundamental distinction from conventional steam generation. Consequently, the bulk of nuclear-powered ships in operation are military platforms, with aircraft carriers and submarines representing the principal types.

Lyle & Scott, founded in 1874, originally specialized in golfing apparel and gained recognition as a label worn by high-profile golfers. In 1975 the company was awarded a Royal Warrant of appointment by the Duke of Edinburgh. Since 2003, the brand has expanded into youth and urban fashion markets while continuing to offer its traditional golfing attire.

Lyle & Scott is a clothing brand that has attracted a number of notable patrons, including the Duke of Edinburgh, Prince Philip, and Ronnie Corbett. The label has developed associations with musicians such as Arctic Monkeys, Kasabian, and Pete Doherty, and counts actor Adam Deacon among its supporters. It has also been linked with television presenters, among them Tim Lovejoy, Chris Ramsey, Simon Amstell, and Holly Willoughby. Additionally, the brand has appeared on screen in the films The Firm and Green Street.

Naples Daily News historically served Collier County, but its coverage has expanded to include Lee County and portions of Charlotte County. The publication produces several editions of its Local & State section, with each edition outlining communities such as Bonita Springs, Cape Coral, East Naples, Fort Myers, Immokalee, Lehigh Acres, Marco Island, North Fort Myers, North Naples, and South Fort Myers.

Naples Daily News, a newspaper based in Naples, Florida, was owned by Journal Media Group, a Milwaukee-based company formed in 2015 as a newspaper-only spin-off of E. W. Scripps Company's media operations. The Scripps Company had purchased Naples Daily News from the founding Collier family in 1986 in a deal reportedly worth more than $160 million and described as the highest earnings multiple paid for a newspaper by any American company up to that date.

Australian corporate law historically drew heavily on United Kingdom company law, reflecting its colonial heritage. Over time, the framework was consolidated into a single national statute, the Corporations Act 2001, which now governs corporate conduct across Australia. Administration of the regime is centralized under the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC), the national regulator responsible for oversight and enforcement.

Australian corporate law regulates company registration and identification through the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC). Upon registration, ASIC issues a Certificate of Incorporation and assigns an Australian Company Number (ACN), a unique identifier that must be quoted on all correspondence and invoices. For foreign entities operating a branch in Australia, the regulator issues an Australian Registered Body Number (ARBN), a designation that functions similarly to an Australian Business Number. Where a company intends to trade, it is required to obtain a Tax File Number (TFN) from the Australian Taxation Office and an Australian Business Number (ABN).

Bridgeport, Connecticut enacted a 29% hike in the property tax rate in 2016 to help close a municipal deficit. The measure was among the largest single-year increases in property tax rates in recent United States history. It followed a 2015 citywide reassessment that valued taxable property at about $6 billion, a decline of roughly $1 billion from prior levels. The combination of higher taxes and falling property values has been a persistent political issue in the city.

In 1639, Roger Ludlow was tasked by Hartford with establishing two plantations—Cupheg at the mouth of the Housatonic River (the site of present-day Stratford) and the harbor at the mouth of the Pequonnock River (today Bridgeport Harbor). Ludlow did not follow that directive and instead founded a settlement at Unconway (now Fairfield), a choice likely driven by concerns over a substantial Paugussett settlement at Golden Hill, a sacred site for the tribe; the settlers may have occupied sparsely populated land around the village. Subsequently, in 1659 the Hartford General Court delineated the formal borders of the Paugussett Reservation.

Newcastle, New South Wales, opened to free settlement in 1822, marking a shift from a primarily punitive outpost toward a growing colonial town. In 1824 the Australian Agricultural Company secured a large land grant to the north of Port Stephens, signaling expanding agricultural activity and investment in the region, while around the same period wealthy colonists began establishing estates along the upper Hunter River. The convict population diminished markedly, dropping from about 1,000 to roughly 100; approximately 100 convicts were employed on the construction of a breakwater, and some 900 were sent to the Port Macquarie penal colony. As a result, the convict colony at Newcastle was closed in 1826.

Newcastle, New South Wales, previously hosted two top-tier National Basketball League clubs, the Newcastle Falcons and the Hunter Pirates. Both outfits folded due to financial difficulties. The city is now represented in the NBL1, the league’s second tier, with the Newcastle Basketball Club fielding both men's and women's teams in NBL1, reviving the Falcons branding for the NBL1 squad.
During the 2004 Libertarian National Convention, following the second round of voting, Gary Nolan addressed the convention and endorsed Michael Badnarik for the Libertarian Party's 2004 nomination.

The Libertarian National Convention is held every two years. At each biennial convention, delegates vote on proposed amendments to the party bylaws, adopt the party platform, and approve resolutions, and they elect the party's national officers and a judicial committee. In addition, every four years the convention nominates the Libertarian Party's presidential and vice-presidential candidates.

At the end of the 2021–22 season, Turkey stood 20th in UEFA's country coefficient ranking, which reduced the number of Süper Lig clubs that could qualify for European competitions in 2022–23 to four rather than the usual five. As a result, the league champion entered the second qualifying round of the 2023–24 UEFA Champions League, while the second- and third-placed teams, together with the winners of the 2022–23 Turkish Cup, advanced to the second qualifying round of the 2023–24 UEFA Europa Conference League.

The 2022–23 Spor Toto Süper Lig season, officially titled the Spor Toto Süper Lig 2022–23 season, marked the 65th edition of Turkey's top-tier football league. The campaign commenced on 5 August 2022 and concluded on 7 June 2023.

By 1901, the Jewish population of Turin and its surrounding areas stood at roughly 5,700. In the 1920s and 1930s, some Piedmontese Jews supported Italian Fascism as the movement gained influence in Europe, and a short-lived fascist Jewish periodical appeared in Turin, La nostra bandiera, which promoted Italian nationalism and early fascist ideas. Nevertheless, the majority of Piedmont’s Jews developed a strong anti-Fascist stance, particularly during Mussolini’s dictatorship and after the 1938 Racial Laws. Following the fall of Fascism on September 8, 1943, some Jews from Piedmont joined partisan efforts. In Turin, the Jewish Primary School is named after Emanuele Artom, a young Jewish man who died for freedom.

Turin's history of Jewish life is characterized by a long-standing communal presence and a notable material legacy. In Turin and in almost all of the related cities, Jewish cemeteries, ghetto-era buildings, and synagogues have been preserved in their entirety, providing accessible physical remnants of the community's past. These enduring sites support ongoing scholarly inquiry and public memory, illustrating the social and cultural dimensions of Jewish life in the Piedmont region and its wider connections.

Within the European Parliament the Greens aligned with regionalist and stateless nationalist movements that supported devolution. In 1984 the Rainbow Group was formed as a coalition of Greens, regionalists, and other left-wing parties unaffiliated with international organisations. In 1989 the Greens split to create the Green Group, while the regionalist factions remained within Rainbow. Following Rainbow's dissolution in 1994, its members joined the European Radical Alliance under the Energie Radicale initiative. By 1999, Greens and regionalists had reunited under the Greens/European Free Alliance banner.

The article on political groups of the European Parliament surveys the formation and functioning of the parliamentary groups, with particular attention given to the concept of cohesion as a measure of internal unity within a group. Cohesion is described as the degree to which members act as a unified bloc or display internal divisions. As part of its analytical framework, the article cites Figure 1 from Thorsten Faas’s 2002 European Integration Online Papers (EIoP) study, which analyzes the groups as they stood in 2002.

Halfway to Hazard released the single 'I Know Where Heaven Is' on July 20, 2009 from their second studio album, Come on Time, which was released on October 19, 2009. Neither the single nor the album charted.

Halfway to Hazard is a musical act whose members have pursued individual projects. In 2012, Warrix released a solo music video titled Rain on the Roof, which features Rob Bironas, a former All-Pro kicker for the Tennessee Titans.

At the solar limb, the chromosphere displays a spectrum dominated by emission lines, with the H-alpha line at 656.3 nanometers among its strongest features. This spectral line results from a hydrogen atom in which an electron transitions from the third to the second energy level, known as the Balmer-alpha transition. Because 656.3 nanometers lies in the red portion of the visible spectrum, the chromosphere is often associated with a reddish hue.

Chromospheres are not unique to the Sun; observations have revealed chromospheric layers around other stars as well.
