Following Napoleon's defeat, the Austrian monarchy asserted full authority over the territory formerly governed as the Illyrian Provinces of France. The notion of creating an Illyrian Kingdom emerged from a blend of external strategic considerations and internal political calculations. Externally, Vienna aimed to halt the spread of Italian and Russian influence in the region, while domestically the plan sought to preserve certain French reforms, safeguard Hungarian influence, and replace the wartime interim military administration at the earliest feasible date.

Deux Mamelles comprises two prominent coastal hills that host notable landmarks: the Phare des Mamelles lighthouse on the seaward hill, and the African Renaissance Monument on the inland hill located farther from the shore. The African Renaissance Monument was erected and unveiled in 2010.
Deux Mamelles, also known as Collines des Mamelles or Mamelles, denotes a pair of prominent hills situated in Ouakam, a suburban commune of Dakar, on the Cap-Vert peninsula in Senegal.

Calouste Gulbenkian Museum houses a notable ensemble of French 18th-century decorative arts, including exemplary gold- and silver-work, furniture, paintings, and sculpture. A gallery is devoted to a substantial body of works by the Venetian painter Francesco Guardi. The collection also features English paintings from the 18th and 19th centuries. A premier collection of René Lalique jewelry and glass is displayed in a dedicated room.

Centro de Arte Moderna (CAM) opened in 1983 as Portugal's first museum dedicated to modern art, following twenty-one years of acquisitions, a construction period of more than three years, and controversy generated by conservationists. In 2024, CAM reopened after a €58 million redevelopment.

In the Barbie Basics line, dolls are identified by model numbers rather than personal names, and each figure possesses a distinct head mold that aligns with its numerical designation. A number of these head sculpts have achieved popularity and have been reused within the Barbie Collector line. Mattel typically assigns names to head molds based on the doll, character, or line where the sculpt debuted, though this naming convention is not universal and exceptions occur.

Barbie Basics refers to a limited-production series of Barbie dolls manufactured between 1980 and 1982. The line introduced a distinctive look, featuring the classic Barbie paired with white Nike sneakers. A production run of 200 dolls was distributed to retailers in Florida and Georgia as test markets. The restricted quantities contributed to the line’s rarity and high desirability among collectors, making these dolls a sought-after, scarce collectible. A notable auction record from 1994 cites a 1982 Barbie from this line selling for $12,000.

The Texas Coastal Bend functions as an ecological boundary that differentiates the geographic ranges of several plant communities. Notably, the California fan palm (Washingtonia filifera) occurs exclusively to the west of this boundary, reflecting a regional separation of flora. This vegetative demarcation is linked to the Balcones Fault, a major geological feature that underpins the transition between plant communities in the area.
The Texas Coastal Bend constitutes a regional portion of Texas and is defined by nine counties: Aransas, Bee, Brooks, Jim Wells, Kenedy, Kleberg, Nueces, Refugio, and San Patricio.

The term deathrock first emerged in the 1950s as a label for a thematically linked strand of rock and roll. Its development is often traced from 1958, with Jody Reynolds’ Endless Sleep, through 1964, when J. Frank Wilson’s Last Kiss appeared, and it has also been applied to the Shangri-Las’ Leader of the Pack. Songs in this category typically center on the death of teenagers and are noted for a morbid yet romantically toned view of mortality, as well as the use of spoken-word interludes and accompanying sound effects. In 1974, the label was revived by Gene Grier to describe the same musical phenomenon within rock more broadly. The term subsequently re-emerged to characterize the sound associated with various West Coast punk bands.

By the early 1980s, the U.S. deathrock scene became increasingly connected with the United Kingdom's emerging gothic rock milieu. Music journalist James Greene observed that gothic rock closely aligned with deathrock. This cross-pollination accelerated through Gun Club's European tour in 1983 and Christian Death's 1984 tour, which exposed artists from both scenes to one another's approaches. Christian Death subsequently moved away from its early deathrock roots toward the gothic rock aesthetic later associated with Catastrophe Ballet. At the same time, English groups such as Sex Gang Children and Alien Sex Fiend began incorporating deathrock elements into their sound, further intertwining the two scenes.

ISO standards undergo periodic review by the International Organization for Standardization to ensure their ongoing relevance to market needs. The current edition of ISO 14001 is 2015, and certified organizations were granted a three-year transition period to implement the changes required by the new edition. The standard emphasizes improving environmental performance rather than focusing solely on the management system, with revisions aimed at making environmental management more comprehensive and pertinent to supply chains. It requires consideration of environmental impacts across the entire life cycle, though conducting a formal life cycle analysis is not mandated. The revision strengthens top management commitments and enhances methods for evaluating compliance. It is linked to the High Level Structure introduced in 2015, a framework also used by ISO 9001, and this alignment promotes more uniform implementation and auditing. Finally, certificate holders are required to identify risks and opportunities and describe how these will be addressed.

ISO 14001, the principal standard of the ISO 14000 family, provides a structured environmental management framework that enables organizations to systematically reduce their environmental impact. Economically, it supports improved regulatory compliance and lowers the risk of fines. Operational efficiency gains include reduced waste, lower resource consumption, and decreased operating costs. The standard's international recognition allows conformance across multiple sites, reducing the need for separate registrations and certifications. As consumer demand for robust internal controls grows, ISO 14001 offers advantages for long-term viability and competitive edge. It can positively influence asset value and public perception, strengthening a company's position in international markets. It also signals commitment to innovation to customers and potential employees, potentially widening access to new customers and partners. In some markets, it may lead to lower public liability insurance costs, and it may help reduce trade barriers among registered businesses. There is increasing interest in including ISO 14001 in tenders for public-private partnerships in infrastructure renewal, and evidence from Canadian highway projects suggests benefits to environmental quality and taxpayers.

Within Brazilian Portuguese, the pronoun você has become the default second-person singular form in formal writing and multimedia communication, a trend largely influenced by media output from the Southeast. In Rio de Janeiro, however, the use of tu has grown since the late 20th century, reflecting ongoing regional variation. The form tu is especially common among younger speakers, indicating a pronounced age-related dimension to pronoun choice. Studies also report a rising use of tu across other Brazilian dialect areas, suggesting a broader national shift toward greater diversity in second-person pronouns.

Portuguese is spoken across all continents, reflecting its widespread use globally. It holds official status in a number of international organizations, including being one of the twenty official languages of the European Union and an official language of NATO. In the Americas, Portuguese is an official language of the Organization of American States, alongside Spanish, French and English. The language is also one of the eighteen official languages of the European Space Agency, illustrating its involvement in multinational scientific and diplomatic contexts.

During Japan's colonial rule over Korea, Governor-General Jirō Minami pursued a policy of cultural assimilation (dōka seisaku). In 1939, Ordinance No. 20, commonly known as the Name Order (sōshi-kaimei), was issued and took effect as law in April 1940. Although the ordinance formally prohibited compulsion, lower-level officials and administrators frequently pressured Koreans to adopt Japanese-style surnames and given names. Consequently, by 1944, roughly 84 percent of the Korean population had registered Japanese surnames, illustrating the extensive impact of the policy on naming practices.

Romanization of Korean names sometimes prioritizes Korean pronunciation when the Hangul representation diverges markedly from forms used in other languages. For the name 다윗, the Revised Romanization renders it as Dawit, aligning with its Korean pronunciation rather than the English form David. Although the Hangul-name corresponds to the Biblical figure known as David in English, the substantial difference between the Korean rendering and the English cognate has led some to advocate for rendering the name as DAWIT in English contexts to preserve the Korean pronunciation in transliteration.

Apache Continuum was a discontinued continuous integration server developed by the Apache Software Foundation. It operated in conjunction with Apache Maven as part of the Maven ecosystem, coordinating automated builds for Maven-based projects. Maven runs builds on a configurable schedule, a capability that Continuum leveraged to manage scheduled, automated builds within continuous integration workflows.

Dynamic Science Stories was an American pulp science fiction magazine that published two issues in 1939, dated February and April. It served as a companion to Marvel Science Stories and was edited by Robert O. Erisman for Western Fiction Publishing. Notable contributors included L. Sprague de Camp and Manly Wade Wellman.

Dynamic Science Stories was a pulp science-fiction magazine published by Western Fiction Publishing Co. in Chicago, with editorial offices located at Radio City, New York. The publication ran as a single volume consisting of two issues, each issued in pulp format and containing 112 pages, priced at 15 cents per issue. A British reprint edition of the first issue appeared in 1939, undated. The editor was Robert O. Erisman, though he was not credited within the magazine.

Privacy, as discussed through George Orwell's 1984, is framed by the portrayal of Winston Smith in the totalitarian state of Oceania, where the Party led by Big Brother maintains control through pervasive surveillance and strict restrictions on speech and thought. The work critiques the deleterious effects of totalitarian rule on individual privacy and on freedom of expression, with censorship serving as a central instrument of power. Scholars draw parallels between the novel's warnings and contemporary debates over privacy and censorship in the digital age, noting that themes of surveillance and control remain salient. A frequently cited example is the role of large social media platforms that monitor user data and enforce online censorship policies for monetary gain, a dynamic that prompts ongoing questions about autonomy, accountability, and the balance between safety, profit, and freedom.

In discussions of privacy on social media, Susan B. Barnes introduced the term "privacy paradox" to describe the ambiguous boundary between private and public spaces within online environments. She observes that younger users tend to disclose more information on social platforms than adults, yet this greater openness does not indicate a lack of privacy concern; rather, it reflects a complex interplay between awareness and behavior. Barnes reinforces this point with a case from a television interview about Facebook, in which a student articulated worries about revealing personal data online. When asked to display her Facebook page, the student nevertheless posted her home address, phone numbers, and photographs of her young son, an example of the tension between privacy apprehensions and actual sharing practices on social media.

Fatick is a city in Senegal notable for its concentration of ancient sites designated as historical monuments and listed on the World Heritage list. Among these sacred locations are Mind Ngo Mindiss, situated along the Sine River where libations and offerings are performed; Ndiobaye, a site where traditional ceremonies take place; and Ndeb Jab, which houses a sacred tree at Ndiaye-Ndiaye. These sites are important sacred places in Serer religion. The Xooy ceremony (Khoy), performed by Serer high priests and priestesses known as Saltigues, takes place in Fatick once a year.

Fatick is a town and urban commune in Senegal, located between M'bour and Kaolack. It is inhabited by the Serer people. The population stood at 39,361 in 2023. The name appears as Fatik in Wolof and Serer languages, while the French pronunciation is rendered as [fatik].

Individualism and collectivism represent a central dichotomy in cross-cultural research, contrasting emphasis on personal autonomy with adherence to group norms and authority. Global studies indicate that societies vary in the extent to which individuals are encouraged to pursue independent goals versus conform to social expectations, with such differences generally reflecting degrees of emphasis rather than fundamentally different kinds of social orientation. Cultural levels of individualism are also correlated with economic indicators, notably GDP per capita and venture capital activity, suggesting economic development is linked to the prominence of individualistic traits. Geographically, economically advanced regions such as Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, North America, and Western Europe are among the most individualistic, while middle‑income regions like Eastern Europe, parts of South America, and mainland East Asia occupy intermediate positions. By contrast, the most collectivistic cultures tend to cluster in economically developing areas including the Middle East and North Africa, Sub‑Saharan Africa, South and Southeast Asia, Central Asia, and Central America. The view that modernization accompanies rising individualization is supported by scholars such as Dumont, Hofstede, Giddens, Bauman, and Inglehart, though critics argue that modernization is not linear and that some collectivist societies are highly modernized; they also contend that the concepts of individualism, collectivism, and modernity lack precise definitions, necessitating more differentiated analyses.

Individualism includes, among its currents, egoist anarchism, a school rooted in the philosophy of Max Stirner, who is among the earliest and most recognized proponents of individualist anarchism. Stirner, a 19th-century philosopher influenced by Hegel, maintained that any constraint on an individual's liberty arises only from their ability to realize their own desires, and that this assessment dismisses religious institutions, state power, and conventional morality. Central to his thought is the imperative of self-assertion as a guiding ethic. He also anticipated the formation of unions of egoists—loose, non-dogmatic associations that survive through the voluntary participation and ongoing consent of their members, seen as an alternative organizational model to the state.
Logographic printing refers to a press owned by John Walter, the founder of The Times. Walter had acquired the printing system from its inventor, Henry Johnson, who devised the method.

Logographic printing emerged in the late eighteenth century with Henry Johnson, a typefounder, who sought to improve the accuracy and speed of printing lottery lists. He devised a system in which the types for two or more numerals were permanently joined, creating fixed, composite characters that could be set more rapidly and with fewer errors. This arrangement produced substantial gains in productivity when printing numbers. Building on this experience, Johnson subsequently applied a similar logographic approach to words, extending the concept beyond numerals.

Vegetius was long regarded as the premier authority on military matters, but his status declined as ancient historians such as Polybius became available to scholars. Machiavelli sought to correct what he viewed as Vegetius' defects in L'arte della Guerra (1521), drawing on Polybius, Frontinus, and Livy. Justus Lipsius accused Machiavelli of confusing institutions across different periods of the Roman Empire. G. Stewechius argued that the survival of Vegetius' work contributed to the loss or obscuring of the sources he cited. These positions typified late Renaissance attitudes toward Vegetius. In the eighteenth century, soldiers such as Marshal Puysegur still based works on this model. Milner described Vegetius' work as enduring a long period of deepening neglect.

Vegetius, commonly identified as Publius Flavius Vegetius Renatus, is best known for his late Roman military manual De re militari, which emphasizes systematic organization and responses to wartime circumstances. The treatise furnishes guidance on establishing and strengthening a camp, including its fortifications and administrative arrangement, and it provides extensive instruction on training troops and enforcing discipline, including measures to curb indiscipline. It also outlines approaches to conducting a battle, from tactical preparation to engagement management, and it covers marching procedures as well as the development and evaluation of military formations. Beyond these, it presents broader methods aimed at enhancing the cohesion, efficiency, and courage of the legion.

Buffett's first annual Berkshire Hathaway letter published after Munger's death portrays Munger as someone who did not seek credit for his contributions and allowed Buffett to take the bows and accolades. The relationship is described as a blend of an older brother and a loving father figure. Munger is depicted as relinquishing control even when he believed he was right, and he never reminded Buffett of his mistakes when Buffett blundered.
On December 28, 2011, Charlie Munger donated ten shares of Berkshire Hathaway Class A stock, valued at approximately $1.2 million in total, to the University of Michigan.

Stephen Bray is an American composer and lyricist who made his Broadway debut in 2005 as the composer and lyricist for the Broadway adaptation of The Color Purple, an adaptation of Alice Walker's novel. His work on the production earned him a Tony Award nomination for his contributions to the show.

Stephen Bray began his musical education with private instruction in Detroit, before enrolling at Washtenaw Community College in Ann Arbor. He later continued his studies at the Berklee College of Music in Boston, beginning in 1978.

The Supersuckers formed in 1988 in Tucson, Arizona, initially under the name The Black Supersuckers, and they played traditional punk rock. The original lineup comprised Edward "Eddie Spaghetti" Daly on bass, Dan "Thunder" Bolton on guitar, Ron "Rontrose" Heathman on guitar, Dan Siegel on drums (later known as Dancing Eagle), and Eric Martin on vocals, all of whom were high school friends from Tucson. In 1989 the group relocated to Seattle in hopes of accessing more venues and to sustain their leather-jacket image in warmer months, and after Martin left in 1990, Eddie Spaghetti assumed the role of lead vocalist. Before signing with Sub Pop, the band issued a number of singles and cover songs on small labels, with their early recordings later compiled on the 1992 release The Songs All Sound the Same. Their Sub Pop debut, The Smoke of Hell, released in 1992, featured artwork by Dan Clowes.

Eddie Spaghetti, a stage name for Edward Daly, serves as the bassist and vocalist of the band, which he leads as its only constant member. The current lineup includes guitarist Marty Chandler and drummer Christopher von Streicher. The group’s most recent album, Play That Rock N' Roll, was released in February 2020.

Gusen concentration camp, located near Mauthausen in Austria, operated under an extermination-through-labor system that targeted real and perceived enemies, a design that made conditions harsher than those at the Mauthausen main camp. Prisoners faced an exceedingly short life expectancy, with many dying within months of arrival, and total casualties are estimated at at least 35,000 from forced labor, starvation, and mass executions. Beginning in 1943, the camp complex served as a major armaments production site for the German aviation industry, associated with Messerschmitt and Steyr-Daimler-Puch. The system was redesignated as Gusen I, and new subcamps Gusen II and Gusen III were added to accommodate the expanding workforce. Inmates were compelled to construct vast underground factories, the principal facility known as Bergkristall, which was intended for the production of the Messerschmitt Me 262 jet fighter. By the end of the war, the operations at Gusen produced nearly a thousand Me 262 fuselages.

Gusen concentration camp functioned as a satellite facility of Mauthausen, with its commandants reporting directly to Franz Ziereis, the SS-Obersturmbannführer who commanded Mauthausen. The inaugural commandant was Anton Streitwieser, who was dismissed in May 1940 after authorities found he operated an unauthorized pig farm and diverted prisoner rations to pigs. From 25 May 1940 until October 1942 (some sources place January 1943) Karl Chmielewski served as the SS commandant; he had joined the SS in 1932 and the camp’s SS in 1935. Under Chmielewski, Streitwieser served as rapportführer, and Kurt Kirchner led the labor service. Chmielewski was frequently intoxicated and personally brutalized inmates, beating, kicking, whipping, and even killing prisoners, and he exercised broad discretion in camp governance, with the period characterized by violence and brutality. Under his command, about half of the prisoners died. From October 1942 to the end of the war Friedrich August Seidler took command and was noted for pursuing a harsher, Prussian-style brutality. Administratively, Gusen operated more as a branch of the Mauthausen main camp rather than a separate subcamp until 1943, though it maintained its own departments, including a Political Department.

The Indus River Delta forms at the mouth of the Indus River as it flows into the Arabian Sea, and it lies largely in southern Sindh province, Pakistan, with a small portion extending into the Kutch region of India. The delta covers about 41,440 square kilometers (16,000 square miles) and is roughly 210 kilometers wide at its seaward entry. Its climate is arid, with annual precipitation typically ranging from 25 to 50 centimeters. Since the 1940s, inflows to the delta have diminished as irrigation systems divert substantial amounts of Indus water upstream before it reaches the delta. The area is home to the world’s largest arid mangrove forests. In 2003, the delta had a population of about 900,000 people, with fishing constituting the principal industry.

Within the Indo-Gangetic Plain, the Terai forms the low, flat belt immediately south of the Bhabar region. It is largely formed from recent alluvial deposits laid down by streams and rivers that reemerge after crossing the Shivalik foothills, creating a zone of new sedimentation. The Terai experiences substantial rainfall for much of the year, resulting in a humid climate and fertile soils. This zone supports dense wet evergreen vegetation, giving it a distinctive ecological character within the broader plain.

The Internet2 community develops and implements advanced networking technologies to support the next generation of the Internet. Its work encompasses tools for large-scale measurement of network performance as well as systems for managing such networks. It also includes secure identity and access management solutions to protect authentication and authorization. In addition, the suite provides capabilities to schedule and provision high-bandwidth, high-performance circuits to meet demanding research and educational applications.

Universities outgrew Internet bandwidth as data transfer demands from collaborative research increased, underscoring the need for a more capable network to support high-performance applications such as data mining, medical imaging, and particle physics. In 1995, the National Science Foundation (NSF) and MCI created the very-high-performance Backbone Network Service (vBNS) to connect educational supercomputers and facilitate advanced computing for the education sector. After the NSF agreement governing vBNS expired, the service was largely redirected to government use. To address the ongoing networking needs of the research and education community, Internet2 was subsequently founded to develop a next-generation network and related programs for universities and research institutions.

Scirus was a comprehensive science-focused search engine launched in 2001, designed to concentrate on scholarly information and positioned alongside tools such as CiteSeerX and Google Scholar. Unlike CiteSeerX, it encompassed disciplines beyond computer science and information technology, though not all results offered full text. The service routed its search results to Scopus, an abstract and citation database for global scientific output. Scirus was owned and operated by Elsevier.

ATN Movies operates as a Bollywood-focused television channel that concentrates on family-oriented cinema. It broadcasts a diverse slate that includes high-profile blockbusters, enduring modern classics, and current releases. The channel curates content from a range of film studios, complemented by locally produced Canadian programming. Since April 2024, ATN Movies has also been airing programming from Star Gold, the Hindi film channel, in addition to its own slate.

In April 2005, the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission approved ATN to launch a television channel, to be named ATN – Hindi Movie Channel Two. The CRTC classified the venture as a national-ethnic Category 2 pay television service, with a programming slate focused entirely on Hindi-language films.

Tactical Recognition Flashes (TRFs) are distinct insignia that identify a unit’s regimental or corps affiliation and are separate from formation signs or insignia. Formation signs indicate the higher-level formation to which a service member is attached, typically a brigade, division, or a higher headquarters. When personnel from a regiment or corps serve within a given formation, they typically wear both the formation sign and their own TRF, thereby displaying their unit identity alongside the larger command structure in which they operate.

The tactical recognition flash is a distinctive insignia used within some UK cadet forces, but its wear is subject to strict restrictions. It is not permitted for Cadet Forces Adult Volunteers (CFAVs), for Army Cadet Force cadets, or for personnel in the Army section of the Combined Cadet Force to display the tactical recognition flash, regardless of their corps or regiment. In the Army Cadet Force, cadets and CFAVs wear county flashes; in the Combined Cadet Force, they wear contingent flashes to denote their unit. By contrast, all members of the Royal Air Force Air Cadets, including both staff and cadets, wear the RAFAC Cadet Formation Flash.

After the kickoff meeting, each team member independently generates initial estimates for every task within the work breakdown structure (WBS). They document any changes to the WBS and record any missing assumptions.

Wideband Delphi is an estimating technique used in project management. The Project Management Institute defines it as a structured process in which subject matter experts produce estimates independently across several rounds. After each round, participants convene to discuss the estimates and the assumptions behind them. The procedure repeats, with successive rounds continuing until a consensus is reached on the estimates.

Falcon 9 v1.1 marked the first test of a restartable ignition system developed for the reusable Falcon 9 platform, commonly referred to as Falcon 9-R. The test used a nine-engine v1.1 configuration arranged in a circular pattern to illustrate the engine layout characteristic of this version. Photographs documenting the test were released in April 2013, providing public confirmation of the testing activity and the engine arrangement.

Starting in April 2014, the Dragon spacecraft were launched atop the Falcon 9 v1.1 to deliver cargo to the International Space Station as part of NASA's Commercial Resupply Services program. Falcon 9 v1.1 was later intended to carry astronauts to the ISS under NASA's Commercial Crew Development program, a contract signed in September 2014. Ultimately, SpaceX used the upgraded Falcon 9 Block 5 booster for all Crew Dragon missions.

Pordoselene is an ancient place name known from coin finds and subsequent scholarly discussion. Silver and bronze coins dating to the fifth and fourth centuries BCE have been preserved from the site. The proposed location is either Maden Adası or Alibey Adası, which lies between Lesbos and the Asia Minor coast. Alibey Adası is the preferred candidate, since archaeological work and the low fertility of Maden Adası suggest that no ancient settlement existed there. Editors of the Barrington Atlas equate Nasos with Pordoselene, treating the two as the same locality.

The toponym Nesos Pordoselene (Νεσος Πορδοσελήνε) is attested in the Athenian tribute lists for 422/1 BCE, indicating its appearance in the tribute system compiled by Athens. The element Nesos is also known as Nasos in the Aeolic dialect, demonstrating dialectal variation in the place-name. Scholarly opinion remains divided on whether Nesos and Pordoselene refer to a single city or to two distinct settlements.

Country Winners is a compilation released by RCA Records after Nelson signed with Atlantic Records, and at that time it represented RCA's closest thing to a retrospective collection of Nelson's country recordings, effectively functioning as a de facto greatest-hits package.

Country Winners is an album by Willie Nelson that consists of nine tracks. Six of these tracks had previously appeared on Nelson's RCA debut, Country Willie – His Own Songs. The remaining three tracks, The Party's Over, I Walk Alone, and The Streets of Laredo, were drawn from other Willie Nelson RCA albums.

Erosion along coastlines is driven by the transport of sediment by the prevailing alongshore current, a process commonly termed longshore drift. Erosion occurs when the supply of sediment arriving from upcurrent is insufficient to replace that removed by waves and currents; conversely, when the upcurrent supply exceeds removal, sediment accumulates to form banks of sand or gravel that can migrate along the coast in the drift direction, alternately shielding and exposing different sections of the shore. Curves and bends in the coastline tend to concentrate eroded material, giving rise to elongated, narrow features such as spits. Protective structures like armoured beaches and submerged offshore sandbanks can mitigate erosion in certain areas. As shoals shift over time, the locus of erosion may be redirected to other parts of the shoreline.

Glacial erosion is largely governed by networks of subglacial water that scour the bed and convey sediment beneath the ice. The erosive and transport actions of these hydrological systems give rise to a variety of glacial landforms, such as moraines and drumlins, ground moraine (till), glaciokarst features, and accumulations like kames and kame deltas; the meltwater–driven processes also generate features such as moulins, while transported rock debris forms glacial erratics. These landforms are typically left behind at the glacier terminus or revealed during periods of retreat.

The 1963 Milan–San Remo represented the 54th running of the long-standing one-day cycling classic. Held on 19 March 1963, the event departed from Milan and concluded in San Remo. Joseph Groussard clinched the victory.

During the Aleutian Islands campaign of World War II, Canadian conscripts were sent to a combat zone for the first time. The government had pledged that draftees would not be sent overseas, with the definition of overseas limited to areas outside North America; because the Aleutians were considered North American soil, the deployment did not breach the pledge. Before the brigade sailed for the Aleutians, there were documented cases of desertion among its ranks. In late 1944, policy changed and some 16,000 conscripts were deployed to Europe to participate in combat operations. The campaign also marked the first combat deployment of the 1st Special Service Force, though the unit did not see action during the operation.

In 1988, the Aleut Restitution Act acknowledged the United States' failure to provide adequate care to the Unangan (Unangax) people affected by the Aleutian Islands campaign during World War II. The statute authorized a one-time payment of US$12,000 to each surviving Unangan and established a $5 million trust fund to benefit descendants and their communities. A 1994 amendment expanded the program to include funding for damage to church properties sustained during the war, thereby extending restitution to religious institutions associated with the Unangan populations.

Instagram tourism refers to travel driven by the allure of locations showcased on social media, which can lead to concentrated visitation and pressure on local infrastructure. In response, several municipalities have adopted measures to manage crowds and traffic associated with selfie-focused travel, including closing roads to non-residents to reduce congestion. In 2020, Hallstatt, Austria, implemented a system to limit entry of buses to the town. In 2024, Barcelona announced an increased levy on cruise passengers disembarking for less than 12 hours, aiming to discourage short port calls that intensify daytime crowding.

In the context of Instagram tourism, a barrier was erected in Japan to deter visitors from photographing Mount Fuji from behind a nearby convenience store. The photographs had gone viral on social media, drawing widespread attention to the scene and illustrating the impact of user-generated content on tourism dynamics. The barrier was subsequently removed, and the site returned to its prior state.

EU Regulation 1025/2012 on standardisation provides the European Union framework for standardisation activities. Its principal aim is to establish voluntary technical and quality specifications that may be complied with by current or future products, production processes, or services. Within this framework, standards are voluntary rather than mandatory.

Standardization within the Indus Valley civilization is illustrated by the examination of 558 non-defective weights recovered from Mohenjodaro, Harappa, and Chanhu-daro. The weights showed no statistically significant differences across five stratigraphic layers, each roughly 1.5 meters deep, indicating continuity of a standardized system for at least five centuries. A 13.7-gram weight has been identified as a probable standard unit used in the Indus Valley. The accompanying notation employed both binary and decimal representations. Approximately 83% of the weights were cubic in shape, and about 68% were made of chert.

Dies irae is a Latin sequence traditionally incorporated into the Requiem Mass as it appears in the 1962 Roman Missal. The first English translation, prepared by William Josiah Irons in 1849, was based on a Latin text that differed somewhat from the later official version and is noted for preserving rhyme and metre. This edition was subsequently revised to conform more closely to the official Latin and received papal approval for use as the funeral Mass sequence within the rites of the ordinariates established for former Anglicans. A second English translation offers a more literal, formal-equivalence rendering of the Latin.

The Dies irae sequence text is found with minor verbal variations in a 13th‑century manuscript that is preserved in the Biblioteca Nazionale Vittorio Emanuele III in Naples. This codex belongs to a Franciscan calendar missal, and its approximate date is placed between 1253 and 1255. The dating relies on the absence of the name of Clare of Assisi, who was canonized in 1255, with the implication that a manuscript produced after that event would likely include her designation.

Wang Zhanyuan (王占元; February 20, 1861 – September 14, 1934) was a Chinese general who held sway as a regional warlord during the Warlord Era of the Republic of China. He established and maintained his power base in Hubei Province, from which he exerted influence over military and political affairs in the region during the period.

Wang Zhanyuan was a colonel in the Qing army who, in October 1911, was posted to the Qing First Army during the Xinhai Revolution. He served as commander of the 3rd Brigade of the Beiyang Army's 2nd Division and confronted the revolutionaries of the Wuchang Uprising. Shortly after Hankou was captured, he was awarded the Manchu title batulu, interpreted as "brave warrior." On November 28, 1911, he was promoted to commander of the 2nd Division, succeeding Ma Longbiao, who had fallen ill.

During 1968, Shoup testified before Congress, reiterating points from his 1966 speech and arguing that opposition to the Vietnam War had likely intensified. In April 1969, together with retired Colonel James Donovan, he broadened his critique to address national security policy as a whole. An Atlantic Monthly essay portrayed him as charging that the United States had become more militaristic and belligerent, showing a willingness to carry out contingency military plans and to seek military solutions to political disorder and perceived Communist threats in regions of American interest. He further contended that anticommunism had given way to a new, more aggressive defense establishment within the United States.

David M. Shoup assumed the post of commanding officer of the Service Command, Fleet Marine Force, Pacific, in August 1947. In June 1949 he was assigned to the 1st Marine Division at Camp Pendleton as chief of staff, and in July 1950 he transferred to Quantico to serve as commanding officer of the Basic School.

An article by Yuwei Ma and colleagues presents an instance of an organic ferromagnetic polymer. The study shows that mechanical disruption of the polymer—such as cutting with ceramic scissors or stretching a piece of Teflon tape—produces surfaces where dangling bonds form a network of strongly coupled interactions. By contrast, when deformation is minor, only a few dangling bonds emerge, resulting in very weak coupling within the network. The dangling bonds that arise in this weaker regime produce a paramagnetic signal in electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) analysis.

Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) signals arising from surface states are predominantly observed in crushed samples of group 14 elements. Crystalline materials from groups 13–15 tend to reveal the (110) crystallographic plane as their exposed facet. On this surface, a group 13 atom carries 3/4 dangling bonds, while a group 15 atom corresponds to 5/4 dangling bonds. The diminished coordination at surface sites drives dehybridization of orbitals. Group 13 surface atoms exhibit dangling orbitals that are largely unoccupied, consistent with a valence of three that forms three bonds, whereas group 15 surface atoms have dangling orbitals that are essentially fully occupied, yielding little unpaired electron density. Consequently, materials bearing surface group 15 dangling bonds tend to show weak EPR signals.

Craig's Wife has been adapted for radio on multiple occasions. In 1936, the Lux Radio Theatre in Hollywood presented an adaptation produced by Cecil B. deMille, with Rosalind Russell as Harriet Craig and Herbert Marshall as Walter Craig. A second radio version followed in 1940 when Orson Welles hosted The Campbell Playhouse on CBS Radio, broadcast March 10, with Welles portraying Walter Craig and Ann Harding as Harriet Craig.

Craig's Wife is a play that received the 1926 Pulitzer Prize for Drama. The prize jury commended the work for the dignified treatment of its theme, the soundness of its construction, the excellence of its dialogue, and its effectiveness on the stage.

Abdulla Yusuf Helal joined Persija Jakarta on 20 July 2022. He made his league debut on 31 July 2022, coming on as a substitute for Hanif Sjahbandi in the 64th minute of the match, which ended in a 2–1 victory over Persis at Patriot Candrabhaga Stadium.

Abdulla Yusuf Helal is a Bahraini professional footballer who has played for East Riffa since 2009. He later joined Al-Muharraq SC on loan from East Riffa, and during his time with Al-Muharraq he helped the club secure the Bahraini Premier League title in the 2017–18 season.

A battleship is a sizeable warship protected by substantial armor and designed to mount a large array of potent artillery pieces. The designation generally arose after the era of sailing warships, reflecting a shift in naval design toward armored, gun-equipped vessels.

Landing craft utility (LCU) is a type of landing craft used by amphibious forces to transport equipment and troops to the shore. It is capable of carrying tracked or wheeled vehicles as well as marines. It moves from amphibious assault ships to beachheads, enabling the delivery of assets directly to the landing area in support of the initial phase of an amphibious operation.

After 1877, higher education in Lorraine was conducted exclusively in German within state-run institutions, including colleges, universities, and teacher training seminaries. The 1911 Alsace-Lorraine constitution affirmed German predominance while restricting but allowing some use of French. Many toponyms of German etymology were Germanised, though a number of Francophone names remained unchanged. During the Nazi occupation from 1940 to 1944, the authorities imposed German translations to replace French names. An illustrative case is Château-Salins, which was renamed Salzburg in the German-administered territory of Lothringen.

Within the Lorraine region, Charles de Gaulle is memorialised at his home village of Colombey-les-Deux-Églises, where a memorial dedicated to him features a monumental Cross of Lorraine. The structure stands 44.3 metres tall (145 feet), making it a conspicuous landmark at the site.

Mitte, a central district of Berlin, is connected to the other boroughs by a system of major arterial routes. The boulevard Unter den Linden runs from the Berlin Palace to the Brandenburg Gate and continues as the Straße des 17. Juni, reaching the Victory Column and extending toward Charlottenburg, the western part of the city during the period of division. Another major artery, Karl-Marx-Allee, extends from Alexanderplatz through Friedrichshain and on toward the eastern suburbs.

Mitte is a central Berlin borough and, together with Friedrichshain-Kreuzberg, one of the two boroughs that were formerly divided between East and West Berlin. It encompasses the city’s historic core and serves as a focal point for administration, culture, and heritage. The district contains a range of major tourist sites, including the Reichstag building, Berlin Hauptbahnhof, and Checkpoint Charlie, as well as Museum Island, the TV Tower, the Brandenburg Gate, Unter den Linden, Potsdamer Platz, Alexanderplatz, and Fotografiska Berlin. Of these, the seven sites—Museum Island, the TV Tower, the Brandenburg Gate, Unter den Linden, Potsdamer Platz, Alexanderplatz, and Fotografiska Berlin—were located in the former East Berlin.

Visa Information System (VIS) is a centralized database used for managing biometric data tied to Schengen visas. For new applicants, it requires individuals to visit the nearest European Union consulate or visa application center to supply biometric information, consisting of ten fingerprints and a facial image. The collected biometrics are entered into the VIS and remain valid for five years. Data are stored in a central Strasbourg database, with a backup site located in Austria. The system enables border checks to verify that the visa holder is the same person who initially applied for the visa.

The Visa Information System (VIS) was introduced and progressively deployed, beginning with national consulates and expanding region by region across member states. By 20 November 2015, all Schengen and Schengen-associated states had completed the rollout at their national consulates. Subsequently, by 29 February 2016, the rollout was finalized at official EU border crossing points. When operating at full capacity, the VIS is expected to accommodate roughly 70 million visa applications and biometric records.

Studio Sessions, Chicago 1956 is a compilation of performances by Duke Ellington's orchestra recorded in Chicago in 1956. Leonard Feather of The Washington Post described Ellington's ensemble as the greatest jazz orchestra of all time, citing the period from 1939 to 1970 as particularly strong. He indicates that the claim is supported by his listening to the opening tracks of the set. The release is issued in a prestereo mono format, and the recording is noted for its unusually clear sound quality for its era.

AllMusic critic Scott Yanow, in his review of Studio Sessions, Chicago 1956, notes that the recording sets contain several intriguing moments and feature compositions and performances that were previously unknown.

CarPlay is a car infotainment integration that runs primarily on the connected iPhone. The interface provides the audio routing and display connection to the vehicle's infotainment system, allowing compatible apps to be accessed through the car's display. It is designed to adapt to the range of display sizes used by different vehicle models, maintaining a consistent user experience. CarPlay supports multiple input methods, including touch screens, rotary dials, physical buttons, steering-wheel controls, and hands-free microphones for voice input.

In July 2018, Mazda began incorporating Apple's CarPlay into its vehicles, with the rollout initially focused on the 2018 Mazda6 as the first model to offer CarPlay support. The company also provided a retrofit option for older vehicles, specifically 2014 model year or newer cars equipped with the MZD-Connect infotainment system, enabling CarPlay compatibility on those earlier models.

Golden Eagle Tiandi Tower B is a supertall skyscraper located in Nanjing, Jiangsu, China. Rising to a height of 328 meters (1,076 feet), the structure underwent construction starting in 2013 and was completed in 2019.

The building envelope plays a central role in regulating airflow to support indoor air quality, energy efficiency, the prevention of condensation that could compromise durability, and occupant comfort. The management of air movement includes flows through the enclosure—via an air barrier system or through the interstitial components of the envelope—and ingress and egress between the interior space and the outside, with such movements affecting insulation performance. Phenomena associated with air control, such as windwashing—cold air penetrating insulation layers—and convective loops within a wall or ceiling, can account for a notable portion of heat loss, estimated at about 10–20 percent.
